A—" I saw your mother-in-law at the theatre last night. She seemed to enjoy herself very much. She laughed herself half to death." B— " Yes, that 's just like her. She alway does things by halves. She is a very unsatisfactory sort of a woman." EXCITED BOY—" Come on, quick! The ould man is batin' the mild woman again." Policeman —" Why don't she come herself if she wants to make a complaint, or have him arrested 7" Excited boy —" She's too busy. She's got him down, and is bumpin' his head ca the flure." A BRAKESMAN on a Rocky Mountain road saved his train from rushing down upon a broken bridge by his prompt use of the famous air-brake. Two old mountaineers passing by with their guns, paused to find out why the train had stopped so suddenly. "That 'ere brakesmin deserves a heap of praise for his quick shot," said one of the hunters, on learn- ing how it happened. "'Taint that 'ere brakesman deserves the praise, seems to, Me," said the other; "I'should say it was that air-brake." Iltumonotra immirrfoxs. "Pray, my lord," queried a gentleman of a judge, "what is the difference between common law and equity?" "Very little in the end," responded his lordship. "At common law you are more quickly disposed of. The former is a bullet which is instantaneously and charmingly effective; the latter, an angler's hook, which plays with the victim before it kills him. Common law is prussic acid; equity is laudanum." REAL COLD WEATHER—A resident in Manitoba says that during the recent cold spell the people in that Artie region bad to blow their fires from morn- ing to night with a bellows, in order to keep the flames from freezing. AN enterprising man has his house and shop connected by telephone. The other day during a storm the lightning entered the shop by the wire while the proprietor was talking to his wife about when he would be home to dinner. As he re- covered his consciousness the first words he spoke were: "All right, Maria; don't hit me again; I'll do just as you say." BALZA% being asked to explain an abstruse pas- sage in one of his books, frankly owned it had no meaning at all. "You see," said he, "for the average reader all that is clear seems easy, and if I did not sometimes give him a complicated and meaningless sentence, he would think he knew as much as myself. But when he comes upon some- thing he cannot comprehend, he re-reads it, puzzles over it, takes his head , between his bands, and glares at it, and, finding it impossible to make hald or tail of it, says, Great man, Baizac ;he knows more than Idol' " "Souse me," he said, as he leaned across the aisle of the car, "but I presume you are reading the morning paper ?" "Yes, sir," replied the other. "Published here in the city ?" "Yes, sir 7" "Will you have the kindness to tell me if you have as yet come across an article headed :—' A Distinguished Visitor to Detroit. The Hon. Benjamin Perkins in Town. Let Us Do This Famous Man All Honour." "No, sir, I haven't." "Some oversight, probably. Probably be in tomorrow. That't all. Much obliged." And he settled back, buttoned up his threadbare overcoat, and realised that 13 passengers were sizing him up, and wishing that fame would also come to them. LATZST INTELLIGENOR"—He was a reporter of a local newspaper. He came into the office of the district postmaster, as was his wont, and asked If there was any news. "No, nothing much," care- lessly replied one a the officials. "Have you heard of the new order?" "What new order?" eagerly asked the reporter, making a move for. his pencil. "Why, that the postmaster-general is not going to issue the postaheards any longer." " Where do you " " Well, we haven't any get your information official information yet; but we know it is so.' That will be a great hardship to the poor," ven- tured the reporter. "I don't see how it will," replied the officiL..l. " suppose i: is done on account of the los:, on the letter postage? " "No. that the reason the postmaster-general decided not to make them any longer," spoke up anothei official. "Well, what is the reason, then 1," asked the sow desperate reporter. " Why,.simply because they are long enough cowl The postina,ter-gel: nu; and the people are very well satisfied with ths present length." The door slammed hard as the reporter went out.

" Hazell's Annual" has become a necessity for readers "I got worse, instead of better, and went to the Lon- who wish to keep pace with the topics of the day. It don Hospital, Whitechapel-road, where I was an out- gains in value every year, so that the issue for 1891

surpasses its predecessors, with its 3,500 concise and explanatory articles. It is a cyclopcedia, (kept up to date) on current political, social, and biographical mat- ters of interest. It is suggestive of the number of bio- graphical sketches of notable men and _women to be . _ . _

informed that the additions this year reach 200. As to the thoroughness with which important topics are dealt with, it may be mentioned that the article on the 'Labour Movement occupies lessthan 16 closely printed pages. The alphabetical arrangement of the articles is very handy for reference ; and for the benefit of those who are possessed ef previous editions there is a special reference index. The editor, Mr. E. D. Price, F.G.S., is to be congratulated on the success of the work,though it is a matter of course to say that he has had the assist- ance of numerous specialists. The annual is well printed and well bound, and published at 3s. 6d. "The Life of W. M. Thackeray" is issued by Mr. Walter Scott in the "Great Writers'" series. As this is the first life of the great novelist that has been pub- lished, and as, too, it is the joint production of Mr. Her- mann Merivale and Mr. F. T. Marzials, it is a matter of -course to say that it will command no small atten- tion, and be widely read. Both biographers have, as might be expected, a genuine liking for Thackeray, and Mr. Merivale, in particular, writes from a considerable amount of personal knowledge. Like all great men, , Thackeray has been at times misunderstood and misre- presented, but when the facts of his career in a " Life " of this kind are made known, it is seen that he is deserv- ing of the highest praise that has been given him. There is a considerable amount of quotation from Thackeray's letters, and it is hardly necessary to say that they are generally very lively reading. Under the circumstances it may be expected that this shilling " Life " will have a very large sale. _ Another valuable shilling book, published by Mr. Walter Scott, is a re-production of Darwin's celebrated "Coral Reefs." The full title is" On the Structure and Distribution of Coral Reefs, by Charles Darwin, edited, written, and introduced by Joseph W. Williams." It is doe to Mr. Williams to state that the introduction which he has furnished is full and painstaking, and thus brings the reader up to date in the controversy, which has been so prolonged, over the theories pro- pounded by Darwin in his celebrated book. The volume is amply illustrated, and, as there is a full index, it is a remarkably handy and cheap production. As regards Darwin's theory of the share which subsidence has had in the formation of coral reefs, those who read the book will be disposed to agree with Mr. Williams in saving— "No ,matter how the future may decide, had Darwin written no other work, and simply rested on his laurels, this book alone, by its very inductive reasoning and patient marshalling ef facts, would have remained as an everlastinc, monument of scientific acumen, ana would have placed him in the front rank of investigators." "The Westminster Review," for February, leads off with an itriportant article on" Child Marriage in India," by Mr. C. N. Barham. The revelations which are made justify the course which the Government are taking in raising the age of consent from ten to twelve, with a view, it is presumed, of getting the age in the end higher still. "The Story of the Labour Battle in Australia," is well told by Jeannie Lockett. Mr. William Schooling deals with "Fairy Tales and Science," and Mr. D. Chamier with "The Ethics of Copy-Right." There is an article on " Domeni another on" Lord Houghton, besides the usual review of contemporary literature and current affairs.

- "The Century for February is an exceptionally strong number. The frontispiece is a reproduction of the por- trait of Talleyrand from a painting by Greuze. The second instalment is given of "The Memoirs of Talley- rand," and refers to his relations with Napoleon Bona- parte. It iVeedless to say that they are exceedingly interesting. The " Memoirs " are being now first pub- lished,and are throwing a good deal of side light upon an important period of French history. The publishers of the" Century "are to be congratulated upon their enter- prise in securing such a valuable work. Amongst the more striking illustrated papers are "The Georgia Cracker in the Cotton Mills,"" The Discovery( of Gold in California," "Theodore Rousseau and the French Land- scape School," "Northern Thibet and the Yellow River." All the illustrations are finely executed, but special praise must be given to the exquisite reproductions of the paintings by Rousseau. "The Newbery House Magazine" opens with an article by the Rev. F. F. Irving on "The Attitude of Catholics towards Biblical Criticism." There is a second paper on" Christianity in relation to Socialism," and amongst the illustrated papers we have "The Church House ;" "The Historical Churches of England," and the story" Changed lots, or nobody cares." Other features of interest are " Some letters of the late M. Chatrian ; " " Sea-water " " A German Industrial Colony ;" Notes by the way," &e.

By F. R. R. We are on the eve of , a General Election in this tight little Island. I. dare say to most of your readers it would be easier to connect the Isle of Man in thought with mackerels and herrings than with polities and elections, .and yet I can assure them at the present time the latter dr.minate men's minds here. "The summer now is over," the greater number of the steamers so familiar to Lan- cashire folk are lying idle in Douglas harbour— desolate and still—the " prom " is deserted; the pleasure resorts are closed.; the herring season has not yet returned; and so the weary and heavy-laden Manxman of summer has become the leisured, easy- going ditto of whiter: and the forthcoming disso- lution of thelieys is the general theme of talk, the coming event whose shadow lies thick upon all. The present House has not lived the allotted. span of seven years. The coming break-up is due to the passing of a Redistribution Bill, a measure which has been striven for by some of our more liberal and go-ahead spirits for several years. Your readers may not know precisely how the representative branch of our insular legislature is chosen ; so in a few words Iwill try to enlighten them. We have two Houses here as in England, an Upper and a Lower. The Upper has nine members, all, be it noted—and the fact is gall and wormwood to our local Radicals—paid officials, men who ex-officio sit in the Council, as it is called, and exercise precisely the same powers of veto and of initiation of mea- sures as your House of Lords. They are the Bishop, the Vicar-General, the Archdeacon (three out of nine—not a-bad proportion of ecclesiastical authori- ties), the Attorney-General, Master of the Rolls, the two Judges or Deemsters (" Doom-steerers ") ,the Receiver-General, and last but not least, the Lieutenant - Governor. All these retain their seats as long as they hold office, and thus the Manx are in the happy position of being gov- erned by their own paid servants! The Lower House, or House of Keys (derivation uncertain) is composed of twenty-four elected representatives of the whole island, which has immemorially been divided into six sheadings (pronounced "sheeding" —an ancient division for the purposes of a levy of ships for the defence of the island), each sheading returning three members. The remaining six are returned by Douglas (three), Castletown (one), Peel (one), Ramsay (one). Now the Redistribution Act which is the immediate cause of the impending General Election, takes away a member from each of the sheadings—Garff and Michael, and gives them to Douglas, which therefore will now return five members. The Act is generally popular, for it was obviously unfair that Douglas, the population of which is two-fifths of that of the whole island, should have only an eighth of the voting power of the Keys. Even the representatives of the dismem- bered Garff and Michael gave a general support to the Bill. The Upper -louse assented, and the dis- solution must follow speedily. We have no "parties" here as you understand the word. Men are Liberals or Tories only in re- spect of their attitude towards imperial politics. I find myself utterly unable to arrange our several local newspapers by any mode of political classifi- cation. There is, however, one distinct line of cleav- age here, not political but religious; not between Liberal and Tory bub between Nonconformist and Anglican. The line runs very clearly through all ranks and orders, and however closely men may be thrown together in business or society, separation is easily and clearly effected at the trumpet call of the churches. It must be allowed, however, that in past elections religious differences have not al- ways, or even frequently, ranked the electors on opposite sides. Rather, the test question has been some petty local matter, some personal affair bulk- ing largely before the eyes of the electors in these small constituencies. Let the worthy member for Peel (let us say) deal meanly with the hands of his herring boats, and it will go hard with the sturdy fisherman of that ancient and picturesque city if the said member does not find himself at the bottom of the poll at the next election ! Bat now we are to have it hand-to-hand fight on the question of churches. The battle cry is to be "Church or Dissent—which ?

The easy-going, tolerant Manx Dissenter has a grievance at last—and I venture to think a very real one. I should tell you that Dissenters are in the proportion of three to two compared with churchmen here, and in their ranks are to be found the bulk of the mercantile classes. The merchants "and—tradesniQll- of the, towns are almost without exception Dissenters. So are the fishermen Methodist for the most part. Now we are blessed with an Academy of the Great Unpaid who admin- ister justice (or injustice) to our portion of the Great Unwashed—forty Immortals to whose earthly denominations are added the mystic letters "J. P.', Will it be credited, that the whole of this distin guished body are churchmen? "Not one of them,' says the Dissenter with set teeth and clenched fist,' "is of us." Time after time, as a vacancy occurs (the number forty is religiously adhered to) the Governor is reminded of the heartburning his par- tiality causes, but 'tis of no avail—the brand of sin on the Dissenter, and he is passed over. In vain it is is pointed out that a majority of the twenty-four Keys .are Dissenters: with us "ALP." plays second fiddle to " J.P." Of course the Governor has his rea- sons; be it remembered he is a Walpole and a Liberal Unionist) "cannot appoint anyone engaged in trade," and so industrious, wealthy merchants are passed over and retired lawyers, volunteer officers et- onane hoe genus are the chosen of authority, and bear their honours not blushingly but with brazen superciliousness which would turn the milk of human kindness in the breast of a Luke or Barnabas into gall. And so the battle cr), is sound- ing—" Give them no quarter; out with the Church- men and favourites.' Douglas has cleared decks for action; our three majors (volunteer and other- wise) are to be replaced by five sterling -Noncon- formists, and throughout the island there are signs of a hot contest and a great upsetting of the estab- lished order of things. But perhaps the prettiest little fight (to use a prize ring expression) is going on in gallant little Peel, about which I will tell your readers in my next.

patient for several months, but I kept getting worse. They said I was suffering vgith shock, liver congestion, and debility. I was then sent to the Brighton, Con- valescent Home, where they treated the fourteen days

and did litttle or no good. In a short time I began to despair, and my husband and others who came to see me thought I was doomed. Thus I went ,on from month to Month, expecting each week would be my last. Again and again I whispered solemnly to myself, 'Before this time next week I shall be dead "I took no further interest in any thing pertaining to this world, but thank God! I have a good husband and a good home. My husband carried me from my bed every day, and placed me in the chair sofa, and tried to cheer me up, and persuade me I would get better. But since I have really got well he tells me he never in his heart believed his own words. "My sister too, came frequently to see me, and did all she could to ease my sufferings; but, being unable to resist what her own eyes showed her, she often said You will never yet better, Caroline.' "But who likes to read accounts of the troubles and sorrows of others? So much do each and all of us have of our own to bear. I crave your attention only for a few words more. "I went on in this way—like one who stands on the crumbling edge of an open graveuntil February, 1890, when a little book was left at iriy shop which told of the remarkable cures wrought by Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup. The narrative of the Peliceman of Holyhead greatly impressed me. I said to my husband, The com- plaint that policeman suffered from is my complaint. The remedy that cured him may cure me.' " [sent at once over to Messrs. Lacy and Co., the Chemists, Whitechapel Road, for a bottle. It did me good. I could eat ; but, better still, the food digested. Before this, when I swallowed a mouthful of solid food it seemed to turn to wind or sour acid and gas, and gave me such pain I fancied I had heart disease. "I persevered with the medicine, and after taking six bottles I never felt so well in my life. I can now eat as heartily as any one, and am never distressed after taking food. "In fact I can now eat a jolly gOod dinner, and I leave you to imagine what a treat that is after being bad so long. •
"My husband and relatives, as well as my neigboUrs, are all of my opinion—that Mother Seigel's Syrup saved my life.
"(Signed) Mrs. CAnoraNE SAGE, wife of Mr. Henry Sage, Basket Maker and Stationer„ 200, Whitechapel Road, London, E."

One point only in Mrs. Sage's statement needs a word of explanation. The fall downstairs, in which her illness apparently began, was in fact the re§ult of the -malady, which had for some time been undermining her nervous system—namely,. indigestion and dyspepsia, and the giddiness which occasioned the fall was merely one of its symptoms.
FEARFUL FALL INTO A QUARRY AT
RUNCORN.
ONE MAN KILLED, AND. ANOTHER MAR-
VE4LOUSLY ESCAPES.

A terrible accident occurred at Weston last night week, by which one mail met his death, and another -was seriously injured. Thos: (rice, of Weston, and Wm. Lever, better known as Clare, of Mill Brow, Runcorn, .are labourers at the Weston Chemical Works, and after receiving their pay at half-past five, they remained in the village drinking. At half-past seven they left the Round House with the intention of going to the Prospect Inn, and took a short cut across the fields. The night was very dark, and missing their way they fell into what is known as the Delph Hole of the Weston Quarries, and which is 120 feet deep. A woman who was' passing along the lane heard the noise of falling rock, and raised an alarm, and P.C. Benfield and several quarrymen descended into the "Hole," and found the two men lying at the bottom. Both' were unconscious, and were at once conveyed to the surface and placed in the Prospect Inn. A cart hav- ing been obtained,the men were taken to Dr. McDougall's surgery, at Runcorn. Lever was at once tarried on to his home, where the doctor dressed his Wounds. He had a severely fractured skull, a battered face, and other in- juries, and there was no hope of his recovery from the first. He died on Saturday morning. Grice,!after hav- ing his wounds dressed, was taken to Weston. He had . sustained most severe injuries to his back and internal organs, and had it not been that he alighted upon his companion at the bottom of the quarry, he would pro- bably not now be alive. The inquest was held on Mon- day by Mr. J. E. Worsloy.—Ann Lever said deceased was herson, and 21 years of age. She proved the.death. —Robert Bate, chemical labourer, said he lodged at the Union Vaults, Runcorn. He was in the Round House, when the deceased asked him to walk across the fields to the Prospect Inn. He replied that he was not going as he did not snow the way. The deceased and another man got over a wall into the field, and witness came on towards Huncorn. It was between seven and eight o'clock. P.C. Benfield deposed to finding the men. In reply to the Coroner he said the top of the quarry was fenced and the deceased I would have to climb a wall two or three feet away from the edge of the quarry.—The Coroner said the accident was very unfortunate but very simple. The deceased left the Round House because the landlord would not supply him with any more, drink. He said he would go to a place where he could get some more and he and his companion set off to walk across the field. They climbed two walls and then fell into the quarry. The quarry was properly fenced, and the deceased was trespassing where he had no right to be. At the same time quarries are dangerous places and ought to be fenced even against trespassers., A verdict of Accidental Death was returned.

The frontispiece for" Scribner's Magazine" is a strik- ing 'portrait of David Livingstone, from a photograph from life by J. G. Mayall, about 1860. 1` Mount Wash- ington in Winter" is from the pen of Mr. G. L. Wilson and is finely illustrated. There is a third taper on "Japonica" by Sir Edwin Arnold, with illustrations by Robert Blum. Another article noteworthy ,alike from text and illustration, is "About Africa," and accompany- ing it are portraits of Bishop Ha.nnington, Speke, Grant, Captain Burton, Paul Chaillu, Captain Clapperton , Major Denham, and Sir Samuel Baker. From a "Box of autographs "by H. Stoddart we have facsimiles of the writing of Addison, Burns, W. C. Bryant, Elizabeth liarrett Browning, Thomas Campbell, Dickens, Haw- thorne, Poe Longfellow, Scott, and Thackeray— a truly wonderful collection. "The English Illustrated Magazine" has for its first article" To the East, Westwards" by Sir G. „Baden- Powell. It is amply illustrated, and the same may be said of the paper on "Norwich," by Mr. R. 0. Allsopp, the illustrations of which are dainty and clever,being by Mr. C. 0. Murray. Mr. Charles Bruce deals with "British Guiana" (illustrated) ; and there is a paper on "Across the North Atlantic in a Torpedo Boat, by an Officer on Board."

"Peter the Whaler" by the late W. Fl. G. Kingston, is a successful reproduction of an admirable story of ad- venture from the pen of a very ready writer. It com- prises over 150 well-printed pages, and if it is read as it deserves to be it will be largely in demand.
WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at the Workhouse, on Wednesday morning. Alder- man Harrison presided, and there were also present —Messrs. Ratcliffe, Davies, Smith, Dignum, Turton, Clarke, Heaton, W. Houghton, T._ Jones, Dobson, J. Houghton, Aukland, Jolley, Hood-Wright, Mather, Balharry, Gill; J. C. Sutton (clerk), S. Sutton (as- sistant clerk), and C. H. Ward (Workhouse master).

- The -quarterly statement of the Palestine Exploration Fund has always something interesting about the Holy Land. With the excellent maps, and illustrations from photographs, the record is invaluable. "Black and White," the new "weekly illustrated re- cord and review" made its first appearance on Saturday, and met, as it deserved to do, with a capital reception. The artistic quality of the work is excellent; and,if so much that is good can be given every week for sixpence, success is certain.
A YOUTH SHOOTS THIS SWEETHEART.

At Birmingham, on Monday evening, Harrv, Oldcroft, a lad of eighteen, was committed for trial by the coroner charged with the murder of a girl named Mansell, only- fourteen years old, who some time ago rejected him as a sweetheart. On the 31st January Oldcroft passed the girl talking to her sweetheart in a passage in Russell-st., and wished them good night. Soon afterwards a pistol shot was heard, the girl was stuck in the heact by a bul- let, and Oldcroft was found near with a revolver in his hand. At first it was thought that the shooting was an accident, as Oldcroft had previously been seen shooting recklessly with the Weapon; but inquiries made after the girl's death, a week later in the hospital, showed that he had entertained deep resentment against the girl for rejecting his attentions, and had on several occa- sions threatened that he would take her life. When ap- prehended Oldcroft said he fired for a lark to frighten the girl and her sweetheart. The Coroner's jury were locked up for more than an hour, and eventually re turned a verdict of " Wilful murder" by twelve to two

The fund for the erection of a memorial to tie late Dr. Hanny now amounts to .21,700. The amount required is .£3,000. The Committee of the Congre- gational Union have contributed £5OO.

Conservative members are just now regarding the immediate future with_much_.more _ease_lhan was the case a short time since, the word having priva- tely gone forth from an authoritative quarter that a dissolution is not to be expected before July of next year. , The extent of the accident to the Cape mail train at Taunton is seen in the fact that £10,795 has been paid by the Great Western Railway for compensa- tion for personal injury in the past half-year. In the corresponding period of the previous year .C 1,908 only was so spent.

• It was on Tuesday night privately arranged that the debate on Mr. John blorley's motion shall have assigned to it the two Government night next week. Arrangements are already being made for whips on both sides, in preparation for the division which will take place on Thursday next.

It was officially denied on Wednesday that the paper in which a baronet whose nathe is now much before the world promised never again to play cards is in the Prince of Wales's keeping. But is there such a paper? Who has it? Did the Prince urge the baronet to sign it? Who let the cat out of the bag? These are inquiries to which definite answers must sooner or later be made.

Mr. Labouehere intends raising the question of the card scandal in the House of Commons. lie will, of course, steer clear of anything calculated to prejudice the coming law action, but that will not prevent him inquiring why Sir Wm. Gordon- Cumming has had to send in his papers and retire from the Guards.

A lady staying recently at a country house where gambling is de rigeur, was taken suddenly ill. Not to be thwarted, the host telegraphed to a friend in town the following characteristic message. "Please send down at once another baccarat woman."

Sir Arthur Sullivan has for many years been desirous of writing a serious opera, and would have done so before this date had not Mr. Gilbert per- suaded him that it was the comic business which English people liked best, and was, therefore, the surest to pay. Sir Arthur used to say if ever he wrote a serious opera he would take Ivanhoe for his theme.

A London Correspondent writes :—I hear that the Home Secretary has received altogether about 70 applications from members of the Bar, mostly practising on the Northern-Circuit, for the office of stipendiary magistrate for Liverpool. The number of eligible candidates has been reduced to two or three. Mr. Matthews will take some days to make the appointment.

In Italy, where suicide has been increasing regularly since 1871, it is observed that the crime is more frequent among unmarried than married men, but with the women it ,is otherwise. More married women commit suicide than unmarried women. Men resort more frequently to guns and revolvers; women to drowning, generally in the summer time, when the water is not so cold„

The Chilians have some queer names for their ships. "Almirante Lynch" and " Almirante Coch- rane" must puzzle the' untutored Chilian sailor a good deal ; but what does he, or, for the matter of that, any other son of a Latin race, make of "O'Higgins"? Fancy calling an ironclad "The O'Higgins!" "The O'Gorman," "The Mulligan," and "The Macintosh" ought to be built at once to complete the series.

Mr. James Redpath, whose death took place in New York on Tuesday, was a native of Berwick-on- Tweed. Ile was best known in this country as an Irish Nationalist. He has shown his sympathy with Ireland in many ways, and recently took an active part in the organisation of the famine fund. Mr. Redpath was formerly a journalist, but he played many parts in his time. He originated the Lyceum lecturing system in America. He was one of Mr. Henry George's supporters when he first began his campaign. His last literary work was the writing of the Jefferson Davis' Memoirs.

Sir John Macdonald's addmss to the people of Canada is a catching document and pm ingenious. He has strained the issue, and makes the coming election a question of whether Canada is to remain "under the broad folds of the Union Jack," or to join the United States. This is the best card which Sir John could play. The question of annexation has not been raised by " the Liberals; they have simply opposed Sir John's ruinous protective policy and advocated closer commercial relations with the United States. Canada May enter into reciprocity with the United States without imperilling the British connection.

The German Emperor,through Goteral von Wedel, has addressed a letter of condolence to M. Herbette, the French Ambassador in Berlin, on the death of Meissonier. He desired that this expression of his sorrow at the loss to the world of so great an artist should be communicated to the Academy of Fine Arts. This news, our Paris Correspondent says, has caused quite an agreeable impression in the French capital, particularly as it comes after the recall of that zealous agent of Prince Bismarck, Major Hiine. M. Ribot, who is now in possession of the letter to M. Herbette, will make the communication to the Academy of Fine Arts.

The factories act amendment bill, introduced by Mr. Matthews, is a large and important measure. Its objects are, first, to give effect to the recommen- dations of the Berlin Conference so far as legislation in this country is necessary; and next, to carry out several of the recommendations of the Sweating Committee. .The provisions of the bill on this sub- ject are very im. portant, and will undoubtedly give rise to much discussion and probably some opposi- tion. The Government regard the measure as one of great importance. They think that it will be popular with the working classes, and every effort i will be made to carry t into law. ,

In the death of the Rev. William Freeman the National Liberal Federation loses one of its most energetic and conscientious workers. Wherever a constituency had to be contested, or a seat was to be won, a telegram from the N.L.F. would always bring Mr. Freeman at twenty-four hours' notice to the spot. His diary, if he kept one, would bear eloquent testimony to the work he had put in at Spalding. Sleaford, Eccles, Bassetlaw, and mcst of the other bye-elections that have taken place dur- ing the last few years. In what may be termed the drudgery of the campaign—the stump orating and the house to house canvassing—his services have been indefatigable and invaluable.

Here is a sketch of the new Australian champion sculler of he world, John McLean, whom we shall doubtless soon see on the Thames. He and O'Connor,. the Canadian, ought to come to London without delay, and give us a spin over the championship course:—" He is (say an Australian journal) a tall man, about six feet in height, very wiry, showing well-developed muscles, and has good limbs, although not heavily built. His chest measure- ment is forty-two inches, and he has a splendid back, which he uses to advantage. in manner he is one of the quietest, most unassuming of men, and a very manly fellow. His backers, Messrs. Spencer, hold him in the highest esteem, and have a very favourable opinion of his skill and honesty.

Herr Joachim, who appeared at the Pops on Monday night, is Hungarian by birth, and will cele- brate his sixtieth birthday this year. He was a prodigy when but a child, and he is now regarded as king of the violin, while Lady Halle reigns as queen of that instrument. His first visit to the metropolis was paid when/ he was thirteen years of age. Every recurring year has welcomed him in London, where for his magnificent playing and his charming personality he is much esteemed. For thirty-two seasons he has played with the greatest success at the Popular Concerts, and in 1889 was presented with a splendid violin in commemoration of the fact that he had played before the public for fifty years. He is modest and retiring, making friends among the chief members of the English aristocracy. Before he depart's, it is hoped he will introduce Brahma' new quintett in G.

Mi. Clarke Aspinall, city coroner, and a jury, held an inquiry on Saturday into the cause of death of the infant child of Thomas Groarke, draper's assistant, 67, Cairns-st., Liverpool. The jury found a verdict equiva- lent to" Willa' murder" agaiiist the mother, who, after cutting the child's throat on the 4th inst., was taken Into custody by a police sergeant, to whom she said she did it because "she thought the devil was going to take it."

THE TREATMENT OF TRAMPS.

The C.I.ERTE, referring to the treatment of tramps at the Workhouse, which has recently been com- mented on, said the tramp wards at the Workhouse had always been supplied with artificial heat, but they had that misfortunate which no manufacturer who used machinery could help—they had a breakdown, and they could not keep up the artificial heat in the tramp wards until they got apparatus for the purpose. The place was then, of course, a little colder than it was ordinarily. He pointed out that that Board and the House Commit- tee were generous in their treatment of tramps, for they had adopted a system in connection with the tramp wards in that Union which few other Unions had been willing to go to the expense of adopting. The rooms at the WOrithouse Were good rooms, they were boarded ,and they had good walls awl close windows and doors, When they had, in addition, artificial heat to warm the bedrooms they had a state of things which few working people could get in their own houses. He th9ught it was / a mistake to say that the reduction in the number of tramps was due to the cold state of the wards, because lie noticed that both at Rainhill and Leigh there had been a corres- pondingly less number of tra:nps, while if they had been driven away from that workhouse they would, cf neeessity,unless they went to lodging-houseshave had to go to neighbouring Unions. He made that statement be- cause at least one newsnaner had made entirely errone- ous inferences from what had taken place.—Mr. HEATON said the old heating apparatus had become too small and it took about three week to replace it.
A WEALTHY PAUPER.

The CLEuR said that other people as well as that Board sometimes came across people who were supposed to be paupers but who had money. Ile then mentioned the case of a man named John Brown who had recently ar- rived at Boston on Board a steamer from Liverpool. The man was filthy and ragged and he said he had lost his paSsage ticket. He was taken on shore as a pauper, but on being seArched £lOOO in gold coins was found upon him. He said he had been in Ireland but got sick of that cogntry. (Laughter.)—Mr. W. HOUGHTON added that he had read that morning of a case in which a man had died of starvation near Dundee although it was found that the man had £lOO upon him. The relief cases were then taken.

At Bolton, on Monday night, a public farewell was accorded Mr. Edward White, a youth of 19, a son of the deputy coroner of the borough, who departs this week to take up missionary work in Central Soudan. A local schoolmaster, Mr. Hermann Harris, joins him, and both were presented with purses of gold and medicine cases, the latter being the gift of Colonel Bridgeman, MX. White is said to be the youngest missionary that has left England's shores.

div.head: GUN-MAKER OF MOSCONV;, OR, VALDIMIR THE MONK.
div.p: THE GUN-MAKER OF MOSCONV;, OR, VALDIMIR THE MONK.
Br SYLVA.NUS COBB, JR.
CHAPTER XVII. TRANSACTIONS OP A NIGHT,

"I dare not! Oh, I dare not !" "But it is your only hope." "And whither shall we go ?" "Anywhere rather than remain here. Oh, my mistress, if you do stay here you know the fate which awaits you. There is no other means of escape from the wicked duke's power." "And I must thus cast myself among strangers— lose my all of earth—" "Hold, Rosalind. By St. Paul! there is surely one in Moscow who will help you. Let us go to the Emperor. Oh, if he be the man I have heard he will surely listen !" " Ah, Zenobie !—the duke is high in power, and his influence is great at court. Peter would not dare tq thwart him." "It may be so, but I do not believe it. And yet, my mistress, just think, for one moment, how you stand in that respect. You have nothing to lose. This life of earth, with all its pain and sorrows, and with its most exquisite tortures,holds nothing worse for you within the bounds of possibilit3 than to be- come the duke's wife. If there were but one chance in the thousand you had better try it. Re- member you cannot possibly lose anything; but the chances are for you. Let us go to the Emperor."
"But how, "Zenobie ?"

"This evening—after the darkness of night has gathered over the city—let us go. I tell you Ido not believe the Emperor will deliberately suffer a great wrong to be done for the sake of pacifying the duke. He has more noble independence than that."

The young countess did not answer at once. She pressed her small white hand hard upon her brow, and thus she remained for some time buried in profound thought. At length she raised her head, and the fire of determination was in her eye. "I will go," she said. "I will go to the Emperor. He will help me if he has a human heart." "You have one satisfaction, my mistress: he can not harm you." "Can not„?"
"I mean that you can but be made to marry with Olga; and all other harm would be as nothing com- pared with that."
"Aye—you are right, Zenobie. We will go this very night." _

The more Rosalind pondered upon this new re- solve the more hope did she derive from it. Ere long she conversed more freely with her attendant, and at times that old smile would struggle f:n. moment upon her face. Yet she had gloomy moments, too. Her fear was too deeply fixed to be swept away so easily. The afternoon passed away, and as the shades of night gathered over the great city the two girls were astir. Zenobie gathered together such articles of clothing as would be needed, and then proceeded to prepare her mistress for the adventure. "Fear not," she said, as she drew on Rosalind's robe of fur, "for there can be no danger worse than that we flee from. Try only to remember that you flee from the duke's foul embracel" This served to nerve the fair young countess up to the task, and her frame ceased its trembling. "I shall not falter now," she said. "But shall we find the Emperor at this late hour ?" "Bless me, tis not late. But even if we do net see him to-night we can do it in the morning. We shall find plenty in the imperial palace who will shelter us till then."

The girls were now ready, and all that remained was to start on their strange mission. With noise less steps they left the apartmedt where they had dressed, and proceeded 'along the corridor to the great staircase. Zenobie knew there would be less danger there than to go down the other way among the servants. Having descended these stairs they came to the great hall which opened one way into the saloons. They took the former course, and were soon in the court. The only trouble -11QW..... was in passing the porter's lodge t,t the gate, for they knew the great gate was not open, and to gain the street they must pass through the room where the por- ter always stayed. Zenobie went ahead and looked in. The porter sat by the fire playing with his dog.

"My mistress," whispered the girl, as she came back, Old John is in the lodge, and we need have no fear. He is a simple, good-natured fellow, andij am sure 1 can get by him. Do you go in advance— cover up your face—don't look at him; and be sure you don't tremble. Leave it all to me. Remember now • you have—" Fear not, Zenobie. Go on."

So on they went:- aniv;l;n they reached the lodge Rosalind went in first and stood by the wicket, while Zenobie followed, and opened the door that looked into the porter'sroom. "Good John," she uttered, in anxious tones, "come and open the wicket for me quick. My good mistress is very ill, and Tilda and I are going for the doctor. Come—be quick." "But why don't some of the men go ?" asked John as he started up and forced his dog back. "Because 'twould take them longer to do the errand than t'will us. But don't detain us. We shan't be long.'. The honest porter had orders not to allow the countess to pass out, but he thought not of that now. He had known the gentle girl from a child, and so well did he love her that he might not have stopped her even had he known she was then wait- ing to pass out. At all events, he could not refuse the present request, so he came out and opened the wicket without furtlpr question, and the girls passed through. "Now—now," uttered Zenobie, in nervous haste, "we are clear of the palace. Here is the street. Our walk is not long." Rosf lind answered not, but drawing her robe more Zlosely about her to keep out the cold, biting wind, she hastened along by the side of her COM- panion. Hope was now alive within her. Me turned one glance behind her, and she could see the light which she had left burning in her chamber. It seemed at that moment,to be the fiery eye of a demon gazing after her, and instinctively she quickened her pace.

Twice during the day did the Duke of Tulla call at the imperial palace without being able to find the Emperor; but in the evening he was more for- tunate. The Emperor was in, and Olga was admit- ted at once to his presence. "Well, my lord duke," said Peter, as Olga ap- proached; "what business calls you from home at this hour?"
"Business of importance, sire. Business of less moment to me than to the state." " Ah ? Proceed."

Only two attendants were with the Emperor, one of whom was Demetrius the Greek,and the place of audience was in one of the private apartments near the bed-chamber, where only privileged ones were ever allowed to come.
"Sire," commenced the duke, "you remember the gun-maker who was before you not long since?"
" Ah—yes. The one who took my Greek's sword from him."
"The same, sire. Have you heard from him since?"
"By my soul, Olga, I had well-nigh forgotten the fellow. Yes, yes—l remember him well now. He was a right stout knave."
" Aye---and a dangerous one, too, sire. A dan- gerous man," said the duke, with a dubious shake of the head.
"Ah!—what has he done?"

"Why' he has been engaged in various robberies to my certain knowledge; and only a few evenings since he knocked down one of our holy priests, and robbed him of all he had. He is at the head of a numerous band of desperadoes." "Is it possible?" "I know it. sire." "By St. Paul! I should not have believed this."
"Nor would I have believed it, sire, had I not received proofs not to be questioned. I, as is my duty. have !ong been anxious to ferret out this gang of robbers—"
"But I pave never heard of them, Olga," inter- rupted Petlr.

I Ah, sire, because I gave direction that you should notbe troubled with the affair. But I have them now. It was only last evening that I got a clue upor them.. We found them in an old building near the iver, here in the Kremlin, and this same Ruric Navel was with them. But he made his escape." `‘ I doremember me now that the fellow had a bold beFring, and a fearless look," said the Emperor, half to iimself; "and if such a man turns villain there rust be danger in it." ‘," Ayf, sir—you speak truly. And now with your

order, I can apprehend the fellow at once." "I can send and have it done my dear duke." "But your officers may not find him. I knovr where he is, and can have him taken at once. He had several hiding places." " Well—then you might do the work with more advantage." " Aye ; and I can have-him tried and disposed of Without further trouble to you, sire." "No, no. I wish to see him," returned the Emperor. "I will give you the necessary order,and you may bring him here." Peter then turned to his secretary, and bade him fill an order for Runic Nevel's arrest. The stout master-at-arms looked on with a troubled counten- ance, and his glances towards the duke were fair thing but loving. He did not seem to relish the business at all, and the expression of his counte- nance would seem to indicate that he did not be- lieve all that the duke had said. However, the order was soon made out, and in the duke's Possession. "Remember," said Peter, "you will bring him be" fore me."

"You shall be obeyed, sire." If the Emperor did not notice the strange, dark look of the duke as he turned away, the Greek did; and he fancied, too, than he knew what it meant' But he said nothing then. Olga bowed low as he clutched the order, and having once more promised obedience, he hurrieu from the imperial presence. As he passed 011, through the wide court he walked slowly and thoughtfully, and with his head bowed; but ono he started up—his hands came together with all emphatic movement, and he moved on more quickly. Ile had gained the street,and approached a small court within which stood a house of enter- tainment, where he stopped. In a few moments more a man came out from the inn, and as soon as he had satisfied himself that the new comer was the duke be spoke. "Olga—is't you?" yes." It needed but a single glance in the dim starligM to recognise the form of the humpbacked priest; lie walked quickly to where the duke stood, Oa the two moved off together. "Now what luck?" Savotano asked, as they gained the street once more. "Good—as good as I could even hope," retsurn.ed.. the duke. "1 have the power for arresting t.DI gun maker,"

- "And for executing him ?" "It amounts to the same. lam ordersd to brilig him before the Emperor; but that is easily raalY aged." nd Here the duke stopped and gazed about him, then bending his head, so that no word could po bly pass beyond his companion's ears, he Cozy tinued :

"You can call upon three of your best men, all_ I can furnish two from among my own servan' ; Early in the morning—by the time the sun is lir; ; they must be at the gun maker's dwelling. Theld must make him angry—of course he will resist—sllo then kill him. It is very simple—very. They cal easily despatch him thus, and then we have oil to tell the Emperor that he resisted the Imperino authority even unto death. So you see this is ervd better than it would have been had I receive_ dircct authority for his death; for then some tore of trial would have been necessary, but nOW Wto have only to go to his house—provoke hiol quarrel—kill him—and then tell the Emp3ror h° it happened. What think you?" ked "Why," returned the priest, with a i chuckle, "I can only say that Master Nevel is oc4" for—he s a dead man." "Exactly. Nothing could be better—nothing., h After the explanation of this fiendish, hello scheme, the• two walked on some distance ' silence. "Stop," uttered the duke, catching his compe°- by the arm. "There come two persons this 141.61. We must not meet them. Here—into this psss' —quick !" It was a narrow, dark passage leading to tohis- next street into which the duke dragged his et°o. panion, and here he meant to remhin until the _ot persons had passed. The fact was, the duke did Doe wish to be seen with the priest at that hour in aid street, and it is no matter of surprise that be shtooo, at that moment have been influenced by guilt)" ' L. 0,.; The two pedestrians came on, and passed the sP.,e where the men stood. They were females, and 0!,),x ot them the priest saw in the face. The feat.llrs , were upturned to the starlight., and he recognar; them. Ile caught the duko quickly and neryoVJ by the arm. "By the host of heaven !" he whispered, "Viss the countess !"
"Rosalind ?" gasped Olga. "Yes—as sure as cleat!, 1"

"Then come—quick! te Savotano understood the meaning of this, ful-„de followed the duke quickly out. At a few'b°l.l"bt Olga reached the females, and one of them he "ITO by the arm. She uttered a sharp, quick cry, en reec she turned her face up,she revealed the fair feat'illod of the Countess Rosalind Valdai The priests a no need to stop the other girl, for she stoPPe;,-,ir her own accord as soon as she found that her. "- tress was captured. " Aha ;" Olga uttered, when he saw that pale ' urr "What now, eh? Where are you bound at thiS seemly hour?" tter' "Oh, God !" It was all the poor girl could 11,61- She saw the dark face of her hated and feared wi,er dian and the last glimmer of hope faded &on soul. jjg "By my soul," the duke resumed, fastening go gripe surely upon the maiden's arm," it is fortoto I have found you, for you might have fallen difficulty else. You were bound for the irePe' palace, eh ?" At first Rosalind thought of struggling fort:3l°,lle but she felt the strong gripe upon her arm, ailuiz knew that such a movement could result °ill her own harm. , "Say," repeated the duke, "were you not n' for the palace?" "Aye, proud duke, I was," the countess reP gazing up into the man's face, "I was trying escape from your accursed power !" otne. " Alm ! But come—we'll turn toward 3,ittle bp. better off there. And this is our Zenobie, is it ?" ePlt The attendant looked up, but she made no I Then Olga turned to the priest. "Savotano, hurry off your men in the ran.„ and then come to me. I'll have work for V", 11°‘ morrow. By Saint Paul! the work delni° longer !" And then, with a sinking, breaking heart. lind Valdai was led back toward the ducal pall-. (To be continued.)

div.p: THE CONCLUDING LECTURE ON NONCONFORMITY. On Thursday evening the Rev. John Yonge, delivered under the above title at the Wycliffe Congregational Church, the fifth and last of his excellent series ot lantern lectures on Nonconform- ity. Mr, YoNGB it commencing said, let them start 'with this idea clearly before them, that until relig- i°llB equality was arrived at, and all religions should be equal in relation to the state complete religious equality would not be arrived at. (Applause.) 200 Years ago, he proceeded, their Nonconformist fore- fathers were wonderfully glad of religious tolera- tion, The achievement of that mere permission to exist was hailed with a feeling of unspeakable relief. By the year 1700,11 years after the Tolera- tion Act was passed, there were registered nearly t5OO places of worship, most of them entirely new. ~,,Khe Toleration Act was regarded as being even the Magna Charta of Dissent. Looking back on it now, however, it was not difficult to see the essen- tial error of principle on which it was based, and the narrow, ungenerous spirit that inspired it. It did not repeal a single one of the oppressive Acts of for Mei reigns. It allowed dissent rather from the worship than the doctrine of the Anglican Church. The struggles of Nonconformity in the reign of Queen Anne were next dealt with, "le Tories during that period introduced a measure to exclude Nonconformists from qualifying tor municipal Offices by receiving the sacrament at church once a year. The conduct of weak-kneed Nonconformists in consent- ing, in their sneaking fondness for social prestige, to Conform to this extent was commented on and compared tO that of those modern Dissenters who preferred to be '4_arried at church, have their babies christened there,and ue buried in consecrated ground by the clergyman, and Would have nothing to do with promoting any move- fluent for the disestablishment of the church. A. picture s thrown on the screen representing candidates for Bao, rament and office in the days of Queen Anne, wait- in an alehouse preparatory to going to the adjacent church to take the former,it being remarked that the one did not strike us as an appropriate adjunct to the other or the bar parlour as a fitting vestibule to the holy table. :rhe measure for depriving*Nonconformists of the privi- lege of qualifying for office by taking the sacrament did not pass till nine years after its introduction, and it prc- rded that no one who did not conform to the Estab- lished Church should hold any public office' and that any official found in a conventicle should be fined 00, and forfeit his office. The Schism Act was also passed in Anne's reign, being pushed Pirough the House of Commons in a single day, I,ts object being to destroy Dissenting schools by provid- ing that every schoolmaster should subscribe a declaration of conformity to the Established Church, be licensed' by a bishop,and receive the sacrament. It was described how On the accession of George Ist the tide turned in favour Of Nonconformists, the two conspicioas Disability Acts Queen Anne, the Schism Act, and the legislation emanding occasional conformity being repealed. In ,1812 some of the penalties of the Conventicle Act passed in the time of the Stuarts were done away with. In the Year 1828 Lord John Russell, carried a measure for the Zneal of the Test and Corporation Acts. The Catholic ..,niancipation Act in 1829, the lewish Disabilities 2,5.111 in 1858, and the removal of marriage, univer- TY, and other disabilities endured by Noncon- '°Mists were mentioned. The hardships imposed tril them by the burial laws existing prior to L.e Burials Act of 1880 were forcibly described, the Zcturer complaining that even now clergymen :ere allowed to take fees for all burials in consecrated und by ministers of other denominations, but Non- rnfermist ministers were not permitted to claim the ...ees for burials performed by the Church clergy in the quo, t.„ nsocrated ground. In the case of Warrington ceme- he found from enquiry made some years ago that tatter had received fees for burials by. Nonconform- ir-5 in the consecrated ground, and taken fees for burial themselves in the unconsecrated ground of about 61(81114 amount. (Laughter.) The abolition of rates in .thrand the disestablishinent of the Irish Church in , 9 'were brought under notice, the lecturer expressing tom'e ?pinion that as the threats of the Ulster Protestants „pitch the Queen's Crown into the Boyne, if the mea- a4r9 Passed, resulted in nothing, so it would be with Present threats of what .hey would do if Home , ron., were granted. (Applause.) The Education Act of u was another subject dealt with, the lecturer point- the increasea desire of the Church party to 7,tte_ngthen denominati al education, and commenting un the fact that ther ere still 10,000 rural parishes Of out a Board Schc; and nine and a half millips .1 the people compelled by law to send their children to schools. It was a crying evil that the country ror rector should be able to cripple Dissenting Sun- , uaY Schools by refusing children education in the week , nnless they attended the church school on Sunday, or , occasions of festival the parson should be able to j schkooid , mei distinctions between the children of the same ; g as a vicar just outside Warrington did not 'pry. lon oing ago. who made the Dissenting children walk nythemselves at the rear of the day school procession.as o tomeugh an inferior class. The question of the Parlia- ntary oath as raised by Mr. Bradlaugh was passed under notice, and reference made to his recent death, , the lecturer, while expressing regret at his dying Without abandoning his unbelief, bearing testi- , 11;olly to the purity and integrity of his life. In con- alding the rev, gentleman said what Noncomformity ; uad sto do was to be true to its divine principles; to go 011 testifying for perfect freedom in matters of faith, to bon destroying disabilities, and never rest content , Until religious equality was achieved. (Applause.) On the motion of the Rev. E. MOORE, seconded by , :!r• J. S. GARLAND,a hearty vote of thanks was accorded , t! Mr. Yonge and to those who had charge of the lantern, alessrs!Armitage and Lea.

Previous to I)ening of the case Mr. Davies told his Honour that tlieneTdd materially shorten the ease inasmuch as his `OO-"„;:,, had at the last hour instructed him that he tet,:4kl not contest the case. div.p: IMPERIAL PA.BLIAMENT.

HOUSE OF LORDS.—MONDAY. , The Lord CHANCELLOR took his seat on the wool-sack at a quarter past four. MISCELLANEOUS.—The Earl of MEATH introduced the County Councils Qualification of Women Bill. The Bill was read a first time. The Litchfield Cathedral Bill was read a second time. The Report of Amendments to the Custedy of Children Bill was agreed to. rhe Presenta- tion to Benefices Bill was read a third time and passed. The House adjourned at twenty-five minutes to five. HOUSE OF COMMONS.--MONDAY. The SPEAKER took the chair at three o'clock. RATING OF MACHINERY.—Mr. RITCHIE in answer to Mr. Duncan, said no instructions had been issued to Boards of Guardians or other local bodies giving direc- tions as to the way in which the ratable value of build- ings containing machine should be ascertained. THE SOUDAN.—Sir JAMES FERGUSON informed Mr. Gedge that every precaution was being taken to mitig- ate the sufferings involved by the famine in the Soudan. ROMAN CATHOLICS AND PUBLIC OFFICES.—Sir R. WEB- STER declined to answer questions as to the eligibility of Roman Catholics for the offices of Lord Chancellor of England and Lord-Lieutenant of Ireland as they involved points of law of considerable difficulty, which could not be dealt with in the limits of an answer. THE SULTAN AND ARMENIA.—Sir J. FERGUSSON, answering to Mr. F. Stevenson, said her Majesty's am- bassador had been instructed to impress upon the Sultan the danger of allowing a continuance of the state of things which had recently taken place in Armenia. Tins Trines BILL.—The Consideration of the Tithes Bill as amended was then resumed.—Mr. D. RANDELL moved a clause providing that in any action under the Act the plaintiff or defendant might require that the matter should be tried by a jury.—Sir M. HICKS-BEACH refused to accept the amendment, which on a division, was rejected by a majority of 51. Another new clause providing that the County Court Judge should not award costs under the Act on a higher scale than would other- wise be applicable met a like fate.—Mr. STOREY even- tually moved the adjournment of the debate, which was agreed to by the Government, but was afterwards by leave withdrawn. The consideration of the Bill was again continued. The House adjourned at 12.5. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TUESDAY. The Speaker took the chair at three o'clock. GOLD COINAGE.—Mr. GOSCHEN told Mr. Montague that the Gold Coinage Bill would not at present be pressed forward, but another measure as to currency would be proceeded with. LIVEROOL POSTMEN AND THEIR HOURS.—MT. RAIKBS, in answer to the Hon. W. H. Cross, said memorials had been received from Liverpool and other postmen asking for a limitation of their hours, and improvement with re- gard to their pay and overtime allowances and for other benefits. The memorials had been referred to a Commit- tee, whose report he hoped shortly to receive. In the meantime endeavours were being made to reduce the period over which their daily attendance was spread. THE TITHES BILL.—Mr. W. H. SMITH said that owing to the slow progress made with the Tithes Bill the Gov- ernment had no alternative but to ask the House.to give it precedence over all other orders of the day, and he moved a resolution to that effect. Sir W. HARCOURT opposed the motion, as he said there was nothing in the present state of public business to warrant it. The motion was eventually carried, as was also one that if the debate on the Bilf were not concluded by midnight it should not be interrupted by the standing orders. The consideration of the Bill as amended was then resumed. The House adjourned at one o'clock. HOUSE OF LORDS.—TUESDAY. The House met at a quarter to four o'clock. Miscnixamnons.—Lord Cnoss presented a Bill to amend the law relating to certain offices in India, and explained that its object was to enable certain high officers to come home on special occasions without vacating their appointments.—The Bill was read a first time. A Bill introduced by Lord Herschel', to render penal the in- citing of infants tobetting and wagering, was also read a first time. Earl CADOGAN moved the adoption of the report of the Select Committee appointed to inquire into the standing orders. The new standing orders were agreed to. The Lichfield Cathedral Bill passed through Com- mittee, and, on the motion of the Bishop of Lichfield it was ordered that it should not ba referred again to a standing committee last session. Their lordships rose at a quarter to five o'clock. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WEDNESDAY.

The Speaker took the chair at ten minutes past two. PETITIONS.—Mr. SETON-KARR presented a petition from the St. Helens and District Temperance Union in favour of Sunday Closing and from working men of St. Helens in favour of the Steam Engines and Boilers Bill. MARRIAGE OF A DECEASED WIFE'S SISTER.—The second reading of the bill to legalise marriage with a deceased wife's sister was moved by Mr. Joan KELLY. Mr. JEF- FREY'S moved the rejection of the bill. Mr. W. M'LAREN had an amendment on the paper opposing the bill on the ground that it did not deal equally with men and women, but the forms of the House did not permit him to move it. The SOLICITOR GENERAL for Scotland spoke in oppo- sition to the bill, the second reading of which, on a divi- sion, was carried by 202 to 155. MACHINERY RATING.—Mr. E. KNATCHBULL-HUGESSEN moved the second reading of the Rating of Machinery Bill. Mr. WINTERBOTHAM having pointed out that the second reading of the measure was carried last year by an enormous majority, the ATTORNEY GENERAL said that as the promoters had expressed their willingness to accept as a standpoint the clause to which they agreed last year, he thought the house might assent to the motion. Mr. GOURLEY and Sir R. PAGET opposed the bill. At half-past five Mr. WINTERBOTHAM moved that the question be put, but the Speaker withheld his assent, and the debate stood adjourned. On the motion of Mr. HOYLE, the Companies Act (1862) Amendment Bill was read a second time. The House adjourned at twenty minutes to six. HOUSE OF LORDS, THURSDAY. The Lord Chanceller took his seat on the woolsack at a quarter-past four o'clock. The Custody of Children Bill was read a third time. COLONIAL GOVERNMENT.—The Earl of DUNRAVEN,III moving a resolution in favour of the Colonial Govern- ments being invited to send representatives to a confe- rence to be held in London, to consider theadvancement of trade within Her Majesty's dominions and the forma- tion of a fund for certain purposes of Imperial defence, said there were tics of blood and sentiment between Great Britain and her dependencies. but the tie of material advantage was to a large extent wanting. The Marquis of SALISBURY said care should be taken only to make use of such conferences when some definite questions or propositions could be laid before the con- stituents of the delegates—questions which the colonists had had the opportunity of discussing before their representatives came here; and looking at the proposed conference from that point of view, he did not see what definite propositions they were to discuss. The Earl of DUNRAVEN expressed his willingness to with- draw his resolution, but at the same time desired to dis- claim any intenion of advocating retaliatory duties. The motion was withdrawn, and the House adjourned'vat six o'clock.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.--Tmunsam The SPEAKER took the chair at three o'clock. LANCASHIRE COUNTY COUNCIL BlLL.—On'the order for uhe secoad reading of the Lancashire County Council Bill, the object of which is to form a general County Lunacy Board, Mr. COURTNEY pointed ont that it was the first instance of a County Comicil proposing to ob- tain a bill, and said it appeared to him to be in excess of the powers conferred by the House on County Councils. Mr. RITCHIE said that while entirely in favour of the principle of the bill, he agreed with the Chairman of Committees that no County Council had power to spend money in the promotion of a bill, end if they did so it would be at their own risk. The bill 'was then read a second time. QuEsTroms.—Lord George Hamilton informed Admiral Mayne that the laying down of line-of-battle ships since 1889 had been so rapid that the' position of the fleet as regarded new construction ,compared with that of foreign countries, was very much improved. In answer to Sir George Cambell, Sir JANES FERGIISSON said Her Majesty's Government had raised no objection to the occupation of Tokar and Handonb by the Egyptian troops, No additional burden would be thrown on this country by the measures that were being taken. TITHE BILL, &c.—On the motion for the third reading of the Tithe Bill Sir WILLIAM HARCOURT and Mr. OSBORNE MORGAN expressed the opinion that the measure would prove a failure. A third reading was carried by 250 to 161. The Electors' Registration (Acceleration) Bill and the Electoral Disabilities Removal Bill were read a second time. The House adjourned at a quarter past 12 o'clock.
