div.head: EXAMINER, SAM RDA Y , FEBRUARY 14, 1891.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SAM RDA Y , FEBRUARY 14, 1891.

the damage done by the escapes of sulphuretted nydro- gen, instructions were given to again call the attention of the United Alkali Company to the matter. The Clerk reported that Superintendent Noblett had paid £3 19s. 4d. to the credit of the Charity fund, being the balance of the ambulance fund. In connection with this Committee's minutes the fol- lowing letters were read with regard to the escape of sulphuretted hydrogen Mr. G. E. Hall, of Rainhall wrote :—" Can nothing be done by the Widnes Sanitary Authorities to prevent the daily and nightly emission of noisome and poisonous gases from the Widnes works? The nuisance here is becoming intolerable; people who have lived here for many years assert that it has never been so bad as for the last six months. When I woke the other night my bedroom was full of the sickening, suffocating stench, causing violent retching and sick headache. A public petition will be sent to the Govern- ment on the subject if nothing is done to remedy this state of things.—The following letter from Dean Finegan was also read :—" St. Bede's Presbytery, Appleton, 1 Widnes, Feb. 9th, 1891.—Dear Mr. Chairman,—During the last six months I have frequently heard this question asked: "Can nothidg be done to stop the offensive smells caused by the Chance'process in the works ?" The reply is that the Local Board has power to stop it if it wishes. I wish to entreat the Board to move in the matter. During the last few weeks the nuisance has been unbearable to those who have to live in the .district. lam very sure no one would like to interfere with the industries either of individuals or of firms, but when any industry becomes a nuisance to a town or a district then, in my opinion, if the nuisance cannot be abated the industry should be stopped. Loud and frequent are the complaints against the Local Board for permitting the nuisance with which those who had to live in Widnes are afflicted. The fact of our having to live in the town is no reason why we should be exposed to such a poisoned atmosphere. It is with great reluctance that I intrude upon the business of your Board, with any complaint, yet 1 think it is well that it should be known that the feeling is very strong in this district on the subject ; and, speaking fromaper- sonal experience, I can assert that more than once the smell sickened me. We feel it the most at night—Satur- day and Sunday nights in partieular. I hope then that as you have the power to put an end to this nuisance, you will do so, and I am sure that those who have to live in Widnes will feel for ever grateful. —I remain yours truly, Thomas Finegan. Letters were likewise read from Mr. Carey on be- half of the United Alkali Company. In one of these, it was stated, with regard to the letter from Mr. Hall complaining of the escape of sulPhuretted hydrogen from works in Widnes, that the subject was receiving the earnest attention of the directors. The following are the terms of the second letter from Mr. Carey to the Chair- man :—" Dear Mr. Gossage.—Chance-Claus Process.— Probably you will be glad to hear that the United Alkali Co. have appointed a special inspector to detect and report upon any sulphuretted hydrogen escapes that he may find in the works from the process. Full powers have been given to him to visit and inspect at all hours, especially at night, and at other times when the men working the process are apt to be less vigilant than usual. I am glad to say that their inspection has been already of service in preventing nuisances. The United Alkali Co. are, as I have said, mpst anxious to do all that is possible to prevent annoyabce, and will, I feel sure, not hesitate at any reasonable expense to ensure that the utmost care shall be exercised in working the pro- cess." A good deal of discussion took place as to the nuisances, and Mr. Hayes moved, Dr. O'Keefe seconding, that seven days' notice be given the Alkali Company to abate the nuisance.—The Chairman mentioned that he had been informed that a patent had been taken out for a method of working the Chance process which, when applied, would obviate the escapes of gases. Mr. Hayes's motion was defeated by seven votes to four, and it was agreed that the Chairman of the Board and the Chair- man of the Health Committee be appointed a deputation to wait upon the Alkali Company and point out to them that they must take action to abate the nuisance or the Board would have to intervene.—The minutes of the committee were then adopted._

div.head: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD,
div.p: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD,

The monthly meeting of this Board was held on Tuesday at the Town -Hall, Widnes. Mr. Gossage presided, and there were also present Dr. O'Keefe, Messrs. Wright, Timmis, Hargreaves, Hayes, Liddle, Taylor, Houghton, Brown, Cook, ,Sadler, and J. T. Allen (clerk).
THE LATE MR. DICKSON. Mrs. Dickson, on behalf of her sons and herself, wrote acknowledging with thanks the vote of condolence on the death of her husband passed at the last meeting of the Board. '

-MEDICAL OFFICER'S ANNUAL REPORT. The Medical Officer submitted his annual report to the Board, from whieh it appeared that there had been 661 deaths during the past year in Widnes, giving a death. rate of 21.32 per 1,000 on the estimated population, 31,000, of the town. The number of births for the same period was 1,206. The number of cases treated in the infectious diseases hospital during the year was 97, and of these only nine ended fatally, a fact which proved the great usefulness of that institution and the excellence of the nursing and care received by the patients therein. Referring to the Chance-Claus'process the Medical Officer reported that since this process had been adopted con- siderable nuisance had been experienced by the inhabit- ants of the township, said to be caused by the emission of sulphuretted hydrogen into the atmosphere. That Board had communicated with every manufacturer using the process, and they had promised that greater care in the working of it should be exercised in the future, but so far, little, if any, improvement was perceptible.—lt was agreed that a copy of the Medical Officer's report should be sent to the Local Government Board.

GAS AND WATER COMMITTEE. The following items were contained in the minutes of the Gas and Water Committee :—Engineer's report dated this day read as follows:—Stock's Well—Deepening Bore- hole in No. 2 well: The contractors have sunk this hole 140 feet, the total depth from the ground level is 49q feet. The nature of the rock is still hard and faulty, and the increase of water up to the present is only slight. Damage to Waterpipes : During the recent frost from December Ist to January 12th, there were 511 burst pipes. This number is about five times in excess of that of the corresponding period last year. Scrubber-washer : This machine is still passing ammonia, the average of the tests being about 12 grains per 100 feet. The contractor's foreman has been over for several days during the past month inspecting the machine and testing the gas. I submit recent correspondence with Walker's on the matter. Gas Main along Marsh road: This work which has been so long delayed by the recent frost, is now well in hand and will be completed by Wednesday next. Sulp- hate Plant 4: This plant has been worked throughout the past month, 44 tons have been sold, present stock 4 tons. The mean rainfall for the month had been 1471 inches. The illuminating power of the gas during the month had been 1757 candles. It was recommended that C. R. Bellamy be appointed to test the quality of the gas and to report—two tests per month, subject to three months' notice to terminate the engagement. A letter was read from W. Christie calling attention to " the poor quality and insufficient quantity of gas supplied," and request- ing " that immediate steps be taken to improve the supply," the letter being referred to the engineer. Recommended that the tender of the Staveley Iron Co. for /5 tons pipes at £5 ss. per ton delivered be accepted. Instructions were given to continue the deepening of the borehole at Stock's Well—say for 50 feet, and to report. The engineer was instructed to appoint a caretaker at Pex Hill. Recommended that the offer of £5 by Mr. R. Collingwood for shooting right at Pex Hill be accepted. Minimum Charge for Water: A deputation attended in reference to this charge and to the charge for fittings for supply of water for building purposes. The question referred to an adjourned Committee meeting and to the Board.—These minutes were passed on the motion a f Mr. WRIGHT, seconded by Mr. BROWN.
HIGHWAY COMMITTEE,

This Committee held a meeting on the 29th January, and the following items were on the minutes :—The Clerk reported that Messrs. Oppenheim and Co. are tak- ing proceedings against Messrs. Evans, Lockett, and Co., in accordance with the Committee's instructions last month. Instructions given to Messrs. Oppenheim and. Co. to take proceedings against Mr. Cotsworth to en- force compliance with the bye-laws, and to recover the costs allowed in the late action. Recommended, that the lamps in Widnes-road from Vine-st. to Deacon-road, be altered to "Bray's," or other similar lamps. Dr. O'Beeffe objected to this. Public improvements.— Lugsdale-road : Draft agreements with the landowners submitted and approved. Recommended that £l,OOO be borrowed to do the following work :—Flagging in Mer- sey-road, Widnes-road, Albert-road, Alforde-at., aid Lugsdale-road. Curbing, &c., in Warrington-road. Sewering in Deacon-road. The estimate for year 1891- 92 £5,827 95., examined and approved.—Mr. Houghton moved, and Mr. Taylor seconded, the adoption of these minutes.—Dr. O'Keeffe objected to the alterations to the lamps in Widnes-road, on the ground of the cost, but the minutes were adopted as proposed.

THE HEALTH COMMITTEE.-THE POLLUTION OF THE ATMOSPHERE.—COMPLAINT FROM DEAN FrIs'EGAN. The Health Committee's minutes contained the follow- ing :—Messrs. J. Hutchinson and Co. having consented to provide ashed for a hand ambulance, it 6 was recom- mended that the offer be accepted, and that they be thanked—the horse ambulance and the other hand am- bulance to be kept at the Police Station until further notice. The nuisance Inspector reported that the com- mon lodging-houses had been inspected and found in order. The Inspector also reported that there seemed to have been considerable escapes of sulphuretted hydrog- en. As there had been several complaints reported of

div.head: FINANCE.
div.p: FINANCE.

The Finance Committee's minutes contained recom- mendations that applications be made to the Local Government Board for sanction for the borrowing of £250 for washhouses, Btc.. at the fever hospital, and £930 for private improvements ; also that Mr. Sankey be appointed a collector.—The minutes were approved. This was all the business of public interest.
DEATH OF A WELSH. CENTENARIAN.

--- The Welsh newspapers on Wednesday recorded the death of Nelly Phillips, at her cottage on the Pembroke- shire coast, near Fishguard, aged 103. She was a spins- ter, and had been bedridden eight years. Miss Phillips witnessed the landing of the French frigates at Fish- guard in 1797. ......-4,—, MR. GLADSTONE ON THE STAGE.

A story is current that one day last week Mr. Glad- stone went to the Lyceum, and as after the first act he was missed from his box, it was imagined he had re- turned to the House of Commons. A rapid change of scene, however, discovered the Liberal leader at the wings talking to Mr. Irving, who quickly pulled him from beyond the sight of the audience. '
A crofter named William Buchanan has been arrested at Ballyjamesduff on suspicion of being the murderer of the caretaker Reilly and his wife at Lisacapple.

div.head: GYMNASTIC ENTERTAIMMENT AT THE
div.p: GYMNASTIC ENTERTAIMMENT AT THE
EMPIRE THEATRE.

On Wednesday evening a grand gymnastic dis- play was given by the members of the Warrington ' Gymnasium, in the Empire Theatre ot Varieties. There was a large audience, including many ladies. Mr. Tiaos. Morris presided, in the absence of the Mayor, and in the course of the evening addressed some remarks to those present. He said he was pleased to see so many patronising the institution in connection with which the entertainment was held. It was what he called a magnificent institution, almost next to the Infirmary, for they had one little lad on the stage that night who had an arm he could not possibly use three or four months ago, and by medical advice he joined the gymnasium to take a gymnastic course, and now was rapidly recovering strength in the arm. The Committtee were extremely thankful to Mr. Leon, the lessee of the Theatre, for allowing them the use of the building more than free. He was one of the kindest fellows that over came into Warrington, to its ith3titu- tions. ((Applause.) He (Mr. Morris) hoped thpse present would patronise Mr. Leon's performances at that theatre. —Mr. Leon said he was extremely obliged for the kind ' words that had been spoken,and if at any time his services were required for any charitable purpose he should be happyto devote them to that object. The entertainment comprised the following items :—Dumb-bell exercises by pupils of the boys' class. High jumping, parallel bar exercises, pyramids, bar bells, boxing, wrestling, hori- zontal bar exercises, heavy weight lifting, vaulting horse, Indian clubs. The high jumping was remarkably good, and the parallel bar performances were exceed- ing clever, the manner in which the acrobats would spin with their bodies round the bar, convert their hands into feet, and perform a variety of other exploits being most striking. Pyramids, were too, a wonderful exem- plification of the strength and suppleness to which the human body may be developed; and the manner in which the gymnasts would sustain themselves in their strained positions to obtain pyramidal formation was truly remarkable. The wrestling, in which Fair Turner and T. Locker were pitted against each other, was a most exciting and strenuous encounter, both men for the most part of the time conducting the struggle on the ground, first one and then the other being uppermost time after time, until an exhausting struggle terminated in the redoubtable Turneri rising a breathless victor. The programme was somewhat diversified by the appearance during the evening of some of the Empire artistes,who gave artistic exhibitions of dancing, and some burlesque boxing. The gymnastic entertainment altogether was a decided success; and it may be said that it induced in the audience themselves the assiduous practice of a certain description of gymnastic exercise, for their applause was uncommonly frequent. The Empire orchestra, under the direction of Mr. E. Woodville, accompanied with selections of music, the various performances.

div.head: SHIP CANAL FINANCE.
div.p: SHIP CANAL FINANCE.

In the House of Commons, on Tuesday, Mr. Philip Stanhope asked the President of the Board of Trade whether his attention bad been called to the re- cent application of the Manchester Ship Canal Company to the Corporation of Manchester for financial assistance, and te the fact that the Man- chester Ship Canal Acts contain provisions for the vesting of the undertaking, under certain circum- stances, in a public trust ; and if, in view of this application, he would afford facilities for the dis- cussion of the Canal Development Bill now before Parliament for the fourth succeeding sesion, or would allow it to be referred to a Select Committee, in order that the whole question of the develop- ment of canals under responsible public authorities might be adequately considered. Sir M. Hicks-Beach.—Yes, sir; my attention has been called to the recent application of the Man- chester Ship Canal Company to the Corporation of Manchester, and to the provisions of the Ship Canal Acts to which the hon. member refers. Ido not quite see the connection between the first part of the question and the second part. At present I have no intention of asking the House to consider the whole question of developing canals under respon- sible publit authorities.

MISS FORSYTHE'S FREAK

The long-tongued clock in the square was striking six as Mr. Jack Pomeroy left his gondola at the Hotel Damilli in Venice. The world said, and foi once was right, that "he was an excellent as well as fortunate fellow. Heir to half a million of money. and all the good looks of his family." Above stairs, Miss Constance Forsythe amuses herself with the harmless game of battledore. She is in"disgrace with her decidedly fussy step-mother, and in consequence remains at home with the rest of the naughty children. "It is a bore, but not' wholly undeserved," she thinks, as she bends and springs and darts here and there through the room. "Fifty-one, fifty- two—three—four—five—six—" the door opens; an incoming head dodges hastily, as the little, feathered shuttlecock strikes fairly between the eyes. _
"That was a centre shot," says Mr. Pomeroy, lazily sauntering into the apartment. "Is that the way you assault all the friends of the family, Mademoiselle 7"
There is a brief pause. Jack is puzzled, and Con- stance embarrassed. Mr. Pomeroy says: "I came to see Miss Forsythe ; the servant brought me here."

"1 am Miss Forsythe—Miss Constance Forsythe; it was very stupid of the servant, but I dare say that is the way the mistake occurred ;" and Con- stance pushes forward a chair, into which the gen- tleman sinks with a feeling of satisfaction. Mr. Pomeroy giving no signs of speedy departure, Constance accepts the situation the tide of conver- sation flows smoothly on, and Mr. Pomeroy takes his departure with a strong determination to return at the earliest moment.

"It will be absolutely necessary to make his peace with Mrs. Forsythe," he tells himself, as, skimming over the moonlit waters, he fashions airy visions with the haunting eyes of lovely Constance For- sythe; and even in his, dreams that night Mr. Pomeroy still listens to theSsportive bump, bump of a tiny, fluttering plaything. It was a week after the meeting of Mr. Pomeroy and the young lady in question. Constance sat at the window, watching the plashing oars of pass- ing gondoliers. Suddenly thought strikes her. She hesitates but a moment, and signals Petronelo, the Forsythes' own special gondolier. Constance settles herself on her cushions, gives a brief order, and glides. majest:cally away in her Adriatic carriage. "To the market I" says Petronelo.

"Precisely." And ten minutes later Miss Forsythe stands among the crowd of boats and barges waiting at the ferry. A few words of voluble bargaining, a trans- fer of small coin, and she takes possession of an un- wieldy fish-boat. Petronele stands aghast as the scheme unfolds. But Constance brushes him aside as if he was an intrusive fly, steps into her craft and paddles gaily away. An accomplished canoeist on the calm ripples of artificial ponds, she is now con- fident, serene, and ecstatic, but a strange sight, alone in her boat her graceful figure swaying to the vigor- ous stroke of her rounded arm.

Presently Miss Forsythe stops to rest, and looks about her at totally unfamiliar land-marks. She 'turns to retrace her steps, and finds that, as far as her knowledge of the route goes, she might as well have been afloat in the middle of the Pacific Ocean. Constance tries the trip ahead. For awhile it is plain sailing. She turns a corner, and lands in the wide lagoon, with an open outlook to the blue and distant mountains.

Miss Forsythe begins to have qualms, as she scans the soundless prospect for a moving object. Yes! there to the left, towers a white expanse of rustling canvass. If she reaches it, it is almost certain to lead her into frequented thoroughfares. Once in the Grand Canal. she will be all right, and Constance settles to the work in hand, determined to overtake that vessel if it cripples her back. Suddenly a miniature whirlpool spins in the course —au area of small billows and churning foam, and upon them, in half a second, Miss Forsythe's un- wieldy bark dances like a cork. She struggles hard to change her course, but the boat is beyond control. The paddles whirl out of reach, a strong aun seems to drag her out to sea, the wash from the departing ship helps, the mischief, and, with a scream of horror, Constance realises the peril of Petronelo's "hidden currents" as her tiny ship races madly into the open lagoon. At this moment Mr. Pomeroy stands on the deck of his yacht Gerlina. He is thinking of that, eventful game of battledore, of the lovely, mis- chievous Miss Forsythe. Presently he shades his eyes with his hand, whistles softly, and peers in- tently at a strange object whirling rapidly on in the wayward tides. "Hang me if I can make it out," and he leans far over the rails in his effort to see. In an instant, as if shot out of a cannon, Mr. Pomeroy propels himself across the deck, gives a wild shout of alarm, and swings himself over the side by the over-hanging chains. In obedience to the instinct (4 self-preservation, Constance, as her vessel rushes out into the tossing waves, throws herself face downward on the seat and clutches tightly the boat's sides. Every instant increased her peril; with a moan of anguish she faces death. Then, at the very climax of her danger and alarm, a friendly hand stays her frail cockle shell, a friendly voice encouragps her, and a stalwart arm lifts her from despair to the yacht's deck.

At the evenihg service on Sunday, the Rev. Mr. Moore, the missionary of No. 6 section of the Ship Canal,referred to the rumoured closing of the mission. He said he felt it his duty to announce tothe congregation that, knowing what he did of the authorities, he could assure them that there was not the slightest possibility of the mission being closed at present. He had received no inti- mation to the effect of its being discontinued, and would certainly have been informed had the vimpany thought of taking that course. The rumour was a pure inven,- lion. On Tuesday evening Mr. Moore gave a lantern exhibition in the Mission Hall. There was a capital attendance, a number of limelight views illustrative of a journey from London i to the Niagara Falls being shown. Mr. Moore explained the pictures depicted on the screen.

A Galway telegram reports that the suicide of Mr. Mann Colleary, head constable of County Galway, by shooting himself through the head. A movement is on foot at Northampton to raise a Brad- laugh memorial fund, which, it is suggested, should be invested in municipal funds and the interest employed in the purchase of books for the Northampton Library.

"Thank God! my darling," cries Mr. Pomeroy, reckless of the few brief weeks since he and Con- stance have met, and totally regardless of the astonished faces of the sailors who gather about them. The secret is out; the whole city may know it for ought Jack cares.

While this last adventure of the madcap Con- stance is running briskly along, the unconscious Mrs. Forsythe and her own daughter, the well- regulated and only blossom of the lady's second marriage, sit in their private box at the opera. Mrs. F. settles her ilthmees, and secretly wonders why Constance is so late, as she hears the call boy's shrill treble shouting: "Overture on, ladies—over- ture on." Where she mirht be:Mrs. Forsythe dared not speculate. She had made it a rule that her step-daughter should not remain out after sunset; but whether it was obeyed was a matter best left uninvestigated ; and the lady glanced smilingly over the sea of faces. Still Mrs. F. is uneasy— quite nervous, in fact, though not for a gold mine would she betray emotion. Campanini sings, con- sequently the patrician world of Venice has turned out in force. From pit to dome the house is crowded; the prompter's bell jingles, the curtain rolls lingeringly up, the dirE.ctor's baton wavers, as a shaking hand is laid on Mrs. Forsythe 's shoulder, and wretched Petronelo stammers out his terrible tale:

"Signorina—the Lady Constance is missing; has been missing for hours." And he turns for confir- mation to the whimpering fisher lad behind him, Screams, smelling-salts, and a jargon of English, German, and Italian follow this announcement; then a crowd of sympathising friends knd a frantic race to the Hotel Damilli. With all her faults Mrs. Forsythe is a tender- hearted woman, and truly mourns over this cruel blow. Ghastly visions of a dead girlish face rise in the rippling waters. She weeps and drives poor Petronelo wild with reproaches. Through the fleet of boats and gondolas that thriang the Grand Canal they fly like a whirlwind; under the Bridge of Sighs to the hotel entrance. Limp with woe, Mrs. For- sythe supported by Petronelo, totters up the stairs, goes sorrowfully to her room, and stops, transfixed and dumb, on the threshold of the door. "Here I am, mother mine," says Constance, in unruffled tones. "it was certainly a narrow squeeze, but Mr. Pomeroy's actobatic ability saved me." And with her provokingly indifferent air she waits for the gentleman to explain. Judging from the warmth of her step-mother's kiss, some time later, it is clear that he doe k this satisfactorily. Ample means, an irreproachable son- in-law, and no wonder that Mrs. Forsythe's wrath melts like snow under az August sun.
PATENT
"Yes," she tells a confidential friend, when dis- cussida the coming marriage, "I have always said that Constance would secure a suitable establish- ment." - -

—;This is precisely the reverse of what Mrs. Forsythe has either said or thought. As they listen to this change of opinion, Jack and Constance exchange glances, but are too genuinely happy and content to contradict harmless inaccuracies in the newly-risen prophet.

The strike at the Cardiff Docks continues. The Car- diff Trades' Council have resolved to break down the federation movement. The ship Bluejacket was taken to Newport Docks, there to discharge. The Bute Dock Company have issued a notice to their workmen requir- ing all persons in their employ to give due notice before leaving their employment. on pain of prosecution. On Friday, at Greenock, Alexander Scott was sent to prison for thirty days for threatening a 'signalman during tlke. recent strike.

Child WE have still something to learn Marriages about Ireland, and a great deal to In India. learn about India. Our great Dependency is so far away that, although our rule involves the well-being of 250 millions of people, Parliament does not give a tithe of 'the time to Indian affairs that it gives to a Tithes Bill. The doc- trine of equality of treatment of the sexes—which simply means that woman is not to be abused— has taken root-hold in this country, and is bearing fruit in the shape of beneficent legislation. But there is no such progress to record as to India. Woman has for centuries been regarded there as the slave of man, and a slave she continues to be. It is not, we imagine, that the male Hindoo is by nature more vicious or cruel than the average of human beings ; the evil is in the main the out- growth of superstition—of so-called religious teaching which has been intended to be beneficial, but has proved to be baleful. A woman, accord- ing to the sacred books of the Ilindoos, becomes so completely a part of her husband, that at his death it is an act of virtue to compass her own death by burning; hence what is known as the suttee ; though it has for some years been abolished by the exercise of English authority. Another abominable custom—that of child marriages—is still tole- rated; and some hint of what it means may be gained when it is stated that the Government, under the pressure of agitation amongst Medical and other authorities, have at last decided to raise what is known as the age of consent from ten years to twelve. Granted that bodily and fUnctional development is quicker in hot countries than in cold, there is not such a difference as to warrant marriage at the early age which is not unfrequent in India. How great is the mischief May be 10 some degree realised when it is stated that it is' common for mere children to become widows, and this means that they can never marry again—never become mothers—for the rule still is "once a. widow always a widow." A single illustration will bring home the extent of this widowhood amongst the young. The combined population of Warring' ton, St. Helens, Earlestown, Newton, Widnes and Runcorn may be said, roundly speaking, to be 200,000; but if the whole of that population were swept away Bindostan could replace it "with an equal number of widows, the youngest of whonl should be ten,and the eldest not exceeding fourteen years of age." But to go further; there are widows in India under nine years of age equal in number, to the total population of Warrington and Widnes It is is appalling to reflect upon facts of this kind, which are detailed in the current issue of the "Westminster Review." Can we wonder that the medical journals have been loud in their pr3test against the barbarities which such a state of things involves? As already suggested, religious teaching,founded on regard for the life principle in nature, but in conjunction with gross ignorance of physiologY, largely responsible for the degradation of women in India; and it is because it affects the religion doctrines of the natives that, in some quarters, thE,' cry is—" Hands off; this is no business of ours. And if it relateito issues of minor moment—rae, re points of superstitious ceremonial—we should be inclined to echo the cry. But it affects the health and happiness of millions of human beings who, be- cause they are committed to our care, are en- titled to our protection. Sutteeism and thug- I gism have been abolished in India, and we do 1164 see why child marriages should not be abolishoc.t It is difficult, of course, to legislate against opinion; but it is understood that public opin7 is with the Government in raising the age from n to twelve. Then there is such a thing as educa' ting public opinion; and something should be don.P

div.p: in that direction. The Hindoos require to learn that it should be a credit to a wife to be able to read and write, instead of, as at present, a reproach to her. The Zenana missions are doing good work as far as they go, but they touch merely the fringe of the population. It is for the Hindoos who obtain an English education to go back amongst their countrymen and tell theta that where civilisationsis at the highest the regard for woman is the greatest; that the oppression of women, as in India, means that men are still degraded—held down by those twin gaolers Super- stition and Barbarism.

Eight Hours MR C. M. PERCY, Mining Engineer, • for of Wigan, who is well known in Miners, this part of the country as a politi- cal speaker, has published a paper on" Miners and the Eight Hours movement." It will be alike surprising and disappointing to many working- men to find that he is opposed to legislative enac- ment with the object of enforcing an eight hours day for miners. In his opinion no case has been made out, for he• holds that "the average miner does not row work more than forty-eight hours per week." This may be so, and yet it may happen that there are miners outside the average, who work longer hours under exhausting condi- tions. It is in the smaller mines where mischief is done, and where the protection of the law is most needed. Mr. PERCY urges that mines are not un- healthy, and that "a person underground in a mine has less risk than a merchant seaman whose re- muneration is considerably less." Indeed,Mr. PERCY has so much to say in favour of letting things alone as to suggest that, in his view, the collier's lot, unlike the policeman's, is quite a happy one. There is no need,however,to do more than mention the difference between "A life on the ocean wave" and a sunless existence "In the deep, deep mine." People who have nothing to do but seek enjoy- ment sometimes spend weeks on the sea; but we do not hear of them tilling their pleasure for as much as a couple of days in a coal mine. We grant that it is material to consider how far restriction of the hours of labour would reduce "legitimate profits," and increase the price of coal; but in this connection it is as well to remind Mr. PERCY that he himself has told us of something Which is a greater burden both to the capitalist and to the public, and that is the unjust operation of "Mine Rents and Mineral Royalties." If we mistake not, the amount of money which is annually paid to ground landlords for rents, royalties and way-leaves, is several millions more than the total EUM paid in wages to miners! There is a margin here to work upon so large that a quarter of it would more than suffice to cover any extra cost which would be in- volved in making the eight hours day in mines uniform throughout the country. We must con- fess that we attach most importance to the inter- ference with the liberty of the subject which the Proposal involves. It is objection able on the face of it that a strong thrifty, collier should be put in such a position by the legislature that he cannot 'work nine hours when interest and inclination Prompt him to do so. But restriction applies to women as well as men, and we have already sanc- tioned the principle of-limitation in the hours of labour for women. The question is beset with difficulties Which need to be well considered before any definite steps are taken; and men like Mr. Rer, who may be regarded as specialists, are to be thanked for writing' fully and frankly on the subject.

"Master of Arts " Veritas ;" " Qui Vive 7 and "Manlius."—Next week.
Another move in Egypt; the Government is re- ported to be occupying Tokar ? What does it mean? Has Osinan Digna, who has been "killed" a score of times, been showing his head again?

It is understood that the Chancellor of the Exchequer is about to revive the old-fashioned one- pound note, and with it we may expect a revival of the comment upon the people who always "live up to their paper.

--- Can it be true that a 'cute Yankee has invented a gun that can throw dynamite shells a distance of five miles, and can be discharged a thousand times in rapid succession? It is to be hoped so, for it is only when the devil's engines are equal to blow- ing everything and everybody to pieces that "the nations will learn war no more."

Mr. Newnes' "Strand Magazine" promises to be as big a success in its way as " Tit-bits." The second number is quite as good as the first, and it is altogether a capital sixpennyworth. The illus- trations are numerous, and the "Portraits of celebrities at different times in their lives" are a decided novelty. It should be followed up.

The Marriage with a Deceased Wife's Sister Bill passed the House of Commons on Wednesday. This is the twentieth occasion on which it has been before Parliament, and it will, we suppose, be again thrown out by the House of Lords—unless, wonder of wonders, the bishops therein have taken to studying the Scripture and exercising common.. sense.

It seems some of the instructions said to have been iisued by the London and North-Western Railway Company with the object of reducing the hours of railway servants were "too good news to be true." Well, well, the dream will be a reality some day. Meantime railway men throughout the country must act on Lincoln's motto; they must "keep pegging away."

The Liberals of the Altrincham Division have a splendid candidate in Mr. Leadam, and, as" worth makes the man," he ought to win. Referring, at Lymm, on Tuesday night, to the jollifications of the Tories, he hit the nail on the head when he said there had been a good deal of bait visible; but it was as well to remember that bait was not for the benefit of the fish.

The •death rate of Widnes for the past year was reported at the Local Board meeting, on Tuesday, to be 21.32 per 1,000. This cannot be said to be high; it is lower, for instance, than that of War- rington, which is over 22. The fumes of .the chemical works are a foe to comfort, and they are injurious to vegetation; but they do not appear to have any great effect upon the mortality of the town.

Here is a suggestive item :—" Mr. C. Price, the county coioner, stated at an inquiry on Monday evening, at Salford, into the death of a child, that since the 2nd December last he had held 38 in- quests in which children had been found dead in bed, most of whom had been suffocated." Query: Have the parents in any case been proceeded against for criminal negligence? And, if not, why not?

It does sometimes happen that the sea can be seen from the promenade at SoLithport, without the aid of a telescOpe. There was a tidy tide on Tuesday, which went straight up to the men who were at work on the new lake, on the north shore, and drove them away. There is hope that when that lake is finished it will, be filled with water; and, with a lake and gardens on each side of the pier, Southport will be "just lovely."

Professor Lippman of Paris has at last succeeded in photographing in colours: This does not mean that any colour in any object can be reproduced; the experiments are confined at present to photo- graphing a brilliant solar spectrum, and a bright painted glass window. But a beginning has been made, and the result is deemed of sufficient im- portance to be communicated to the French Ac- ademy of Sciences.

The Emperor William's example is having effect —Kings are "coming to." His Majesty of Bel- gium actually, on Monday, received a number of delegates of the Council of Industry. He talked like an ordinary mortal, referred to his limited powers under the constitution, and promised to do all he could to help them. Really, if this sort of thing spreads, Labour may take heart of grace with a faith renewed in "the good time coming."

On Thursday evening in Wycliffe Church, War- rington, the Rev. John Yonge gave the last of the present series of lectures on the struggles and progress of Nonconformity. They have been highly appreciated, and, as they have been admirably pre- pared, they have served their purpose in stimul at - ing that love of liberty which, like hope, springs eternal in the human breast. Mr. Yonge has now commenced to deliver the lectures at Lymm and at Frodsham.

The Duke of Westminister has been expressing himself as in favour of' restricting the sale of intoxicating liquor not only on Sunday but on other days. He is an influential man, and he has a way of his own in enforcing his views. As his leases have fallen in, he has "reduced the number of licensed houses on his estate from forty-five to eight." Very good; but why shouldn't the com- munity be empowered to do a good thing as well as the Duke of Westminster. ?

In his letter to Mr. O'Brien breaking off negotiations, Mr. Parnell says :—" The seal of confidence which covers what passed between us renders it impossible to invite the public judgment upon it at the present time." This regard for "the seal of confidence" is very, very 'pretty as coming from the man who has outraged the nation by his violation of a confidential interview with the most eminent statesman of the age. We shall have him next posing as a model of honour and virtue in public and private life I

Judging from a letter which Canon Dodd has sent to the Runcorn Rural Sanitary Authority, he seems to be having a very hard time of it with an old cottage and with an old woman who occupies that cottage. He has been ordered to repair the dwelling, but the prolonged frost has added to the difficulties of the situation. It is a part of the endowment of his living, so he cannot, as he would like, pull the place down and cart it away. "The Sorrows of Werther " are as nothing to the sorrows 1 of the Stretton parson.

Mr. Spurgeon as back to the Tabernacle, on Sunday, 'like a giant refreshed with new wine," after his three months' holiday. He talked of "crashing like thunderbolts through every diffil culty," and " giving God no rest," which is hardly fair considering the long rest which the preacher has himself enjoyed. The steam is evidently up, and he means to go ahead—until the next break down. His sermon abounded in good things, and he fired off a hard-hitting epigram when he said "nothing did sleep so soundly as a church, especially after a revival."

Like those of the "Heathen Chinee," the ways of the magistrates of the Warrington Bench are peculiar. John Mullins was con- victed, on Monday, of the' chat() of A ex- posing his child George .so as to endanger his health." He was told that he had rendered himself Habib to three months' imprisonment; it was shown that he was "a bad lot," having been fined for "drunkenness, assaults, and theft," and yet the magistrates announced thai "they had decided to dismiss the case that morning." It was very hard on the morning. Oh,for a stipendiary!

div.head: ACCIDENT AT WIDNES.
div.p: ACCIDENT AT WIDNES.

Whilst following his employment at the works of Messrs.. Gaskell, Deacon, and Co., on Sunday, James Vineret, of Cross-st., fell from a plank, and fractured his leg. He is progressing favourably at the Accident Hospital. UNIVERSITY EXTENSION LECTURES AT RUNCORN. '

The third of 'a series of lectures on' The growth of the political systems of Europe" was delivered by Mr. H. J. Mackinder, M.A., Bethesda Lecture Hall, on Friday even- ing. The subject was" The Romans," and was profusely illustrated with lime light views. UMRELLAS RE-COVERED at the shortest notice.—J. &W. DUTTON'S, San key-st., Warrington.—Advt.

div.head: TENNESSEE MINSTRELS AT RUNCORN.
div.p: TENNESSEE MINSTRELS AT RUNCORN.

With the object of aiding the funds of the Catholic Schools at Weston, the Tennessee Minstrels of Liverpool gave an entertainment in the Public Hall on Wednesday evening. There was a good audience and the entertain- ment was of a very diverting character. PREMIER SAFETIES. Cash or Hire.—Garland, Warrington. —Advt. _
WIDNES IRISH NATIONAL LEAGUE.

The weekly meeting was held on Sunday afternoon, under the presidency of Mr. P. Whelan. A statement of accounts for the past six months was submitted and con- sidered satisfactory. The meeting for the selection of candidates to contest the Local Board election was post- poned. , ST. AMBROSE CRIIRCMVIDNES.

In aid of the Church Pastoral Aid Society, special ser- mons were preached in St. Ambrose's Church, Widnes, on Sunday. The Rev. G. Lakeman, M.A., of St. Helens, occupied the pulpit in the morning and the Rev. Dr. Preston in the evening. There was a good attendance at each service. GOSPEL UNION MISSION RUNCORN.

In aid of the mission an entertainment was given on Saturday evening, by the Weston Point Band of Hope. A programme of songs, dialogues, and recitations was gone through in good style, and the members were cor- dially thanked at the conclusion of the entertainment. Mr. Thomas Cooke presided.

div.head: RUNCORN -CONSERVATIVE PLUI3 BALL.
div.p: RUNCORN -CONSERVATIVE PLUI3 BALL.

The first ball in connection with the Conservative Club was held on Friday night last week, when about 150 ladies and gentlemen were present. The room had been gaily decorated with flags by Mr. R. Abel. Mr. J. J. W. Potter was the M.C., and the music was supplied by Mr. Wood's Quadrille Band.

UMBRELLAS RE-COVERED at the shortest notiee.—J. & W. DUTTON'S Sankey-st., Warrington.—Advt. ROBBERY FROM THE PERSON AT WIDNES. Yesterday at Widnes Police Court, Mary Jane Reilley, of Nelson-st., was committed to the Quarter Session on a charge of stealing 325. from the person of Roger Powell, captain of the schooner Richard Cobden, which is at present lying in West Bank Dock. The prosecutor had been drinking with the woman who is a well-known character.
BissixETTEs.—J. S. Garland, Ironmonger, 51, Bridge-at., Warrington.—Advt. RUNCORN BRICKLAYERS' SOCIETY.

The annual supper of the Runcorn Branch of the Bricklayers' Society was held at Wilson's Hotel, on Thursday evening when about 40 persons were present. Mr. James Wilson occupied the chair. The toast of suc- cess to the Bricklayers' Society was proposed by Mr. Walter Joinson, and Mr. William Ashley, of Halton, res- ponded. A musical entertainment was provided by Mr. J. Ravenscroft and Mr. Jas. Wood, junr. RUNCORN BURIAL BOARD,

The monthly meeting was held on Wednesday under the presidency of Mr. S. Taylor. The monthly report stated that the interments for ten months ending Janu- ary 25th numbered 407, last year 332 ; increase 75. The fees received during the same Period amounted to £373 6s. 4d. last year £3OO ; increase £73 6s. 4d. The Fin- ance Committee recommended the payment of accounts amounting to £3. BRIMLAS E-COVERED at the shortest notice.—J. &W, DUTTON'S Sankey-st., Warrington.—Advt. ST. PAUL'S CHAPEL, RUNCORN.

In our advertising colums will be found an announce- ment of special services to be held in St. Paul's chapel to-morrow (Sunday) when the pulpit will be occupied by the Rev. Marshall Randles, of Didsbury College. On Monday afternoon the Rev. T.Champness, 'Joyful News," preach, and in the evening a pulpit meeting will be addressed by Mr. Champness Sister Josephine, and Rev. Pulford Williams.

div.head: BETHESDA CONCREGATIONAL GUILD.
div.p: BETHESDA CONCREGATIONAL GUILD.

Under the Auspices of this Guild,the Rev. S. B. Handley' of Stafford, on Monday evening delivered a lecture entitled "A holiday trip through Belgium and up the Rhine." The large audience which had assembled, were treated to an interesting and entertaining account of Mr. Handley's Continental travls,and his descriptions of the charming sceneryof the Rhine were enhanced by the exhibition of a number of photographic views by means of the lime-light. Mr. W. H. Handley was the exhibitor. The chair was occupied by the Rev. John Simpson, and on his proposition a hearty vote of thanks was passed to the Lecturer.

div.head: RUNCORN VOLUNTEER BAND.
div.p: RUNCORN VOLUNTEER BAND.

Full particulars of a concert and ball to be held in the Public Hall on Monday evening, will be found in our advertising columns. The affair has been organised by the members of the Volunteer Band, with the object of raising the funds to purchase aset of first-class instru- ments of which the band is much in need.—The band has been in existence for forty years, and has been con- nected with the volunteer movement since the establish- ment of the Runcorn corps to which it has been of great assistance and benefit. There are several members of considerable individual merit and as a whole the band is a credit to the town. It is to be hoped the public will attend the concert in large numbers, and this aid in obtaining the £6O to £BO which is required.

div.head: WIDNES FREE LIBRARY COMMITTEE.
div.p: WIDNES FREE LIBRARY COMMITTEE.

The monthly meeting was held on Wednesday under the presidency of Mr. H. Wade Deacon, and there were present Messrs. Pankhurst, Lee, Midwood, Brookes, S. Robinson, J. T. Allen (clerk.) Accounts amounting to £99 Ils, were passed for payment. It was resolved that a map of Lancashire be purchased from Messrs. J. W. Deacon and Company. The, sub-committee appointed to consider the question of providing atn additional room for boys to the reading room recommended that a tem- porary room adjoining the reading room be provided, and this recommendation was adopted. It was decided to purchase books to the amount of £7O. The Clerk (Mr. Allen), presented a statement showing an estimated ex- penditure of £450 for the ensuing year, ending March 25th 1892. The Librarian reported that during January the daily average number of visitors to the reading room was 493 last year 512. The number of books issued was 5,030, being an increase of 75 in the lending 'department and 13 in the reference department. The receipts amounted to £4 Is. 11d.
PEESONAL REMINISCENCES IN EGYPT.

At the invitation of the Brunswick Mutual Improvement Society, Mrs. Robert Garnett, of Penketh, delivered a lecture at Runcorn, on Wednesday evening, in the Wesleyan schoolroom, which was crowded with an appre- ciative audience. The title of the lecture was "Personal reminiscences of travels in Egypt," and Mrs. Garnett in a chatty style, which occasionally rose to eloquence, des- cribed the scenery, the people, and their customs, and her remarks were illustrated by \numerous views, thrown on a screen by means of a lantern manipulated by the Rev. Mr. Meek, of Widnes. There were also displayed for in- spection a number of curios, and on the stage were several ladies and gentlemen attired in the picturesque costumes of Egypt. The Rev. Dr. Preston occupied the chair, and, as a traveller in Egypt, testified to the fidelity of Mrs. Garnett's descriptions. The usual votes of thanks were passed.

THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY FEBRUARY 14 1891. I DEATH AND FUNERAL OF MR. A. CAMERON OF RUNCORN. The announcement of the death of Mr. Alexander Cameron, on Tuesday, was received on all hands with expressions of regret. For many years he had suffered from diabetes,but he had followed his occu- pation uninterruptedly, and it was not until a fort- 'slight age that he became unable to carry out his duties under the VI, late Star Line. His strength sank rapidly towards the finish,and his death,wiiich took place on Tuesday morning, came as a shock to his family and friends. Mr. Cameron was the son of the late Mr. R. Cameron, chemical manure manu- facturer, of Halton, and he is brother of Captain Cameron of the Germanic and of Mr. Robert Camer- on, the well known bicyclist, who for many years Was President of the West Lancashire Bicycle Club. The deceased gentleman, who had only attained the age of 38, ears, was in his early life, traveller for a commercial ['use, but he had a strong inclination for the sea, and ten years ago became a purser on board one of the West India and Pacific Steamship Company's Vessels. Wtlile in this sir- vice he had an attack of yellow fever, and there is no doubt this dread disease undermined his con- stitution. He then became connected with the , famous White Star line of steamers, and only on the day previous to his death he was apuointed chief purser on board the Majestic, the Cortrodore boat of the fleet. He was held in the highest esteem by his employers, and he was a great favourite with the passengers fot his kind, genial, and bright nature; and from all parts of the country his widow has received letters of condolence with her in her great grief. Mr. Cameron married a sister of Mr. James llandley, of Garston,*and he has left his widow and four daughters to mourn his loss. THE FUNEIZAL. took place yesterday afternoon at Bethesda Chapel, and the processien left -the deceased late residence in Green- way-road shortly, after three. Preceding the hearse there walked several officers representing the White Star Line, and Captain Jarvis and Cant. I. Jarvis, and Messrs. J.Bell and R. H. Bell all of Garston. There were also a number of local tradesmen &c.including Messrs. F. Beck, J. Bate, B. W. Jukes, J. Slade, J. R. Frith, W. H. Chadwick, R. Pierpoint, J. Unsworth, H. W. Jukes, A. Lightburn, H. Chadwick, S. Walton, F. Scott, W. Littler, S. Viratsm &c. Following the hearse were five coaches. In the first were the Revs. S. B. Handley; J. Simpson, and T. Cole and Dr. Gemmell : 2nl Captain Cameron R.N.R. and Mr. Robert Cameron (Fludderstield) Mr. Mc.Kerrow and Mr. Kinna : 3rd Messrs. W. Handley, J. Handley. J. P. and T. Handley: 4th Messrs. G. F. Handley, H. W. Handley, T. B. Handley, and A. Handley: sth: Messrs. C. Handley, F. J. McCarraher, F. Whalley, and J. Rhodes. En route to the chapel the windows of the dwellings and of the tradesmen's places of business were darkened as a tribute of respect to the memory of the deceased. The Rev. J. Simpson having read the funeral service, the Rev. S. B. Handley, of Stafford, brother-in-law of the deceased, delivered an oration ever the body, in which he paid a tribute to the character and abilities of Mr. Cameron. Mr. Humphreys then played the Dead March in Saul, and the coffin was borne into the grave yard and deposited in its last resting place, the conclusion of the service beinc, read by the Rev. J. Simpson. The coffin we hidden 'beneath a number of floral tributes. The duties of undertaker were carried out by Mr. James Kirkham, and Messrs. Yarwood Bros. supplied the hearse and coaches. •

- THE GYMNASTIC COMPETITION. The champion team of the Warrington Gymna- sium will to-day meet a team of the picked athletes of the Liverpool Gymnasium, in the competition for the shield of the National Physical Recreation Society. The contest takes place at the Myrtle-st. Gymnasium, Liverpool. It is understood that both teams are in the best of condition, and as they met last year in the final, it may be expected that a close and exciting contest will take place. EXTRAORDINARY DROWNING CASE. On Wednesday evening an extraordinary drown- ing case occurred at Lowton. It appears that Elizabeth Leather, aged 73, widowed farmer, occu- pied Fair House Farm, Lowton, and resided with her sons. About five o'clock she left the house in the absence of her sons, a,nd was not seen again until nearly nine o'clock, when her dead body was found in a pond adjoining the house. No reason whatever can be assigned for the rash act, which has caused excitement in the village, where she was well-known and greatly respected. EMIORATION.—Intending emigrants to New York, Boston. Philadelphia, San Francisco, Canada, China, Japan, Aus- tralia, or New Zt-alard, should take tickets (lowest rates) at the " Examiner" Office, by Cunard, Guion. American, and other lines.— John Walker, agent, "Examiner' Office, Bewsey-et.. Warrington.—Advt. A GOLDEN WEDDING AT WARRINGTON.

_ Mr. Thomas Royle, of Dial-st., Warrington, cele- brated his golden wedding on Sunday, he having been married on February Bth, 1841. Mr. and Mrs. Royle have brought up a large family, some of whom were present on Sunday, with a goodly num- ber of grandchildren. Their son William, with his wife and family, had made ample provision for the old couple to enjoy themselves on their Jubilee day, and Mr. Royle said, in reply to the toast of their good health, that he had not only been married 50 years, but he had been a member of the Oddfellows, M.U., over 50 years, having joined the Order in September, 1840. UMBRELLAS RE-COVERED at the shortest notice.—J. &W. BUTTONS Saukey-it., Warrington.—Adrt.

THE SUDDEN DEATH IN A PUBLIC HOUSE. "Truth "has the following comment on a recent Warrington case, but falls into the error of treating it as a Liverpool incident :—" I cordially agree with the remarks made by Mr. Husband, the deputy- coroner for South-West Lancashire, that the prac- tice of publicans insuring the lives of their customers cannot be too strongly deprecated. It appears that it is not an unusual thing amongst certain publicans of Liverpool for them to insure the life of some irredeemably confirmed- toper, whether customer or employe, and then cause the policy to be assigned to themselves. At least this was proved to be the case when Mr. Husband held an inquest upon one Rohan, who had been allowed to take up his residence in a Liverpool public-house, and passed his time in doing odd jobs, varied by bouts of drinking, since upon Rohan's death from delirium tremens it was discovered that his master, the landlord, held a policy for £lB effected upon his life. . UMBRELLAS RE-COVERED at the shortest &W. DUTTON'S Sankey-st., Warrington.—Advt. WIDNES SCIEN CE AND ART SCHOOL.

div.head: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIA.NS.
div.p: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIA.NS.

The fortnightly meeting of the Prescot Board of Guardians was held at the Union Workhouse, Whiston, on Thursday afternoon, when there were present Major .T. Wareing (in the chair), Rev. S. A. K. Sylvester, Rev. Dean Finegan,Messrs. W. Tyrer, C. B. Johnson, Marsh, J. Birchall, (*roves, Lowe, Davies, Peover, Jas. Burchall, Ranson, Kenwright, Ellison, Mercer, Syder, and S. H. Hartley (clerk). Tim DIVISION OF WIDNES DISTRICT. - The Clerk reported that he had received a communication from the Local Government Board asking for details in regard to the proposed re-arrangement of the Widnes relief district. He added that he was forwarding the information desired.—The Chairman said they might be a set of puppets and knew nothing judging by the questions they were asked. (A laugh.)

„. • THE WORKHOUSE FIRE EXTINGUISHING APPLIANCES.— The Clerk stated that a letter had been received from the Liverpool, London and Globe Insurance Company, intimating that owing to the precautions taken to pre- vent the outbreak of fires at the workouse and the means at hand for subduing fires the directors had decided to make an allowance of 10 per cent. on the renewal pre- mium. A cheque for £32s. 10d. was enclosed. Courry RECEIPTS.—The Clerk stated that he had received a precept from the County Council for the payment of £3,943 ss. 6d. before the 24th March.—The Chairman asked how the Guardians were going to raise that amount.—The Clerk said he had allowed for it in the estimate. _ . .

..... ESTIMATE or EXPENDITURE.—The Clerk submitted the following estimate of expenditure for the ensuing year. In maintenance, £2,500; children in schools, &c., £1,200 ; out relief, £7,000 ; lunatics in asylums, £2,500; instalment of loan, £420 ; interest, £440 ; salaries, £2,500 ; Workhouse officers' rations, £3lO ; Assessment Committee's expenses, £250; school fees, £640 ; vaccin- ation expenses, £260; registration expenses, £2O; esz tablishment expenses, £1,900 ; county . rate, contingencies, £2,272 ; total, £25,028, as compared with £24,754 the actual expenditure of the corresponding period in 1890.—The estimate was adopted. THE GOVERNAIL:NT INSPECTOR .—TIIO Clerk reported that a printed copy of the report of Mr. Henley, the Government poor-law inspector, on the pauperism of the county had been forwarded to each member of the Board.—The Chairman did not agree With some of the observations of the inspector, and said lie thought he could demonstrate that be was totally wrong in regard to the Prescot out-relief districts as compared with others.—The Rev. Dean Finegan remarked that those , Guardians who sat on the Widnes Relief Committee were very much astonished and pained to read the remarks. The severe winter seemed to have swept off a number of men who had left widows and children helpless, and he did not see what was to be done except what they had done.—The Chairman remarked that they might sonic day have an opportunity of ventilating the subject. THE LIVERPOOL INFramA.lty.—The hon: treasurer of the Liverpool Royal Infirmary wrote askinc, for an , increased subscription from the Guardians. He pointed , out that during, the last year 10 patients were sent frem the Union and were in the hospital for 264 days. Two of the patients were also sent to the Convalescent Hospital. The Boards contribution to the Infirmary funds was far short of meeting the expenses of the patients sent from the Prescot Union. On the motion of Mr. James Burchall seconded by Mr. Lowe it was resolved that the annual subscription be increased from five guineas to twenty guineas per annum. THE WIDNES RELIEVING OFFICERS. —The Guardians representing Widnes district were appointed a sub-com- mittee to arrange for suitable effice accornodation and a safe for the Widnes relieving officers. This was all the business.

PARR'S BANKING COMPANY, LIMITED. Yesterday an extraordinary general meeting of this Company was held at the Bank Premises, War- rington. Mr. J. C. Parr presided, and the other directors present were Colonel Gamble, Messrs. N. Eckersley, P. Stubs, E. Greenall, A. Turner, and C. F 4 Parr. There was only a small attendance of shareholders. The meetinovas called for confirming, or otherwise,the following special resolution which had been passed at a meeting held on the 23rd Jan viz :—`• That the articles of association of the Com- pany be altered by the insertion therein of the following article, namely:—No. 114 A.—The eividend extraordinary dividend, or bonus payable upon shares in respect of which any person is, under the Company's articles relating to the transfer and transmission of shares, entitled to become a mem- ber, or which any person under those articles is entitled to transfer, shall, unless the directors in their uncontrolled discretion otherwise appoint, be retained until such person shall become a member in respect of such shares, or hall duly transfer the same, and every transfer of such shares shall carry with it all dividends, extraordinary dividends, or bonuses which may have been retained as herein ptovided."—On the motion of the Chairman, seconded by Mr. Eckersley, the resolution was con- firmed. Members of the Provident Association of London Limited should apply to Jonn Podmore. Bewsey Chambers, for ticket for admission to the local ballot to be held in the coming week.—Advt.

div.head: ANNUAL DISTRIBUTION OF PRIZES
div.p: ANNUAL DISTRIBUTION OF PRIZES

The annual meeting and distribution of prizes, took place on Monday evening in the Baths Assembly Room. There was a numerous company present. Mr. F. 11. Go§sage presided and he was supported by the Rev. Chapman, Messrs. Alder- man Muspratt, J.P., C.C., T. Snape, C.C., H. Wade Deacon, J.P., J. Brock, J.P., E. Carry, D. Wright, J. Morrison, F. J. Poole, V. C. Driffiela, J. Showan, J. T. Allen, J. S. Sinclair, P. Cook, and Dr. O'Keefe. The Chairman, in his opening remarks, pointed out that the classes would in future be carried on by the Local Board and afterwards by the Corporation, if the town "was incorporated, and he hoped they would in the future be carried on as successfully as, or more suc- cessfully than they had been in the past. (Loud applause.) The Secretary (Mr. .T. Morrison) prescnted the 16th annual report which stated that the classes continued to be well attended. During the year 38 students were under instruction in art, and 176 in science; 139 students , presented themselves at the Government examinations, with the following result :
Exam- Per- ined. Passed. cent.

Art Plane and Solid uteometry Machine Construction Building Construction Sound Light. and Heat. - ll Inorganic Chemistry (Theoretical) ... 45 Inorganic Chemistry (Practical • 24 i This s the first year of Mr. Angell's connection with the school, and the Committee congratulated him on the suc- cess of the students under his instruction. (Applauge.) Mrs. Brock then distributed the prizes to the success- ful students, a list of which has previously appeared in this journal. Mr. Alderman Muspratt said it was his pleasing duty to move a vote of thanks to the Committee for conduct- ing the classes during the past year. They knew how the classess had been conducted during the last sixteen years. On the whole, they had been successful, but they must accord a great deal of praise to the masters for the , success of the students. At the same time the classes could not have been so successful but for the labours of the Committee ; and of the members of the Committee he would like to single out Mr. Morrison, who had been the heart and soul of the Committee itself. He noticed that a great portion of the students had taken up chemistry, but he pointed out that the indu4try of Widnes was not dependent upon chemistry alone, but upon engineering and building and maid-line cOn- struction, and he was sorry to see that those classes were not as well attended as the chemistry classes. The Government had at last becre aware of the impor- tance of technical education to the welfare of this coun- try and the community at large. They had passed during the last two years two measures which enabled them to anticipate a very great development in technical educa- tictn. They in Widnes would obtain a portion of certain money from the County Council, after the Special Corn-' mittee, of which their friend Mr. Snape was the chair- man, had fully dealt with the matter. He looked for- , ward to a great development of the chemical industry in this country. The United Alkali Company, which had just been formed, would not lose sight of it; in fact, they had already appointed Dr. Hurter, manager of the chemical laboratory, to investigate all new processes, and see where the manufacture of articles could be improved. They could not have men too well trained for their work. He asked them to see that they had a good return for the money spent on those classes, in helping on primary and secondary education. (Ap- plause.) Mr. Thomas Snape seconded the resolution, and said referring to the £5,000 applied for by the Widnes Local Board, that was one-eighth of the sum to be handed over to the county by the Government, and as more than 100 applications had been received, he did not think they would be successful in getting the full amount applied for. Referring to the need of students in the subjects allied to the chemical industry, he said the great progress in the chemical trade had not been by the dis- covery of chemical principles, but the application of those principles which were in the laboratory long before. He urged upon all the young people to take advantage of the sch•ol, in order that their own lives might be filled with prosperity, and that the town of Widnes might be a centiT of light and leading to the county and country at large. (Applause.) The motion was carried unanimously by acclamation. The Chairman, after acknowledging the vote. crncluded by moving a vote of thanks to Mrs. Brock for kindly distributing the prizes. Mr. H. Wade-Deacon, 3.P., seconded the motion. Mr. J. Brock, J.P., in responding on behalf of Mrs. Brock, emphasized all that had been said by Mr. Muspratt and Mr. Snape with regard to the study of mathematics and building construction, with the present subjects now being taught.

div.head: CORRECTION.
div.p: A CORRECTION.

In our report last week of the meeting of the Town Council we gave Councillor Bolton's name amongst those who voted both for andoagainst an amendment on the Sanitar*Committee's minutes. This, of course, was a mistake—Councillor Bolton only voted for the amendment. JOURNALISTS' MEETING. The annual meeting of the Warrington. sub-dis- trict of the National -Institute of Journalists, was held on Wednesday evening, Mr. W. Gill presiding.. The report submitted by the Secretary (Mr. Iteid) showed an increased membership, and was other- wise of a favourable nature. All the officers were re-elected.

THE THEATRICAL PERFORMANCES AT LATCHFORD. The statement of accounts in connection 'with the recent amateur dramatic performances at the Parish Room, Latchford, shows that the gross rec3ipts were £4O is. 11d., and the expenditure £27 Os. 11d., leaving a balance of £l2 12s. to be handed over to the day schools, in behali of which the per- formances were given.

div.head: ELECTIVE AUDITORS.
div.p: ELECTIVE AUDITORS.

Tne letion ot two elective auditors for Warring- ton will take place on the 2nd March. The retiring auditors—Mr. J. Harrison, of Egypt-st., and Mr. J. Bolton, IVilderspool Causeway—have been re-no- minated, Mr. Hrrrison by Councillor J. Shaw Green, seconded by Mr. J. S. Garland, and Mr. Bolton by Mr. John White, seconded by Mr. W. Sharpe.

div.head: MORE MAGISTERIAL REMISSNESS,
div.p: MORE MAGISTERIAL REMISSNESS,

At the Warrington Borough Police Court, on Tuesday morning, at ten o'clock, the hour for com- mencing the business, only Mr. R. Garnett was present; and at. ten minutes past, no other magis- trate having arrived,officers were sent to obtain one. The result was that at 25 minutes past ten Alder- man Holmes joined Mr. Garnett on the bench,but on other magistrate made his appearance.

div.head: SOIREE AT THE CO-OPERATIVE HALL.
div.p: SOIREE AT THE CO-OPERATIVE HALL.

Miss Praeger's soiree in connection with her class was held in the Co-operative Hall, on Wednesday evening, when there wereoo couples in attendance. The platform was decorated with plants, fairy lamps, &c., which had a pretty effect. Great credit is due to ;I.i,SS. Praeger for the manner in which the arrangements were carried out. Mr. 0. J. Praeger supplied the music with his usual ability, and dancing Was kept up with much spirit until two o'clock. _ _

div.head: BUTTEMISIMET-ST. IVESLEYIN MISSION.
div.p: BUTTEMISIMET-ST. IVESLEYIN MISSION.

On Sundayauniversary services were held in this Mission, and were well attended. The preaches were—in the afternoon, the Rev. T. Ross, and in' the evening, Mr. W. Brough. On Monday evening a largely-attended concert was held in the Mission. The programme that was submitted was a varied and excellent one; including performances on the pianoforte, piccolo, and cornet, songs, and readings. All those who took part acquitted themselves in a very creditable manner. FUNERAL SERVICE AT PADGATE.

The funeral sermon of the late Mrs. Antrobus was preached at the Padgate Wesleyan Chapel, on Sun- day morning, by Mr, Elijah Ford. He remarked that the deceased was taught in their Sunday School, and was a member of society, but now she had gone to live with God, which was far better, and their loss was her gain. At the conclusion of the service Miss Bennett, of Bruche-avenue, played the " Dead March" Hi " Saul" on the organ, the congregation standing during the performance.

div.head: POPULAR ENTERTAINMENT AT LATCHFORD.
div.p: POPULAR ENTERTAINMENT AT LATCHFORD.

The last popular entertainment of the season took place in Christ Church Parish-room, on Monday evening. There was a good attendance. The pro- gramme, which was an unusually attractive one, had been left in the hands of Mr. Broadbent and the Misses Broadbent. The various items,. which were of a miscellaneous and interesting nature, were admirably rendered, the following ladies and gentle- men taking part:—The Misses Todhunter, Miss Ethel Heap, Mr. Roper, Mr. Gooch, Mr. Arthur Cros- field, Mr. W. B. Greener, and Mr. Harold Broadbent.

div.head: PRESENTA.TION TO MR. JOSEPH MOUNFIELD.
div.p: PRESENTA.TION TO MR. JOSEPH MOUNFIELD.

As an acknowledgment of fifty years' services in connection with the Brick-st. Sunday School, Mr. Joseph Mounfield, sen., was, on Tuesday even- ing, presented with a very valuable timepiece and two bronze ornaments. Prior to the presentation a tea was held which was well attended, as was also the subsequent meeting. The presentation was made on behalf of the teachers and officers of the school, by Mr. W. Hudson, who referred in complimentary terms to Mr.Mounfield's long and active connection with the school. The timepiece bore a suitable inscription.

div.head: STACKS BURNED Af ARPLEY.
div.p: STACKS BURNED Af ARPLEY.

On Tuesday night, shortly before nine o'clock, some stacks, belonging to Mr. W. Owen, butcher, of Warrington, and situate at Arpley, near Walton Arches, were discovered to he on fire. The. alarm was at once raised, and the Warrington fire brigade, under the superintendence of Mr. Turner, were soon, at the scene of the outbreak. It was found that two stacks were ignited, hut the flames had got' such a hold of one that it was decided that the efforts of the men should be directed to saving the second. A third stack was in close fproxomity but this was entirely saved. The fire continued through- out the night. The outbreak is supposed to be due to incendiarism. The damage which is estimated at about .E2OO, is completely covered by insurance, in the Caledonian Company.

div.head: DOCK STRIKES.
div.p: THE DOCK STRIKES.

The Mersey tugboatinen on strike had a meeting at the Malakoff Hall, Liverpool, on Wednesday night, and de. ciped that, owing to the attitude of the tugowners, they should stand firmly against the propcsed agreement and seek employment elsewhere. _

The dockers in the export sheds at the Roval Albert Docks, London, with few exceptions, struck- vvork on Thursday; but the import men continue at work. Boy- cotted companies are still employing Federation men. All tips and cranes at the Bute Docks, Cardiff, are being worked with the exception of one. Later dispatches say that the dockers on the Shaw Savill and Albion's import steamers have joined the strikers. The Cardiff Trades Council have promised to support the strikers by all the means ia their power, and action is being taken wich view to prohibiting engineers repairing any dock machinery worked by non-unionists. Yesterday the strike at the Liverpool Docks collapsed, the men agreeing to put their Union buttons in their pockets.

div.head: SUICIDE IN A STABLE,
div.p: SUICIDE IN A STABLE,
AFRAID OF BEING HANGED YET HANGS HIMSELF.

On Wednesday afternoon at the Parade Room, Police Court, Warrington, Mr. W. T. Husband, de- puty coroner, held an inquest on the body of James Donaldson, aged 31 years, a native of Airdree. Scot- • land, who was found hanging by the neck, in a stable on Monday last, quite dead. John Kincaid, of 5, Whitfield-street. said he was a rivetter, and came last May with the deceased, who was a rivet- ter's labourer, from Greenock. He identified the body as that of James Donaldson. lie left his work on the 19th of December. lie had been drinking. Witness saw the body on Tuesday, at the Manx Arms, and idontified it as that of James Donaldson. Ann Littlewood, 4, King-street, said the deceased had lodged with her some time. On the 20th September last he went to Wigan, and on the 2nd of November, he not having come back, she found him at the county police office there. He was afraid that a man named Brockett who lodged with her was going to hang him. She had not seen Brockett since a fortnight last Saturday. The deceased was taken to the Wigan Workhouse Hospital, and she brought him home from there last Thursday. She found him rather strange in his talk. He was out of his senses at moments and then rational again. He began that night about Blockett again,saying he had seen him mak- ing a stool and some ropes. About twenty minutes to eleven the next night he went out and did not return. She wired to Wigan in the morning about him, and in- formed a sergeant of police at Warrington. Ellen Has- lam, a girl who worked for her occasionally, sent her little brother to tell witness that Donaldson had hung himself in a stable,and she went and identified the body. —Hannah Oxley, wife of John Oxley, 31, Dd.kin's-yard, deposed that about a quarter to twelve on Monday morning, on account of what her little boy told her, she went to a stable used by her brothers for keeping tools I in, behind the house,and found the deceased there hang- ' ing by a muffler, and she then brought her husband. The deceased had no right to enter the stable.—P.C. Smith deposed to being called to see the body in the stable. The deceased wasin a kneeling position, and must have been dead all night. In witness's opinion the case was one of determined suicide.—The Coroner having addressed the jury, they immediately returned a verdict that deceased hullo. himself whilst in an unsound state of mincl. • b

The congregational tea meeting and conversazione in connection with St. Barnabas' Church was held in the schoolroom on Tuesday evening. There were 'about 150 present for tea, but at the after meeting there was a much larger attendance. The following ladies had charge of the tea tables :—Miss McGhie, Miss It. Allton, Mrs. Looker,_ Mrs. R. Smith, Mrs.
YOUNG MEN'S CHRISTIAN ASSOCIATION.

The first of a series of social meetings in connec- tion with the Warrington Y.M.C.A., was held on Tuesday evening at the Hall, Bold-st. About 70 members and friends were present at tea. The tables were presided over by the Misses Balmford, Barker, N. Barker, and Harrison. Afterwards an excellent entertainment was given before a large audience, Mr. W. H. Butler being in the chair. Songs were given by the Misses Hislop, Florrie Jones, Sherlock, and Unsworth,and Messrs. Griffiths, Jackson'and Kidd. Messrs. Garland and Sudlow, contributed two pianoforte duets, and Miss Uns- worth a violin solo. Mr. Fogg also gave two recitations and Mr. H. Dntton a reading. Mr. Travis ably accompanied. Mr. Woodier is deserv- ing of credit for having so tastefully decorated the room for the occasion. A hearty vote of thanks was given to the Chairman, and to the ladies and gentlemen who had contributed towards the even- ing's entertainment.

_ Roscoe, Mrs. Woollacot, Miss Steward, Mrs. Platt, Mrs. Evans, and Miss Fanny Smith. After tea, the Vicar, in a short speech, said that last year they did not have their annual tea meeting, but he was de- termined that it should not be missed again, and was pleased when the other attractions were taken into consideration, to see such a large gathering. It was very gratifying to him to think of the kind manner in which the friends throughout the town had helped them. (Applause.) They seemed to be rather fortunate at St. Barnabas', as their friends always helped them when they were in need. He had experienced the greatest kindness ever since he came to the parish, seven years ago. He hoped their work would go on happily and properly during the present year. de wished to thank the subscribers and collectors. Mr. Woollacot had collected over
