div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.

CHARGES OF THEFT AGAINST A 80. At the Borough Police Court yesterday, Michael Law- ler, a boy, son of a carpenter, living at 48, Hardy-st., was charged with stealinc, en Tuesday articles of cloth- ing from the,premises of Frank Connelly and Thomas Worrall, both living in Lythgoe's-tane. There had been several other tlicfts of clothing in the neighbourhood, during the week, and on the application of Chief Con- stable Hunt, the prisoner was remanded till to-day. THEFT AT A LODGING-HOUSE.

At the Borough Police Court on Tuesday morning, John M'Dermott,was charged with stealing, about six 'o'clock the previous morning, at the lodging-house of Wm. Preston,Bank-st.,a quantity of pork sausages and bread, value 10d., the property of James Tobin, a Ship Canal lahourer,lodging, there. The prosecutor left the provisions on a shelf, and the prisoner was seen to eat part of them and put the rest in his pocket. The complainant missed his breakfast and got up. and went out to look for the prisoner, losing his breakfast and most of his day's wages, in consequence. The prosecutor told tbe magistrates he did not wish the man to be punished; and Mr. Preston said prisoner had lodged with him 12 months, and had never committed a theft there before. The Bench sent him to prison for seven days' hard labour. CHARGE OF RUFFIANLY ASSAULT BY A NAVVY. At the Warrington Borough Police Court on Monday, James White, a navvy, employed at Latchford on the ship canal, and a native of Leicestershire, was summoned on a charge of assaulting Thomas Kelly, employed in the same section of the ship canal, and lodging with the defendant at the model lodging-house in Old road. Chief- Constable Hunt said that about half-past 9 on Saturday, night the complainant, accompanied by a fellow-work- man, went to the Packet House beerhouse and had a glass or two of beer. He left at 10 o'clock, accompanied by Joseph Starkey, and they were proceeding down the Old road when they were met by the prisoner, who was accompanied by James Leitch. The prisoner without a word struck Starkey a violent blow in the mouth and felled him to the ground. He said" What did you do that for "? and the prisener replied with an oath that he would serve the other man the same. He then felled Kelly and kicked him in the ribs and in other places. He had a belt (produced) wrapped round his hand at the time. The complainant had to be taken to the Infirmary, and lay there unconscious from Saturday night to Sun- day night. The prisoner was apprehended at the lodg- ing house.—Joseph Starkey and Catherine Knockton, gave evidence corroborative of Mr. Hunt's statement, and the prisoner was remanded for a week, to admit of the complainant appearing. SHAMEFUL NEGLECT OF A CHILD. John Mullen was charged that he on the night of the , 31st ult., exposed his child George Mullen, aged 8 years, ' so as to cause unnecessary suffering and danger to his Amsen said on Saturday week about mid- night, he was in the Market place, and saw the boy in the street, with-obt hat, shirt, shoes or stockings. He was at a potato stove picking up chip potatoes. Witness got hold of him and asked him what he was doing, and he said he was looking for his brother. Witness sent him home with a man. The night was .cold and wet. Chief- Constable Hunt said ,the boy was out half-starved and almost naked, having nothing on but his trousers and braces, and for him to be out like this at a quarter to twelve at night as he was, really amounted to criminal neglect.—The defendant said it was no fault of his: the boy was put to bed with his brother and sister at 6 o'clock, and after being in bed about two hours got up to go to the back, and he went out in the streets with his feet bare and no shirt on, having no change of shirt as witness had had so very little work of late.—The Chief-Constable said the family of the defendant was one Of those the Mayor had caused enquiries to be made about, after the children had been relieved at the spun kitchen, and a very pitiful report had been made as to their con- dition.—The defendant in reply to the Mayor said he was doing a little work at present, and admitted that he took a "drop of drink." He thought when the boy went out that he would come back.—Alderman Harrison: You never troubled yourself about him.—The bench dismissed the case, but the Mayor t, admonished the defendant strongly, and cautioned him as to the result if his children were found in the streets again.—Alderman ,utton said this was the prisoner's 26th appearance and in Septeniber last he was brought up for allowing his son William, aged 7, to be exposed.

div.head: MINOR CASES.
div.p: MINOR CASES.

WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. MONDAY.—Before the Mayor (Mr. R. W. Francomb) In the chair, and Aldermen Harrison and Sutton. FIGHTING.—John Cußerton, militiaman, was brought up under a warrant charged with fighting in Dial-st., on the 20th of April last, and was bound over to keep the peace for six months.—This was his Bth appearance for fighting—Tim Collins, for fighting in Bridge-st., on the 2nd inst. was bound over to keep the peace for 6 months, and mulcted in the costs. Dnumc AND DISORDERLY.—Thomas Taylor, labourer, Silver-st., was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Winwick street, on Saturday night last, with assault- Ing P.C. Clough on the same occasion, also with being drunk and disorderly on the 13th of July, 1889. He was sent to jail for a month. Ralph Taylor, Silver.st., and Patrick Burke, 3, Old Gardens, were charged with being drunk and disorderly in Winwick street on Saturday night. Burke was also charged with assaulting P.C.120, Cooper, and P.C. Corcoran atthe same time and place. Prisoners were each sent to jail for a month. Samuel Dag.nall. hawker, drunk and disorderly in Winwick-st., on Saturday night, was dismissed, he being a youth and this being his first offence.—Ellen Burke (14th appear- ance), lodging-house keeper, drunk and disorderly. on Monday night, in Dial-st., was fined 10s. and costs, or 14 days, and Patrick Burke, her husband, was fined ss. and costs or 7 days for the like offence on the 31st ult. John Lawton, forgeman, and James Griffin, hawker, drunk and disorderly in Winwick st., were fined—the former ss. and costs,and the latter 10s. and costs.—Joseph Bate, drunk and disorderly in Rose yard, on Sunday night, was dismissed. DISORDERLY END REFUSING TO QUlT.—Michael Melia was charged with being disorderly and refusing to quit the Packet House beerhouse on being requested to do so. Mr. Browne appeared for the prosecution' and said he obtained an adjournment of the case on Friday—when the defendant appeared to the summons—because there were two other cases to be brought forward arising out of the same circumstances. The defendant di not now appear and he would ask for a warrant for his apprehen- sion. It appeared that the defendant went to the beerhouse on Tuesday last and asked for some beer, the daughter of the landlord, Mr. Monks, being in the bar. By the in- structions of her father, who was at Stockton Heath,she refused to serve him. He used filthy language, and she told him he had better go out, and he used an objec- tionable expression to her. Frederick Shaw, who hap- pened to be in the house, told him that for doing so he deesrved ducking in the river.and at Mrs. Monks's request put him out. Melia struck him and got hold of him by the) muffler, so that Shaw had to strike him again to prevent himself being strangled.—A warrant was granted for Melia's apprehension.—Frederick Shaw wes then charged with fighting in fighting in Mersey-street, on Tuesday. Mr. Brown said he was instructed by Mr. Monks to say that Shaw was simply interfering on his behalf. The defendant was dismissei. CREATING A NCrISANCM.—John Stokes and James Jones, charged by Mr. Norman. inspector of nuisances, with allowing nuisances to exist in certain outbuildings, were fined is. costs each. - - —. . _
-„—. ASSAULT.—Martin Harvey, for assaulting Patrick Kil- duff in Friar's Gate, on Saturday night, was bound over in the sum of £lO to keep the peace for six months; in default a month's hard labour.

DRUNK IN CHARGE OF A TRAP.—George Lang, sen., was summoned for being drunk in charge of a horse and trap at Bridge Foot, on the night of the 30th ult. The officer who proved the case said the defendant was.driv- ing three gentlemen to Frodsham, and he had a collision and the shafts were broken. He was flied ss. and costs. FURIOUS DRIVING.—Joseph Whittle, for furiously driving a horse and spring cart in Bank-street, on the night of the 2nd inst., was fined 2s. 6d. and costs. ALLOWING A CART TO STAND.—Aaron Brimelow, charged with allowing his cart to stand longer than neces- sary in Golden Grove-road, on the 31st ult., was dis- missed with a caution.
CHIMNEYS ON FlRE.—James Birchall and Louisa Lomax for having their chimneys on fire were fined is. and coats each,
TUESDAY.—Before Mr. R. Garnett (chairman) and Mr. Alderman Holmes.

SCHOOL OFFICER'S PROSECUTIONS.—The following con- victions were obtained by Mr. G. Riley, school attend- ance officer :—William France, foygeman, Watkin-st., 2s. 6d. fine; (the defendant in this case lives near the school her child attends; and Mr. Riley remarked that he always found that the nearer the school the worse the attendance).—James Hayes, forgeman, 9 Buckley Court, ss.—John Glynn, forgeman, Silver-st., ls.—Thomas Berry, labourer, Haydock-st., 55.—During the hearing of the last-mentioned case Chief Constable Hunt said it was customary to bring these people up on Tuesday on which day they were not prepared,.to pay, though they would be better prepared on Monaay. When they could not pay at once they were allowed till Saturday, and they would come down and pay two or three shillings at a time'. Time went on and they were fined repeatedly, and he had to send Constable Chantler to collect these fines. The magistrates had no idea of the trouble the police had in collecting these sums, and he was quite sure the legislature never intended that the police should go round collecting this money. It would be much better if a penalty were nut on, and enforced in case of non- payment. —The Chairman said the fines were im- posed with the alternative of 7 dais' imprisonment, and if they were not paid action would be taken without bringing the defaulters before the magistrates again.— The Chief Constablel-, But in the cases I complain of they are brought up every fortnight; and then they cannot pay the fines accumulated.—Mr. Rileysaid if the penalty were enforced the women would pay rather than let their husbands go to, prison.—The Chairman told Mrs. Berry, the last-named defenglant's wife that if her son did not attend school regular!, in future he would be cer- tainly sent to., the training ship " Clio." George Andrews, labourer, 26, Bciwcoek-st., George Forster, railway plumber, 14-9, Knutsford-road, and Patrick Kil-

martin, Ship Canal labourer, Old-road, were each Ened 2s. 6d., Thomas Allen, labourer, Crossley-st., ss. and John Henry Broughton, news agent, 75. 6d. WEDNESDAY.—Before Alderman Holmes (chairman) and Mr. J. Fairclough. NON-MArrrrENANcs OF A WIFE.—Wm. Patten appre- hended under a warrant, was charged by dr. Basil Shearer, on behalf of the Warrington Board of Guardians, with leaving his wife Ann Patten, chargeable to the Union, from the 17th till the 29th of June, 1889. Mr. Shearer said the expense to the Board, including the cost of the prosecution was 365., and offered to withdraw the case if the prisoner would pay. The prisoner said he could pay so much a week, but some one in court paid the amount down, and the case was withdrawn. CHARGE OF WIFE ASSAULT.—The prisoner Patten was also charged with assaulting and beating his wife on the 4th of March, 1889, but as she did not appear, the case was dismissed. INDECENT BEHAVIOUR.—EIiza Smith, for indecent be- haviour 'in Buttermarket-st., the previous night. was sent to prison for a month. FRlDAY.—Before Mr. John White (chairman), Alder- man Harrison, Dr. Gornall, and Dr. White. _ _

CHARGE AGAINST A CONVICTED THIEF. - Thomas Mitchell, a convicted thief, was charged with being found loitering about the premises of St. James's Church soon after midnight that morning,for an unlawful pur- pose. It appeared that the prisoner had been hanging about the churchyard, and hestated that he merely wanted to have a ‘; lie down" for some hours, as he had been turned out of his lodgings. The case was dismissed. _ _

DIM/B.—Andrew Duffy,' di-unk in John.:St—., early that morning, was fined ss. including Costs. NON-MAINTENANCE OF RELATIVES. —Frederick Hall, publican, of Liverpool, for non-compliance with an order to allow ss. a week for out-door relief to his father, was sent to prison for 14 days.—Michael Logan, of Stamford- st., summoned for leaving his mother chargeable to the Union, was ordered to pay 2s. 6d. a week and costs.— George Jackson, employed at the White Cross Works, was charged I-Jy his wife, Clara. Jackson, with refusing to maintain her. Mr. Forshaw appeared for the complain- ant. An order was made for allowance of 10s. a week, and the magistrates advised the parties who were at present separted, to live together again, which they were disposed to do.
_ DAMAGING A WINDOW. - Margaret Stokes, was charged with wilfully smashing the window of Mary Stokes, her mother-in-law, on Monday night, but was dismissed.

WARRINGTON OCCASIONAL COURT. SITURDAY.—Before Mr. Ziba Armitage. MISMLANEOUS.—Rebecca Battersby, of Golborne, who has been several time previously charged with theft, was now charged with stealing two books from the shop of Mr. James Starr, stationer, High-st., Gol- borne, on the 6th inst. Evidence was given to the effect that on the day in question she visited the shop to make a purchase, and after she had left the books were missed. Information was given to the police, and the prisoner was apprehended. She was remanded, to enable the police to make inquiries.—At the same court, on Mon- day, Martin Concannon, a labourer, was fined , ss. and costs for being drunk at Rizton, on Sunday. The magis- trate present was Mr. James Tinsley.

div.head: RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS.
div.p: RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS.
MONDAY.—Before Major Hazlehurst and Mr. James
'Handley.

Dft lINKENNESS.—SamueI Giegory, labourer, was charged with having on the 2nd February been drunk on the licensed premises of Mr. G. W. Cooper, the Wilson's Hotel, and refused to quit when requested by P.S. Woolley. He pleaded guilty and was fined ss. and costs Bs. 6d.—For being drunk a similar fine was imposed upon John Howard, Isaac Johnson, William Griffin, Thomas Hayes, and John Sefton Ball. MISCELLANEOUS. —A fine of ss. and costs was inflicted upon John Moore for obstructing Trinity-st.—William Jones was ordered to pay 9s. for permitting the chimney of his dwelling to be on fire.—Sarah Ann Meakin was convicted of disorderly conduct, and was sentenced to 14 days' hard labour. A sentence of seven days was passed upon a vagrant named Arthur Reed, for begging. THEFT.—Margaret Molyneux pleaded guilty to having on Saturday stolen from a stall on the Market Ground two dress bodices, a skirt,and other articles belonging to Ellen Craddock, a second-hand clothes dealer. She was sentenced to 14 days' hard labour.

div.head: WIDNES POLICE COURT.
div.p: WIDNES POLICE COURT.
MONDAY.—BefOre Mr. H. Gaske 1 and Lieut-Colonal
Gaskell

DRIINHENNKSS.—For this offence Thomas Burke,Michael Barlow, Joseph Green, Catherine Hynes, Ellen Mitchell, William McCliffin, and Ann Goulding were each fined ss. and costs.—Margaret Wall was fined 7s. 6th and costs for a like offence.

ALLEGED RESISTANCE OF THE POLlCE.—Charles Malone, a youth from Sankey-st., was charged with assaulting and resisting Constables Walley, Evans, and Tweddle. While the officers" had a man in custody on Saturday night, the prisoner and a number of others threw stones and a quantity of slush at them.—The prisoner denied that he had thrown any stones, but admitted that he had a piece of "pot" in his hand .—Theprisoner was cautioned, and dischapaed. on promising to pay the costs.

GOTBORNE v. BOLTON ASSOCIATION.—GoIborne had a visit from the Bolton Association on Saturday afternoon, when the teams faced each other before a good number of onlookers. Golborne played a gallery game, but dur- ing this half neither side scored, and the game ended in a win for the homesters by two goals to nil.

div.p: FOOTBALL.

Secretaries of Football Clubs are requested to note that reports of matches played on Saturday must be sent to the head office, Bewsey-street. Warrington, not later than ten o'clock on Wednesday morning.

div.head: RUGBY.
div.p: RUGBY.

WIDNES V. WIGAN (" A " Tats.)—Played at Widnes on Saturday, before a fair attendance. Half-time score: Wigan" A" 3 minors; Widnes "A," 2 minors. Final result : Widnes " A " 5 minors; Wigan" A," 3 minors. Sr. HELENS REOS' "A " V. WIDNES ST. MARY'S IST. The first match between the above this season was played at City-road, St. Helens, and attracted about 1,500 spec- tators. Final scores :—Widnes S. Mary's Ist—one goal, three tries, two minors ; Rees A '—two minors. WIDNES V. WIGAN.—One of the finest matches parti- cipated in by the Widnes team took place on Saturday, when they succeeded in vanquishing the champions of the West Lancashire League, on their ground at Wigan, by 2 tries, 2 minors, to 1 try and 1 minor. This is the first time this season that two tries have heen scored against the Wiganites on their ground, while, for the same period, they have, only been subjected to defeat once. This makes the event all the more creditable for Widnes' and the spirit and combination displayed by the Widnes team surprised even their most ardent followers. In the scrimmage they were equal to their opponents, and the Widnes backs played as one man, and the sel- fishness visiblein previous matches amongst the Widnes team was conspicuous by its absence. Evans and Drum- mond worked well together at half-back, and the plucky play of the latter was frequently admired. RUNCORN V. DOICINFIELD.—The Runcorn Club having a vacant date, made arrangements almost at the last moment to play a match on Saturday. at Dukinfield. Runcorn, however, did not put anything like its ordi- nary strength on the field; but the match was sufficiently interesting to draw together a large body of spectators. Faulkner started the ball, which was returned by Gled- hill, and then ensued a series of smart passes, Dukin- field scoring a minor. Play was very fast, and Abrams, Hughes, and Davies treated Dukinfield to a sample of grand passing; but Haslam came to the relief, and de- f ended the home lines smartly. Houghton was pre- vented for a time from playing' and Crompton, eager to break the ice, put in a grand kick, and was within an ace of dropping a goal. The passing tactics of Faulk- ner, Davies, Abrams, Crompton, and Pendlebury gave a, , chance to the last-named to score. The game was ex- citing throughout,and in the second half,Riley secured a try, and Houghton kicked a goal, the scoring at the ' finish being—Runcorn, 1 goal, 1 try, 2 minors; Dukin- field, 2 minors. WARRINGTON RANGERS V. HALTON VlEW.—Played at Warrington, before a fair number of spectators. The visitors kicked off, and after scane exchange of kicking, I play was taken to centre, but the Rangers' forwards, by a combined dribble, got well into their opponents' terri- tory where Potts obtained possession, and dropped al splendid goal. This early reverse roused the visitors,but the strong defensive play of the home backs repelled any serious invasion. From some loose play Potts I Picked up, and made a fine run through the midst of his opponents, and a try was a certainty, when he foolishly threw away the chance by preferring to drop at goal al- most on the line, and a minor only was recorded. Half- time was now called, the score reading—Rangers, 1 goal, 2 minors; Halton View, nil. Whitfield re-started, and the home team pressed. The grand tackling of Wade and Bleasdale prevented further score. By several mis- kicks on the part of the homesters the Viewites rushed the ball over, and a try was secured by Conner, which Manley converted into a goal. The score now being equal. both teams put in all they knew, play becoming fast aikd determined; but eventually the game was taken I to the visitors' half, and from a line out Kenwright burst 1 away in grand style, and passing at the right moment tol Potts, that player knocked aside all opposition, and scored a splendid try, but he failed to land a goal from a favourable position. With the etception of minors no further score was made, and the Rangers retired victors by 1 goal, 1 try, 4 minors, to Halt ui View 1 goal and 1 minor. _

WARRINGTON "A " V. LEIGH. - The Warringtonians journeyed to Leigh, on Saturday, and, as is now a cus- tomary occurrence, found an exceptionally strong team awaiting them, the team comprising half of the West Leigh club, 'whilst special training had been indulged in for the combat. Leigh started, and after the usual exchanges between the backs,ofificer got away with a sprint to the visitors' 25, Davies returning the oval to midfield. For some time packs and scrambling play oc- cupied, the game being somewhat enlivened with a run

div.head: EXAMINERI SATORDAY; FEBRUARY 14,1891.
div.p: THE EXAMINERI SATORDAY; FEBRUARY 14,1891.

by Collier. Here Jolley got away finely and kicking across, the oval was snapped up by Webster, who gal- loped in grandly, the place failing. Although Barnes replied to the drop out, a rush by the homesters carried play well into the visitors' lines, when Lalley, Buckley, and Phillips dashed away in fine style, transferring play to the home quarter flag. Off-side play spoiled the drop out, the attack being maintained for a while, until Knowles, Kilgarry, Hackett, and Holcroft were notable in a rush to the quarter flag. Grand kicking by Jolley,. Knowles, and Sampson was followed by Leigh running up and Officer scoring, the place being a failure. Some exciting play ensued, a pass from Davies enabling Jolley to punt to midfield, the position being further enhanced by strong forward play by Molyneux, Cragan, and Hackett. Phillips here ran across and passed to Jolley, but the oval was quickly transferred to half way. A grand rush by Barnes, Knowles, Buckley, and Davies only resulted in a minor. There was a rough and tumble tussle hereabouts, the homesters eventually get- ting to their antagonists' lines, where Sampson. tackled Briscoe grandly, a fine relief being ultimately effected by Lalley, half time arriving with the score level. Re- suming Warrington, by the aid of Knowles, Holeroft, Kilgarry, and Cragan, got right up to the line, the pres- sure being maintained by Webster. ,1% fter this a grand bit of play by Jolley deserved a better fate than the soli- tary minor which resulted. Barnes then floored Hindley under the posts, but the ominous outlook was only tem- porary, as a kick from the ruck caused the struggle to wage in neutral territoiy,a mull almost letting in the home- sters. For a time the combatants vied with one another on the touch lines until Davies got grandly away right into his opponents' 85, the opportunity being supple- mented by a rush of the Warrington forwards.Lalley scoring a rattling try under the posts, the place kick be- ing charged. Soon afterwards another glaring piece of off-side play allowed the home lot to get close to the line, Collier running in smartly amidst frantic cheering, the place kick failing. The remainder of the play calls for little comment, although Jolley and Daniels were on seicarate occasions within an ace of scoring, the final re- sult reading—Warrington, 0-24 ; Leigh, 0-24. reams: —Warrington: Full back, Sampson • three-quarter backs, Webster, Jolley, and Daniels; half backs, Davies and Lal/ey ; forwards, Molyneux, Cragan, Kilgarry, Hackett, Holcroft, Buckley, Barnes, Knowles, and Phillips. Leigh: Full back, Hindley ; three-quarter backs, Poole, Collier, and Briscoe ; half backs, Pendle- bury and Officer; forwards, Horrocks, Holloway, Clark, Lawson, Phcenix, Sutton, Collier, Ramsdale, and Harri- son.

a game to be stopped owing to either darkness or fog and victory awarded to the side which then happens to be leading would be a lesson to certain dilatory clubs, and it should stimulate them to make the best of the un- certain light of a winter's afternoon. The League sets a splendid example which someof our big Rugby teams would do well to follow.

Something like a sensation wag caused by the defeat of Wigan by 'Widnes, and on the ground of the West Lancashire League champions, too. True, the xtent of the defeat was only a try, but it counts all the same. The chemical men got both their points before the Wigan players had properly settled down, and try as they would they could not recover the lost ground. The record of the Wigan team urte date is :—Played 21 matches, won Ig, lost 2, drawn 1. Total score foi, 27 goals, 32 tries; against, 1 dropped goal, and 8 tries. 3o other Lanca- shire club can anything like approach thst.

The team that crossed the Channel to do.duty for Eng- land' against the Frish fifteen at Dublin might have been stronger in several instances, but it was quite strong enough. Ireland had hardly ever a chance of doing mis- chief, and in the end they were very decisively beaten.. The absence of such men of sterling worth as Christopher- son, Midworth, and Strang made no appreciable differ- ence in the play of tilt Englishmen, who were at all points superior to the " Frome Rulers." From the time that ".Dickv " iuockwood' scored the first try for the visitors the issue was never in doubt, the Irish players being both out-paced'and out-manceuvred. At half-time England was leading' by a couple of tries to nil, and the final verdict was in their -favour by two goals and three tries. The honours of scoring were divided between Lancashire and Yorkshire.. Roger Wilson, who was drafted into the team- as deputy for Budworth, and Lockwood each ran in twice and Toothill once, whilst Lockwood placed both the goats. Both Jowett and Wood had made the attempt befOrs the Heckmondwike three- quarter was given a trial in this department, and then he was twice successful. The English backs were infinitely better than those on the other side, one or two of the Irishmen being conspicuous failures. The three Lancastrians. Berrv,Wil§on, and Kent, all did themselves credit, the Trldealey half back and Leake supporting each other finely.

div.head: WARRINGTON v. LEIGH.
div.p: WARRINGTON v. LEIGH.

The return match between the above clubs took- place at Wilderspool on Saturday. The day was fine,, and advantage was taken of it by a large crowd, the Leighite having a following of nearly six hundred. There would be over five thousand present when Frank Turner kicked off, and Ashton foiling the return, Warrington looked like scoring in the first minute. Smith snapped up the oval from the home forwards' toes, and a sharp run and kick gave his side relief. Play was located at half-way, when Evans with a strong run forced his opponents back, and a short bout of passing between the same player and Barnes found the game in the mouth of the railway goal. The Leigh forwards by the aid of short rushes again cleared, only to find Coop, Massey,. and Frank Turner exchanging kicks; the latter having at shot at goal, the oval falling short, and Davies easily clearing. Jolley, Barnes, Fair Turner, and Berry each at this juncture became prominent, and Massey punting well, Jolley got clear away, but the fatal whistle was- sounded, much to the disappointment of the home sup- porters. The home halves now wakened up, and for the first time made their presence felt. James Bate, with some clever work, got as far as Coop, who responded to Boscow, only to find the home custodian as safe as ever, and Leigh were again on the defensive. Berry and Holmes came away together, and their quick following up and tackling was neutralized -splendidly on one occa- sion by Coop. Erwin and Graham by judicious kicking harassed the home defence, but Jolley, Donohue, and Frank Turner came away from the pack, and their pro- gress was not stayed until they had reached the Leigh 25. Again the visitors relieved, and again Warrington ' attacked, but this time with better luck, for a beautiful piece of combination between Jas. Bate. Barnes, and Massey saw the home skipper taking the final pass in neat style, and a try was the result. Fair Turner essayed the place without success. A similar sequence of passes between the two Bates and Barnes was wit- nessed immediately on the restart, but Leigh tackled successfully this time, and although Coop dropped well, Boscow could not get passed, and Leigh contented them- selves with defensive 'tactics. A fine piece of play by James Bate was ably seconded by some smart rushes, in which Ashton and Thorniley were the shining lights. Loose play in front of the Leigh posts saw Barnes with the oval, and a shot at goal went a trifle wide. Another minor fell to Warrington's credit, from a mark taken by Frank Turner, but a beautiful return and quick following lip by the elder Turner again saw Warrington on the aggressive. After Evans had spoiled Davies in his endeavour to clear, from a pack James Bate passed finely to Barnes, who dodged Smith and the second try was recorded. The kick at goal was, again at fault. Massey soon after was hurt, and Warrington practically played 14 men the remainder of the game, Jolley being placed at three - quarter. A fine run by Smith raised the hopes of the Leigh partisans, but these were soon dashed to the ground when Jolley, Ashton, Povey, and J. T. Bate rushed the ball through the now over- taxed defence, and James Bate backing this up with a useful dribble, the ball was worked over, Holmes com- pleting the try. Still no goal was nlaCed. Thorniley chargel the kick off, and all but scored. Luckily, the Leigh men were all up, and by a sharp series of passes, aided by some clever kicking on the part of McMasters. Coop and Graham, the Warrington 25 was reached, and although Fair Turner tackled Coop near the half-way on one occasion, Smith got clear the next moment, and a smart drop resulted in a goal, this bringing half-time ' with the score as—Warrington. 0-3-2; Leigh, 1-0-0. Coop re-started, and only a faint reply being given, Leigh early forced their only rilinor of the match. Berry was now conspicuous with a fine run, and got the oval well inside the Leigh 25. Ewin put in several eaart kicks, which gained neutral ground, but a sharp burst by Fair Turner, Donohue, and Berry saw Coop saving daringly. The home backs now gave their opponents a taste of their quality, and a fine series of passes between the two Bates, Evans, Barnes, and Jolley was luckily foiled by McMasters. Boscow and Coop exchanged kicks, and again with advantage to the Warrington back. Sharp practice in the line-out between Berry and J. T. Bate gained considerable ground, and then a sharp series of passes along touch ended in Frank Turner being knocked into touch a foot from the line. This was in- deed hard lines for Warrington, and although Coop saved his side from disaster on many occasions in marvellous fashion, the homesters still plodded on with the hope that victory would yet be theirs. James Bate forced Davies to concede a minor immediately after, but fortune favoured the smart Warrington half backs a moment later, for getting possession near the half way, he out- witted the opposing backs, and Coop being in a dilemma as to which course to pursue, Bate romped over the line, and Warrington regained the lead once more. This evidently had its effect, for the pressure now became doubly strong, and although Coop many times cleared, Evans and Barnes never failed in their mission to drive their opponents back. Near the call of time a short passing movement ended in Holmes scoring the last point of the match, and Barnes being at fault with the place, the final score read as Warrington, 0-5-4; Leigh, 1-0-1.

Teams :—Warrington: J. Boscow, back; Barnes, Massey, and Evans. three-quartets; James Bate and J. T. Bate, half backs; Ashton, Fair Turner, F. Turner, Donohue, Jolley, Thorniley, Holmes, Berry, and Povey. Leigh : Davies, back; Coop, Smith, and Holt, three- gnat ters ; Shovelton and Ewin, half backs; Lawson, R. Taylor, P. Taylor, Graham, Gregory, McMasters, Black- burn, Aldred, Langford. Referee, Mr. Clegg, Wigan Football Club.

Sr. HELENS CELTIC V. SUTTON VICTORIA.—This match was played on Saturday afternoon, and resulted in a win for the Celtic by three goals to one. WHISTON V. TRANMERE ROVERS.—Played at Tramere on Saturday last, before a fair number of spectators. Final result: Whiston, 3 goals, Tranmere Rovers nil. HAYDOCK V. BLACKPOOL SOUTH SHORE.—This match in the second round of the Lancashire Senior Cup, was played at Blackpool on Saturday afternoon, Blackpool finally winning by five goals to nil.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND
ATHLETICS.
FOOTBALL-RUGBY.

There was little to choose between the counties of Westmoreland and Cumberland on Saturday, the first named carrying off the honours by a goal and a try to a try. It was very late in the game when Johnson man- aged to score for Cumberland, who as a rule were busily occupied in defensive tactics.

Whilst England were thus enjoying themselves at Dublin, Scotland were doing equally as well against "gallant little Wales." With a decent place kicker in the team the defeat of the Welshmen would have been very heavy indeed. As it was it amounted to three goal- and six tries. the Welshmen having to go quite empty- handed. Of the four tries obtained during the first half not one was improved upon. Two of the goals were dropped by Stevenson and Clauss.

The official announcement regarding a referee's duties is a step in the right direction. Some clubs are notori- bus for unpunctuality and late starts, but the, power now vested in the referee ought to wake them up. For

div.head: ASSOCIATION'.
div.p: ASSOCIATION'.

Four of the ties for the Lancashire Cup were disposed of on Saturday, the event of the afternoon being the defeat of Burnley by D'arwen, the game taking place at Turf Moor. Thus in eight days the costly Burnley team has been swept out ofthe two chief cup competitions. Newton Heath just won theirs verurs Witton.

If further testimony were needed of this truism it was furnished by the final tie for the Scotch Cup. The competing clubs were Dumbarton and the Heart of Midlothian. The former had not once been beaten this season, and yet they lost the cup by a goal. Before this the Hearts had knocked out the Third Lanark by four goals to one, and the Volunteers had previously dis- posed of tho Queen's Park by exactly the same margin. The unlooked for victory of the Hearts should give a fillip to football among the the E'dfnburgh clubs.

The North End are rejoicing that they have Ross, jun., and Kelso back in their ranks. The two Scotchmen have been long absent, ".Jimmy ". suffering from a severe attaak of sciatica, and their loss has told a tale. The great value of the two men is seen in the fact that di- rectly they rejoin their.comrades the Preston team win two important League ffxtures with consummate ease. To heat Burnley by seven goals to none and West Brom- wich Albion by three to one were two excellent perform- ances. North End have four more League matches to go through, and if they can pull them all off they may again be champions. Of course the odds are against then. Derby County gave another specimen of their curious form by beating Sunderland, who for weekshave been carrying all before them. They never calculated on having their colours lowered at Derby, and it only goes to prove that the very best team is not invincible.

div.head: IRELAND.
div.p: IRELAND.
THE LISACAPPLE MURDER.

On Sunday night the constabulary at Ballyjatnesduff ariested a man named William Buchanan on suspicion of being the murderer of the caretaker, Patrick Reilly, and his wife at Lisacapple a week ago. He was remanded for inquiries. Buchanan is a cotter living about a mile away. In his house were found some clothes stained with blood, and concealed in the thatch was a large iron bar, bearing marks of blood and grey hairs.

div.head: IRISH LEADERSHIP.
div.p: THE IRISH LEADERSHIP.

At the churches in the Mitchelstown parish on Sunday the officiating priests read an appeal from Dean Oregon, Deaikof Cloyne, requesting the people to hold aloof from the central executive of the Irish National League,which, as at present constituted, has forfeited the confidence of the people. The appeal was issued in consequence of Mr. Harlington's recent circular.
THE IRISH DIFFICULTY.
FAILURE -OP-ITECIOTIATIONS.

A telegram to Wednesday's "Freeman's Journal" stated that after a hastily-arranged conference late on Tuesday night, at which three members of Mr. Parnell's Parliamentary following were present, a note was handed to Mr. Justin M'Carthy in the House of Com- mons, conveying the abandonment by Mr. Parnell and his followers of any present hope of coming to a satis- factory understanding with the other side. Mr. W. O'Brien, writing to the secretary of the Walker-on/Fyne branch of the National League, says—" Neither Mr. Dil- lon nor I will expose ourselves to imprisonment until we have done all in our power to end the present deplorable strife in the ranks of the Irish party." Mr. Parnell has written to Mr. O'Brien stating that he withdraws from the Boulogne negotiations because,in his opinion,the interests of Ireland, more especially as regards the Home Rule question, would not be properly safeguarded under the terms suggested. He invites Mr. O'Brien's endorse- ment of his action as guided by a desire to settle the question in accordance with the best interests of the national cause. The anti-Parnellites, on the other hand, express themselves confident of eventual victory. Mr. W. O'Brien, on Wednesday night, gave a'communication to a Press representative, in which the "recklessness and injustice" of Mr. Parnell retaining the leadership are referred to. THE IRISH LEADERSHIP. MEETING OF ,THE ANTI-PARNELLITIES. The Preas Association states that the meeting of anti- Parnellitie members of the Irish Parliamentary party was held at one o'clock, on Thursday, in Committee- room No. 15 at the House of Commons. Among those present were Messrs. Jtatin McCarthy. Sexton, T. M. Healey, Sir John Pope Hennessy, Dr. Tanner. Dr. Corn- mins, Messrs. J. Tuite, Donald Sullivan, T. A. Dickson, and Sir Thomas Esmonde. Mr. McCarthy took the cliair amidst applause, there being then about 30 members in thr room. Some digcussion, it is understood, followed Mr. McCarthy's statement, which was conducted with- out acrimony. • A resolution was passed to the effect that while firmly maintaining the position taken up on the 6th December in regard to the leadership, they regretted the fate of the recent negotiations undertaken in the hope of bringing the minority again into harmiony with the party. A seeond resolution requested that a meeting of the Nation- al Committee should be convened for an early date in Dublin.
ARREST OF MR. W. O'BRIEN AND MR. JOHN DILLON.

Mr. John Dillon. M.P., and Mr. William O'Brien, M.P., have returned to undergo the sentences passed upon them by the Coercion Court at Tipperary. They left Boulognefor Folkstone on Thursday afternoon, and were arrested as they left the steamer at the latter place. Tt-ey were afterwards, in custody of Scotland Yard detectives, conveyed in a special saloon carriage attached to the mail train to London. As the arrest was quite un- expected by the public there was no demonstration either at Folkstone or when the prisoners reached Charing Cross. At the latter station, however, they were welcomed by several Parliamentary supporters of Mr. Parnell. The greetings over, the hon. members were driven almost unnoticed to New Scotland Yard, where they were visited by several of their Parliamentary colleagues, and where they remained for the night. Questioned in the House of Commons by Mr. Justin M'Carthy, Mr. Bal- four said he had no information as to the arrest of Messrs. Dillon and O'Brien. He imagined that the question should be addressed to the Home Secretary. Mr. Matthews said he had not received information of the arrest; but in reply to a query whether he expected to receive such inforthation he said, "It would not sur- prise me at all."

div.head: RELIGIOUS BIGOTRY IN RUNCORN. BY A NONCONFORMIST,
div.p: RELIGIOUS BIGOTRY IN RUNCORN. BY A NONCONFORMIST,

There has just passed away amid the eulogiums of friend and foe, a man who for a large portion of his life laboured hard to "fight the bigots," and hundreds were the pounds contributed to him by working-men and others for this purpose. In, these modern days, we have often been told that Bigotry is dead, but although it is often cloaked beneath a smile and a handshake, it now and again rears up its head with the same brazen-faced impudence as of yore. This expression is drawn from me, Mr. Editor, by at pertisal of the sermon preached by the Vicar of Runcorn and published in this month's Parish Magazine at the request of "one or two:" And a fine storm of indignation has it aroused amongst the great Nonconformist body, but especi- ally the Wesleyans of the town. The sermon "appears as preached" and "kind indulgence is- requested for what little blemishes. and slips are to. be found in iit,'lotherwise one would be tempted to remark that the logic was quite equal to the composition. With the sophistical' reasoning as to whether regeneration takes placebefbre conversion, or whether conversion and regeneration are one and the same thing, ram not concerned; but I wish to, attract attention-to the feeling which impels a clergyman from his-pulpit to denounce another re- ligious organisation in the town—an, organisation which he is compelled to admit is doing great good. This sermon was preached on the Sunday mcrning previous to the meeting in St. PauPS Wesleyan Chapel in aid of the Bondon Mission, and the Vicar, after warning his hearers against the errors of modern Wesleyanism,tens them "it would be wiser andbetter to avoid giving support to such religious effOrt outside your own, epurch, as you are nolv in- vited to countenance, and assist." " he con- tinues, "I go and take-my place upon a- Wesleyan orany Nonconformist platform; I thereby recog- nise their organisation as forming a legitimate part of the Catholic Church. Now, an instructed Churchman cannot do this." The Rev. Dr; Freston, M.A.,.the vicar of Holy Trinity Church, was-present on the platform in the Wesleyan Chapel on the oc- casion-referred to, but, of course, the rev.. &actor is an "uninstructed Churchman," and needs a few lessons from Canon Wood in order to bring him to that perfection of religious charity that he may, without compunction, ostracise every other "sect" but his-own.

An inetructed churchman "knows that the Saviour- founded one visible church under the Apostles—he believes that the Body usually called the Church of England is for this country the duly true, legitimate, and historic branch of that one church,—and he cannot, therefore, for popularity or peace put on one side his conviction, and admit that there are many churchez." Upon what this belief is founded Canon Wood does not condescend to infOrruue, but Macaulay who may be regarded as an equally high authority as Canon Wood, in his essay on" Gladstone on Church and State" 'asks —" 18 there such a visible body? Was there such a visible body in the year 1500? It not why are we to believe that there is such a body in the year 1839 '?"-(or-1801.) If there was such a body in the year 1500, what was it? Was it the Church of ROme ? And how can the Church of England be orthodox now,if the Church of Rome was orthodox then ?" My reading of history teaches me that if one church can claim to, be the " one visible body" it is the Church of Rome,and that" the orders of the Church of England are generally derived from the Church of Rome." The Church of England,says Lord Macaulay, "sprang from a compromise huddled up between the eager zeal of reformers and the selfishness of greedy, ambitious, and time-serving politicians." I am no Catholic, my Ndficonformiy will withstand the assault of both Roman and Episcopalian, but Canon Wood if he be true to his reasoning, and to his desire to be-joined with the historic church,,ought at once to transfer his allegiance to the Roman Catholic Church, which "saw the commencement of' all the Governments and of all the ecclesiastical establishments that now exist in the world, and we feel no assurance that she is not destined to see the end of them all. She was great and respected before the Saxon had set foot on Britain, before the Frank had passed the Rhine, when Grecian eloquence still flourished, when idols were still worshipped in the temple of Mecca." If it is the historic that isto be the ruling force in determining the Vicar's religiousnpinion, surely here is the Church where his aspirations will be best met, and where the units* is far more visible than in the Establishment, one half of which is travelling Romewards and the other half who knows where ?'

I prefer to found my religion 'on an intelligent reading of the Bible, and to believe that "all religion hath rela- tion to life, aTici the life of religion ia to do good;" and not to set sect, against sect and man against man.. Candour ' compels the Vicar to confess that God uses these Noncon- formist organisations for the benefit of mankind, but it does not followrhe says, because God permits an organ- isation to-do good that such an organisatien ought to be. recognised as a true branch of the Church, How to characterise such an arrogant assumption as this words cannot tell. To thus question the wisdom of the Supreme and to declare to be false that which the Lord evidently accepts as true worship, savours much of blasphemy. "We do not doubt," he continues, "that the prayers, alms, and toil of Nonconformists are blessed and accepted by God. No doubt they are useful, but how much more ' useful would they be if they would acknowledge the ; truth and rejoin the one body." But the Church of Eng- ' land has no place for Nonconformists. Thereis no place in the Establishment with its formularies,. its govern- ment, and its vestments, for an enthusiastic laity desir- ous to be active in the service of the Lord. There was no room for a Wesley there, and there is assuredly none for his millions of followers. Nonconformists are " use- ful," and the Vicar is apparently under the necessity of taking from a book which he no doubt heartily disap- proves—General Booth's "Darkest England."—the only case of practical Christianity, followed by conversion,. with which he illustrates his sermon. Are there no•such conversions recorded in his own Church? Is its religion so robbed of fervour by empty formalities that the con- verted are not numbered amongst its ranks? It is. to be hoped not,but still he has to go outside to give an ex- ample of reclaiming the wicked. This sermon, from which I have just made a few quo- tations, towards the conclusion, asks if " the useless religious competition, the heartburning and jealousies and rivalries, the terrible waste of strength and money, the evil example set to the world—the startling fact,, that if religion is pushed out of the schools, the jealousy of Non- conformists will have done it—he asks if these things are counterbalanced by the records of conversions which might as well have taken place if the workers were all members of the Church of England." I would ask what does the vicar think he has accomplished by his ill-con- sidered sermon, and the ill-concealed bigotry it contains, but heartburnings, jealousies,and rivalries? What feel- ing prompted him to warn his flock from' fraternising with another religious denomination but jealousy and rivalry and a fear that some members of his congregation did they enter within the doors of a Nonconformist Chapel, and witness the display of religious enthusiasm there to be seen' might begin to doubt that the priests of the Church had the true Apostolic succession and that the Church of England was the "me visible body ?" Perhaps the key to this outburst is to be found in his reference to religious education in the day schools, but he ray rest assured that his intemperate zeal will bear fruit such as he never anticipated when he penned words calculated—would it be too strong to say intended ?—to grieve, injure, and offend the Nonconformists of Run- corn.

div.head: ANOTHER WOUNDING CASE AT WIDNES.
div.p: ANOTHER WOUNDING CASE AT WIDNES.

At Widnes Police Court, on Monday, John M‘Guire, of 35, Nelson-street, was charged with un- lawfully wounding John Coyle and Mark Coyle. From a statement made by Superintendent Noblett it appeared that at midnight on Saturday, the prisoner and prosecutors had a disturbance together, and it was alleged that the prisoner struck the other teen en the heads with a hammer (produced), and caused a number of serious wound., penetrating to the bone, which had been dressed by Dr. Mac Lennon. On Sunday, so the superintendent was informed, the prosecutors removed their bandages and were out of the house drinking, and they did not now appear to support the charge. The prisoner was remanded until the following morning when the prosecutors appeared and supported the allegation. Dr. MacLennan said .John Coyle had four wounds on his head, varying inlength from half an inch to two inches. Mark had one incised scalp wound two inches long. The clothing and hair of both men were saturated with blood. The wounds were of a dangerouS character —The prisoner was committed to the Quarter Sessions or trial.

EPPS'S COCOA.— GRATEFUL AND COMFORTING.—" By a thorough knowledge of the natural laws which govern the operations of digestion and nutrition, and by a careful applica- tion of the fine properties of well-selected COCOA, Mr. Epps has provided our breakfast tables with a delicately flavoured bever- age which may save us many heavy doctors' bills. It is by the judicious use of such articles of diet that a constitution may be ,gradually built up until strong enough to resist every tendency to disease. WARRINGTON MUSICAL SOCIETY'S CONCERT.

The third concert of the season of the Warring- ton Musical Society was given in the Public. on Tuesday evening. The concert was largely attended though the hall was not crowded, and-the success- with which it came off proves that the society continues to make advancement under its new auspices and conditions, to an extent that must allay all anxiety on account of the changes it, has made: The vocalists were all members of the society, the fact of this independence of extraneous aid making the success al/ the more creditable. They were as follows :—Mrs. Dobson and Miss Mein, sopranos ;. Mr. R. Fairclough, tenor; Miss Faiishaw% contralto; Mr. W. A. Wallington, bass. Mr. F. W. Reynolds, pianoforte, and Mr. F. H. Crossley, violin, were the solo instrumentalists, the latter also act-- ing as conductor. The overture "Marionette" (Gurlett)'by the orchestra, was a masterly perform- ance,one on which it would be difficult to bestow too high praise: A song by Mr. Fairclough "The light of home "'followed and was very artistically sung, though we hardly think the piece is of the character best adapted to his voice. Miss Mein succeeded with a German song "Die Bekehrte," by Max Strange, to the original of which a translation of Goethe'S words was appended in the programme, enabling the audience the better to judge of the lady's thoughtful and artistic rendering of the song. Her charming voice,with its clear resonant quality and fine compass, delighted all. The better-known of the two enteaCtes,to Schubert's "Rosamund "was next performed by the orchestra with all the delicacy of treatment which the beautiful theme demand, and a vocal quartette "Softly Fall the Shades of Evening" (Hatton) by Mrs. Dobson, Miss Fanshawe, Mr.. Fairciough, and Mr. Wallington was a very creditable performance,though there was ob- servable occasionally some defectiveness as to time. Mr. Crossley's violin solo (with orchestral accom- paniment).wßomance" (Svendsen) was splendidly executed,. and earned for im a vociferous encore, in response to which he played, to the accompaniment of the pianoforte alone, a pavatina by Adelmann. Miss Fanshawe'S song "The Flight of Ages," was much applauded, Beethoven's concerto for piano- forte and'orchestra in C Major Op. 15 next following, Mr. F. W. Rhynolds pre siding at the solo instru- ment. The whole of the three movements comprised in the work were executed with precision and expression and the perform- ance earned enthusiastic plaudits. Mr. Rey- nolds was compelled to re-appear to receive personally the expression of the audience's appreci- ation. Part 2bd opened,with the performance of a quartet for violins, viola and violoncello in D minor, Allegro moderato—Andante Arenuetto e Trio— Allegro viilace; the composition being by Mr. F. H. Crossley, old• the artistes being himself, Miss M. Nunncrlef, Miss J. Nunnerley and Mr. C. R. Cross- ley. It speaks highly for the merit of the piece and foras execution that the audience could sit, through such a lengthy performance not only with com- posure, but with apparent pleasure. Mrs. Dobson then sang in exquisite style "The merry birds (Gtumbert) and was deservedly encored, giving in equally delightful manner " I mayor may not." Mr. Wallin on followed with "The demon king," which created' Much impression, his part being ably sus- tained, though a stronger voice would have been better suited for such a piece. Mr. Reynolds gave another , pianoforte solo. Miss Mein in beautiful style sang "B'ecauSe " for which she was recalled, and' another vocs.l quartette by the same performers as the first was given. The concert was then brought to a close with a finely rendered "Trium- phal March by Prout. Mr. P. H. Crossley officiated as conductor with his characteristic ability. The pianoforte, we may mention, was supplied from the establishment of Mr. R. H. Pearson, Bold-st.
THE CLERICAL SCANDAL AT NEWTON: EXTRAORDINARY APPEAL.

Last week we gave publicity to the fact that the wife of a clergyman at Newton had left her home, under conditions which has given rise to excite- ment and unpleasant gossip. Since that time the matter has been referred to in such a public manner by the Rev. 11. Monk, vicar of Newton, that there is no longer any obligation to suppress the names of the chief actors in the proceedings. The lady who has so ruthlessly broken her marriage vow is Mrs. Pughe, wife of the Rev. H. Pughe who up to last week was the curate of St. Peter's, Newton. The other party to the affair, is a solicitor named Owen, and is brother to a lady, residing in Newton. Report says that the acquaintance has been continued for several months past, and although plainly notice- able to many of the residents, yet the husband was ignorant until lately, of the state of affairs. The culminating point has now been reached,, and being unable to any longer remain from the side of the new object of her affections, Mrs. Pughe hasleft her afflicted husband, and is now said to be living with her lover at Southport. She has also forsaken her two children, a. boy and a girl, who, however, are too young to recognise their mother's wrong-doing. It is also said that Mr. Pughe has been left with a heavy pecuniary burden, but report does not say whether the erring wife is responsible for this or not. However that may be, the Vicar of Newtorr the Rev. IL Monks, finds it incumbent upon himself to do something to relieve Mr. Pughe's present necessities,, and he has accord- ingly issued an appeal to his parishioners from which we make the followingextract _ _

During the week of its preparation I have found myself unexpectedly single-handed in the work of the parish; for on Tuesday my colleague'placed in my hands his formal resignation of the assistant curacy, which he had previously asked me to ac- cept; and on the same day I received permission from the Bishop of the Diocese to accept it. It is unnecessary that I should allude to the painful in- cident, which has induced Mr. Pughe to. take this very proper step, while it is necessarily so fresh in all our memories, further than to say that it is one which demands, and assuredly will call forth, the sincerest sympathy from all who knew. him. Dur- ing nearly six years he has always stniven in the most loyal spirit to carry out my wishes in the good works he has successfully undertakens and perhaps there are few who know under what a heavy load of family affliction and domestic trialhe has always cheerfully seconded every effort for the well-being of the parish. I feel it my bounden duty to bear this testimony to the value of his work, and to as- sure him thus publicly of deep sympathy with him in the crushing blow which has so cruelly overtaken him. Seeing that he has so promptly taken the right course, in resigning a position which had be- come untenable, I hope the sympathy drawn out towards him will take the practical shape of assist- ing him to meet his immediate necessities, and that he will not be allowed- to occupy a worse pesition than if he had adopted any Other course instead. Although by resigning he forfeits his legal dein to receive any consideration beyond his stipend pto that date, when it is remembered that he is in a moment deprived of emolument and saddled with heavy burdens, it' will be admitted that he has a strong claim upon us all, and particularly upon the subscribers to the Curacy Fund. But in this, as in all matters,we must be just before we are lenerous, and in the first place Mr. Pughe is morally entitled to receive the three months' stipend of £4O, which would have been his had the circumstances ad- mitted of his giving the usual three months' notice of. resignation. This seems to me to be our first duty, and the least that we can do for its due dis- charge. I hope the response to this appeal will be on a more liberal scale, and I intend myself to con- tribute a sum of £25. I shall be happy to receive the contributions of sympathisers,and all sums sent to me will be applied in the manner I have indi- cated.
THE NORTHAMPTON CONTEST.

6REAT LIBERAL VICTORY. The nomination of candidates for the vacancy in the Parliamentary representation of Northampton took place on Monday, when Dr. Aveling, Socialist, Mr. R. A. Germaine, Conservative, and Mr. M. P. Manfield, Glad- stonian Liberal, were nominated. An objection was raised to D. Aveling's nomination papers; but it was withdrawn, subject to his ending by two o'clock the de- posit required by the returning officer. When two o'clock arrived, Dr. Aveling had not provided the money required, and his nomination was, therefore, declared void.

The pollingfor the election for a membenof Parliament for Northampton, in the pittce of the late Mr. Brad- laugh opened on Thursday mroning, at eight o'clock. Since the contest of 1886 the register has-been enlarged by 1,200, bringing the total:, number of voters up to 10,895: The eandidates—Mr- Moses Philip Manfield (G.L.) and Mr.. R. A, Germaine (G)—were early at the polling places,. and the election was without any disturbing incident. Save scenes at one or two of Mr. Germaine's meetings, the whole contest has been very quiet. Parliamentary agents were -.engaged from Birmingham, Worcester, Nottingham, Gloucester, Peter- borough, and North Hunts. The poll closed at eight o'clock, and the ballot-boxes were removed to the Corn Exchange, where the counting was concluded under the supervision of the Mayor (Mr. George Norman), who acted as returning officer. At a quarter to eleven o'clock the poll was declared, as follows : Mr. M. P. Manfield (GL) Mr. R. A. Germaine ,(C) 3,7339

Liberal majority The crowds in the Town-square and adjacent streets raised a tumultuous shout on the Mayor announcing the figures, the cheers being so persistent that it was some moments ere the newly-elected member couldmake him- self heard.

The news of the result of Northampton election reached the precincts of the - House of Commons at twenty minutes to eleven. The magnitude of the majoritv made a great sensation. It was utterly unex- pected in the most sanguine calculations. There was the greatest enthusiasm at the National Liberal Club, the figures being received with reiterated cheering by a large gathering of members who had met for the announce- ment.

PREVIOUS ELECTIONS: The figures for the last two elections were :- 18.85. Mr. H. Labouchere (I) Mr. C. Bradlaugh (L) 4,315 Mr. H. C. Richards (C) 1886. Mr. H. Laoouchere (L) Mr. C. Bradlaugh (L) 4,353 Mr. R. Turner (U) 3,850 Mr. T. 0. H.. Lees (C) It will be seen that the Liberal majority, on Thuisday, was increased by no less than 1210 votes.
PEER'S "ECONOMIC "BUILDING SOCIETY._

The annual meeting of the First Warrington Peer's " Economic " Building Society was held on Tuesday evqping in the offices King-st. Mr. T. chall, tne president, occupied the chair, and the other directors present were Messrs. J. Albinson, T. J. liaise, S. Jones, J. Mounfield, jonr., A. Rathbone. ana, S: Taylor. There was a good attendance of members.
DIRECTORS' REPORT

The directors in their.report said " they had again written off a reasonable amount of the formation and other expenses, but the profit not being so much as last year,,tney did net propose to add any bonus to member's subscriptions. This was owing to the fact that three of the members who had obtained approriations during the year (holding together it.shares) had sold them to the Society, which the directors with a view to obtaining the best possible price for the use of thisrnoney had refrained from selling. They,however, intended disposing of these during the coming year, and had every confidence that a substantial profit would be the result. The membership had steadily increased,, but the total number had not yet been made up, and as the advantages of the Society would be considerably. greater when this was accom- plished,the directors .ur.ed the desirability of every mem- ber,doing his utmost taring that about as soon as pos-• sible. Tenders might be submitted at any time for sums of, from £lOO, and rising in amounts of £5O to £400." The report and balance sheet were then adopted.

ELECTION OE DIRECTORS, &C. , Messrs.. Albinson, Hulse, and Mounfield were re- elected directors. Mr. Rathbone expressed a wish t re- tire, and Mr. Johnson was elected in his place. Mr. T. Roberts was re-elected members auditor.
AN APPROPRIATION.

An appropriation meeting was also held, Mr. Birchall again presiding. Messrs.. Dobson, Leigh, and Lake were elected to officiate at the ballot. On a ballot being taken, the number 245 was drawn, and this entitled Mr: ,JamesStrange,,jun., to the use of £2OO free Off interest A vote of thanks to the Chairman brought the meeting to a close.

div.head: RITNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: RITNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

Colonel Ashton presided over the fortnightly meeting held at -Dutton Workhouse, on Tuesday. Present—Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, Rev: Dr. Gastaldi, Messrs. P. Speakman, C.C.,A. Th omas, J.P., Mclntyre, W. Whitlow, J. Weir, Aaron, W. Fisher, Phillips, Bretherton, Smith, Kirkham, Yarwood, Forster, J. Whitlow, Parr, Brandreth, Turner, J. Baguley, J. W. Baguley, Lewis, H. Linaker (clerk), and H. G. Lina: ker (deputy clerk).—The Clerk reported the death of Mr. W. Fermston, registrar of births and deaths, of the Daresbury sub-district, and read a letter from the Registrar-General suggesting the amalga- mation of the Budworth and Daresbury districts.— On the proposition of Mr. Speakman, seconded by Mr. Mclntyre, it was resolved to amalgamate the districts, and Mr. W. R. De Prez was accordingly appointed registrar for the Daresbury sub-district. —On the recommendation of the Finance Commit- tee, accounts amounting to £32 were passed for payment. It was resolved that the Assessment Committee obtain counsel's opinion re the rating of Appleton Quarry.
A RUNCORN PUBLICAN CONVICTED.

Before Major Hazlehurst and Mr. James Handl eyat Runcorn Police Court on Wednesday, James Taylor, landlord of the Rose and Crown Beerhouse, Church- at., was summoned for having on the 3rd inst., supplied drink to two drunken men named Daniel Bibby and John Jones. He was further charged with' unlawfully permitting drunkenness to take place on his premises.—Mr. A. Fletcher, of North- wich, prosecuted on behalf of the police and Mr. C. H. Lewin,of Widnes defended. From Mr. Fletcher's opening statement it appeared that about three o'clock on the day in questien, P.S. Woolley and IP.S. Edwards saw three men obviously under the influence of drink, come from the defendant's house and shortly afterwards they visited the house. Bibby was leaning on the counter with a pint of beer before him in a drunken condition indeed. In answer to the sergeant's inquiries the landlord admitted that Bibby was drunk, and that he had'supplied him with two pints, one previous to the one on the counter, which the defendant said he would put into a bottle for him, and he could take it home. One of • the navvies present volunteered to carry the beer for him. Jones was asleep near a table on which beer had been spilled. He was very drunk but quiet, and a summons was taken out against him, but he had since absconded. Bibby refused to give his name and he was taken into custody, and he wagso helpless in the street that the two officers had to keep him on his feet. Next morning the magistrates fined him five shillings, or seven days, and he was now in gaol expiating his offence.— Mr. Fletcher commented upon the reprehensible state of affairs these facts disclosed, and informed their worships of the penalty to which the defendant was liable.—This statement was borne out by theevidence of the constable, and Mr. Lewis said his evidence was in direct contradic- tion to that of the police. There was no doubt that this house was frequented by a rough class of customers, but the defendant had kept it for 16 years and no conviction was recorded against him. Bibby lived at a model ledging-house near by, and he had one pint during the morning. After dinner he came again and said he had no money and asked a man named Barnaby to stand a pint, but he refused but pushing his pet before him, told him he could take a drink. When the officers came in Taylor denied that he said he had served Bibby with two pints, but that he said " this man wants to stand him a pint and if he does, he will have to carry it out in a bottle." Jones had not been in the house more than five minutes, and the defendant had ordered him out several times. He had never been served.—The defendant was sworn, and cenfirined this statement and said he never served either men with drink. Evidence was also given by Barnaby, Walker, Rhymes, George Chapman, Ship Canal navvies, who declared the men were not served with liquor. The Bench decided to convict on the charge of permitting drunkenness, and fined the defendant 40s. and costs 255., Which included the advocates fee of 10s. 6d. As this was the first conviction against the defendant, hislicensa was not endorsed.

RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY. The Atnightly meeting was held at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday. Colonel Ashton presided, and there were present Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, Mears. Mclntyre, Parr, Smith, Aaron. Turner, Brandreth, Weir, J. Whitlow, Bretherton, Foster, W. Whitlow, H. G. Linaker (clerk).

THE SHIP CANAL COSTS. The Clerk said he had received a letter from the solicitors to the Board (Messrs. Linaker and Linaker) asking what were the approximate amount of the costs of the Authority in connection with the Manchester Ship Canal Company, incurred in defending the rights of the Authority. He thought there was no doubt the Cern- pany would pay these costs. He would provide the solicitors with the requisite information.—Mr. Aaron said no doubt the secretary of the Company desired to know so that he might lay the matter before his Board of Directors.

div.head: CANON DODD AND HIS COTTAGE.
div.p: CANON DODD AND HIS COTTAGE.

The Inspector of Nuisance read the following letter he had received: " Stretton Vicarage, Warrington, Feb. 9th, 1891. Dear Sir,—lf you had had the courtesy to com- municate with me about the old cottage in Well-lane, Stretton, before bringing the matter before the Sanitary Authority,you would have known that orders have been given long ago for the repair and re-thatching of the pre- xnises. I only allowed Mrs. Millwood to go in from sheer compassion, when she had nowhere to put her furniture, and no other cottage was available for nerself and her children. She has scarcely paid any rent since she has been there, and has been a most troublesome tenant into the bargain. (Laughter.) The builder who has had my orders for some months, excuses himself on account of the prolonged frost, and says that even now two or three weeks must elapse before the thatch is ready to be put on. The cottage is so old that it is very difficult to repair it properly. It is of no value to me as the annual cost consumes all the rent, and I heartily wish it could be pulled down and carted away. (Laughter.) But I have no power to do this, as it is not my own private property, but forms a Portion of the valuable endowment of this living. (Daughter.) What can be done to the place will be done as soon as the straw is ready, but I think it will be best for Mrs. Millwood to seek another habitation elsewhere as she will never be cpntent where she is. Yours faithfully,Henry R. Dodd." The Inspector said he did not ask for any action.to be taken ; he should witch that the property was repaired.
THE REBEWICS NUISANCE.

On being informed that no instructions had been re- ceived from the Local Government Board with respect to this matter, Mr. Aaron said the dryer the weather became and the stronger became the nuisance which consisted of sulphuretted hydrogen. The manner in which the Local Government Board were neglecting this matter was not fair. The Guardians were mere cyphers and if they were all of the same mind as himself, they ''Would not attend the Board at all. Re proposed that the Clerk lay the circumstances before the member for the Division, Mr. J. T. Brunner, M.P. and ask him to bring the subject before Parliament.—Mr. W. Whitlow agreed with Mr. Aaron. The authority were being treated in a very slighting manner, in this matter, which was more serious than the Local Government Board thought. Mr. Whitlow seconded the motion.—Mr. Weir said he had had a father and a son farming land adjoining this brook, and they had , both lost a lot of cattle, and he ,thought it was high time that something was done.— The Clerk thought little good wouldte done by writing to the member, as the Local Government Board a Month ago said they would write as soon as they had arrived at a deeision.—Mr. Brandreth : All particulars must be given, and Mr. Brunner will be glad to do it.— The motion was carried with only one dissentient (Mr. Mclntyre). ME WATER SUPPLY OF DUTTON, &C.

The Inspector of Nuisances (Mr. Farriniton) presented a report respecting the water supply to dwelling-houses situate in Northwich-road in the townships of Aston and button. He said the total number of houses in the town- ships stated was 14, containing a population of 62, of Whom 38 were adults. The whole of thesa houses were Without a wholesome and sufficient water supply rwithin a reasonable distance. The total amount allowed by the Public Health Act for the provision of a water supply to this number of houses wag £l2l 6s. Bd., which would be aPportioned as follows :—Preston estate, £l7 6s. Bd. ; kston estate, £69 6s. Bd. ; London and North-Western hallway Company, £34 14s. 4d. The Inspector also IT- Ported that 13 dwelling-houses situate in the township of Preston e'th' Hill were without a wholesome and suffi- cient water supply within a reasonable distance. The total amount which could be expended in providing a NvEt!er supply to these houses would be £ll2 13s. 4d., which was apportionable amongst the Ship Canal Com- -11411Y4 North Stafford Canal Company, and three other oWners. In his opinion a water supply could be pro- evyled to the whole of the 27 houses for less than £234 tjargeable and he would be glad to confer with and ad- -4 "18e he various owners or their agents respecting the Provision of the water supply. He suggested that notices 13hould be served upon the several owners to provide hater to their respective properties.—The Board decided act uPort the Inspector's suggestion.
