Sir,—lt may interest your readers to know that at the time the Vicar was preaching his extraordinary sermon in the Parish Church, the Rev. W. D. Walters, of the London Mission, was preaching at the Wesleyan Chapel from the text found in the 49th and 50th verses of the 9th chapter of St. Luke :—" And John -answered and said 'Master we saw one casting out devils in Thy name,' and we forbade him because he follovreth not with us. And Jesus said t unto him Forbid him not; for he that is not against us is tor us."—Yours faithfully,
ARTHUR HIGGINS Al bert-st ~ G reenway-road, Runcorn.
INFRA DIGNIIM.

Sir,—l see my old friend Mr. Dignum has again rushed into the arena. Now, I• was quite willing to allow Mr. Gandy and he to play among the branches of the tree of assumption without interference from myself. My object is to examine the root of that tree and to lay thereto the axe of fact and investigation. But Mr. Dignum is unwise. He should let sleeping dogs lie. But he has been delivered—of what think you—(an argument from facts ?)—No! a " goak." Now, sir, I always regarded my venerable friend as being one from whom it would be as hard to extract a joke as it proverbially is to get one into a Scotehman's head! But does my seraphic friend think jesting comports with the dignity of the subject we have in hand? He and he alone is responsible for its introduction. If motley is to be the only wear, and the cap I make for others fits him, let him wear it, bells and all. But would the covering of Mr. John Dignum with ridicule—and it would not take much to do that—would this many way advance the cause I have at heart—the cause of ascertained truth, v. fabled error? I think it would not. lain amazed, amused, and instructed by this his last escapade, in appearing before a discerning public without a shred of argument to his back and masquerading in the painted vestments of a clown. When we have nothing further to attest, it is worse than useless to be standing and Corybanting in the witness box. As a witness in this case Mr. Dignum is pumped dry. He may stand down.—Yours, kc., - JOHN PEERS. The Haws, Penketh, Feb.lBth, 1891.

div.head: CADISHEAD POST OFFICE.
div.p: CADISHEAD POST OFFICE.

Sir,—ln your recent notes of Cadishead news, refer- ence was made to the removal of the post office' to new premises, and a box being placed near the centre to somewhat satisfy the inhabitants. Now, sir, the public of Cadishead have been treated in this affair by the authorities with something like contempt. Letters have been senti to Mr. Raikes by several of the residents. There was a protest from the Highway Committee; and a petition was sent to Mr. Johnstone, Manchester, signed by most of the business men and other residents, which was simply ignored; also a petition signed by over SOO was' sent to Mr. Raikes protesting against the removal, but nevertheless it has been removed. The residents are being put to great inconvenience in consequence, as a pillar box will not sell stamps, postal orders, or money orders, and people have to run here and there to procure a stamp or take a walk to the premises, which is about as much out of the way as your central office in Warrington is from your business centre; but in this case it is quite uncalled for, as the premises are a shop taken, but not by the postal department. You may ask how was it they at the head office did not look into the matter ? The officials replied by saying they were supposed to know what was best required, without any interference of the public. We have a box put near the Coach and Horses to meet the requirements, and a most unseemly affair it is, both as to position and convenience. Only to-night, I was coming away after posting letters, when I was accosted, with the remark "Oh do you go to the Coach getting your glass on the sly ?" I shall expect the temperance party to take the matter up, for the position is,to say the least,degrading, being within a few yards from a urinal. As things have been arranged by the officials we must submit, or go to the House of Commons demanding an investigation.— Yours &c., Cadishead, Feb. Bth, 1891.
LETTER BOX.

THE VICAR OF RUNCORN AND DISSENTERS. thoroughly agree with your correspondent Mr. Charles Finch's condemnation of the recent animad- versions by the Vicar of Runcorn upon Dissenters. Such attacks are narrow, bigoted, and unspiritual-minded in the extreme. I suppose that by the words "one fold and one shepherd" he would have us understand the Church of England and Christ. I am much inclined to think from what I know of the Church of England that even if all men were united in its fold the shepherd might be Christ, but would be more likely to be no higher a one than the Archbishop of Canterbury. The Vicar also, I suppose, fancies, and would ha ire us fancy that in desecrating the passage by construing it in the spirit in which he reads and would have us read it,he is carrying out the spirit of him who uttered it. I would remind the rev. Canon of the utterance by the same authority, immeasurably broader than his own pitiful declamations against Nonconformists, "Other sheep I have but not of this fold." I would remind him, too, of another utterance—that of one of tbe Christian fathers, who are held by many to have been the fathers also of all ecclesiastical intolerance and persecution that has ever existed, St. Justin :—" He that i virtuous is a

Christian though he be otherwise an atheist." This quotation may be too strong even for Mr. Finch, but I hold it contains the very essence of true Christianity,and that the saying of Christ about his "other sheep" has a closer connection with it than could ever enter into the conception of men of the type of the Vicar of Runcorn. Mr. Finch may not improbably be disposed to quarrel with me for making this statement, assuming him to be a Nonconformist, for, alas ! experience has pr9ved that even Dissenters as a rule, have far from risen to that magnanimity and breadth of view which is true Christianity,and which its founder, unlike his pretended followers, so much exemplified. I say with the poet— For modes of faith let graceless bigots fight: He can't be wrong whose life is in the right. , Let the clergy of the Church of England prove that they can realize this standard of Christianity ; let them make their church worthy of universal confidence and devo- tion, a chairch that has ceased to be a chiefly aristocratic institution where contrary to the Scriptural injunction those that wear a gold ring and have goodly apparel, have the preference over the poor and the humble; let it disdain to be content any longer with being meanly bolstered up in its place of power by the State, then, as Mr. Finch says, we may talk about that universal re- union the rev. canon of Runcorn so ardently desires. But this will never come about while such bigots as he exist to circulate broadcast from the pulpits in which they usurp the places of true men, their [bigoted, pernicious, and revolting nonsense. The conditions I have named are the smallest under which the people at :large could be brought to aim at there-union the rev. Canon desires. But I must say that considering the constitution of human nature, and the corruption and abuse which all history teaches is the inevitable ultimate result of unlimited power, how- ever beneficently and fayourably exercised at first, I have no desire to see that unity of Christendom which is the dream of so many well-Meaning and pious men. Of course the absolute inclusion in one church of every in- habitant is a moral impossibility ; but if the Church of England or any other church once became so powerful as to be able to dominate all other churches the ascend- ant denomination would assuredly soon or late, as Buckle the author of the " History of Civilisation " says, commence the persecution of the others. This would be the -case because of the fact that our institutional religion is a gigantic organised hypocrisy—if that can be called an hypocrisy in which almost everyone is playing a game of sham whichalmost everyone knows to be such—and the veryextent to which this organised hypocrisy has carried out its endless and bewildering ramifications, is but an attestation of the almost universal absence of individual religion. Under such conditions, I say with Buckle, in the very multi- tude of sects lies our safety, and the preservation of our civil and religious liberties. The sects being so numerous, each one takes care that the other does not obtain undue power, and thus through the innumerable theological dissensions and divisions, any renewal of the age of ec- clesiastical persecution is made impossible. What we want is not reunion of churches, but a re- union of hearts and souls, the reunion of human kind- ness and human brotherhood. In the closing up of humanity to form this there will be no space left for the narrow creedalism of fossilized parsons ay, indeed, or—for that matter—for the do-nothing unproductive- ness of useless aristocrats, and the shameful extortion- ateness of grinding capitalists. With these the clergy of the Church of England have always,as Carlyle says, been in alliance to keep mankind in darkness and ignorance. Heaven forbid that there should ever be a reunion under them of all the churches. With the power it would give them' with the desire they would have to prevent thsir church again losing its supremacy, with also all the re- sources of a far advanced civilizatien at their`command, they would in time constitute a much more formidable and terrible despotism than ever it has been in the past, or there has eve* been any example af in history.—Yours faithfully, _ _
ECLECTIC.

div.head: WHAT IS A CHRISTIAN?
div.p: WHAT IS A CHRISTIAN?
"Error is mortal, and cannot live; Truth is immortal, and cannot die.

" The clergy are at present divisible into three sections : an immense body who are ignorant, and speak out; a small portion who know, and keep silent; and a minute minority who know, and speak according to their knowledge." T. H. Huxley.

Sir,—Mr. Dignum says he had no idea that a second letter on this subject would be necossary. Of course he thought he had given me my quietus, which was very modest of him, to be sure. He accuses me of an obvious fallacy regarding Professor Beet's meaning,,and says that I entirely miss the drift of his excellent work. Now I decline to allow that either of these statements is true, but assert on the contrary that Mr. Dignum's letter is nothing less than an evasion. Ile evades and tries to obscure the issue. I don't mean to say that this is his intention, but this is really the effect of his letter. Professor Beet says the gospels are anonymous; that the names commonly attached to them do but embody a very ancient tradition. Now, who is correct, Professor Beet, or Mr. Dignum ? Mr. Dignum instances the case of a work which was issued anonymously, but which, he says, all the world knew to be written by one of the Chambers Brothers. "Thus," he says, "the reputed author was long well-known, though his work was issued without any name attached." Yes ! all the world knew that the work in question was written by one of the Chambers Brothers. But this, surely, is a very different thing from saying that the work was issued with the name of, say, Richard Chambers attached to it, but that th 3 work was anonymous, since the name attached to it did embody a very ancient tradition. If it were issued with the name of Richard Chambers attached to it, and all the world knew that Richard Chambers was the author would anyone dream of saying that it was "anony- mous, since the name attached to it did but embody a very ancient tradition ?" No no, my friend; it won't do. If all the world knows that the gospels were written by Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John why should it be necessary for whole volumes to be written to prove it? What Mr. Beet says on page 99 of his book, that the Ist Epistle of John and the Gospel now bearing his name "are undoubtedly from the same pen," proves nothing, unless it be that the Ist Epi§tle of John is anonymous also. At the best it is only a surmise—or a matter of Opinion.

My friend declines the invitation of Mr. Peers "to range untrammelled o'er the world of extraneous thought," and yet, with a light heart, he takes aerial flight tnto the regions of ancient ecclesiastical history, on something even less substantial than Mrs. Shipton's broomstick. I must confess that lam greatly surprised. Surely no one knows better than Mr. Dignum that ancient Christian literature and the Christian Fathers can be made to prove a.nything. My friend had better not play with edged tools. Now, this subject of the Fathers and early Christian literature is a very large one. Many volumes have been written on it, and in a newspaper correspondence one can hardly so much as touch the fringe of it. There are quite a number of writers—not anonymous ones, bear in mind—but for the present it will perhaps answer the purpose if I refer to one or two of them. Mosheim, the Christian historian of the church, tells us the early Fathers counted it pious to lie and cheat for the good of the church ; and F. H. Preston tells us that " the Christians of the first three centuries were of all men of whom we have any record,the most unprincipled liars and forgers: that Origen, Jerome,Eusebius, Chrysostom,and the early Fattkers of the Church established the science of pious forgery as a justifiable practice under the name of economic."

My friend mentions Irenoeus. Irenceus was the first to allude to the gospels about a century and a half after the time of Christ. Previous to this we have no mention of them, and they were presented to the world upon no other authority than his. A little later on we hear of many gospels and sacred writings being in circulation which were actually read and quoted as the word of God. Upwards of fifty of these Acts and Revelations and Gos- pels were at one time considered the "divine word," and were accepted by the Primitive Christians as of equal authority. At length it became necessary to settle authoritatively whicli books were true and which were false. Several Ecumenical Councils were held for this purpose. The first one was held at Nice which had to decide which of these books were, and which were not, the inspired Word of God. "This was done," says one of the Fathers, " by placing all the books under a com- munion table, and upon the prayers of the Council the inspired books jumped upon the communion table.whilst the false ones remained under." At another, council the manner of choosing was by vote. Now these records are matters, not of opinion—but facts of history which any of your readers can ascertain for themselves. Mosheim records the most astounding things about the early Christians and the early Fathers of the Church. Space forbids my dwelling any further on the subject, and so I come back to my former position. A man can be a Christian without believing in either the Fall or the Redemption. Christ never so much i as mentions them. His religion is a very simple one. It is a religion of humanity: it teaches the fatherhood of God and the brotherhood of man. It insists on no theological tests, or the acceptance of any creeds or dogmas. By this," says Christ, "shall all men know that ye are my dis- ciples, if ye love one another." In the 25th chapter of Mathew, we have an account of the Son of Man coming to judge the earth. Those who pass into life eternal are not the orthodox and the unctuously pious but those who had fed the hungry, clothed the naked, visited the sick and those who were in prison. The rejected ones were not those who had had intellectual troubles about ' the dogmas of the church—not even Atheists or Agnos- tics—but those who had neglected known duties; who had disregarded the cries of the noor and the outcast, the hungry, the naked, and the sick. And yet one of my ministerial friends told me the other day that. unless I believed the story of Jonah .and the whale, I did not believe the Bible, and therefore I did not believe in the Lord Jesus Christ, and so I should everlastingly perish. I believe in the teachings of Christ. I believe that his life and His teachings are the salvation of men. I don't believe the Gospels were written by his disciples. They were preachers not writers. They were ignorant men and could' not write. It was nearly two hundred years after the death of Christ that the oral teachings of the Apostles were collected together and put in much the same shape as we have them now. But the "pious fathers" of the early church interpolated many things
to suit their own purposes, and the miraculous element of the Gospels I ascribe to this cause. Yours truly, JOHN GANDY.

DUKE OF MANCHESTER.

The late William Drogo Montagu, Duke and Earl of Manchester, Viscount Mandeville, and Baron Montague of Bimbolton, in the peerage of Great Britain, was the eldest son of George, sixth Duke, and was born on tho 15th Oct., 1823, and consequently he was in his 67th year at the time of his death, on March 21st, last. He married in July, 1852, Countess Louise Frederick Augusta von .Alten, second daughter of Charles Fran-

, of Hanover, by whom he left two sons and three daughters. He succeeded his father in 1855, was educated at the Military College, Sandhurst, and entered the 11th regiment in 1841% He became a captain in the Grenadier Guards in 1846 and retired from the army in 1850. From 1843 till 1846 he was aide-de-camp to Sir Peregrine Maitland, governor of Cape Co/ony. In 1848 he (then Viscount Mandeville) entered the House of Commons as Conservative member for Bewdley, which he represented till 1852, when he was returned for Huntingdonshire, continuing to sit for that county till he was raised to the peerage in 1853. The late peer was made a knight of the Order of St. Patrick in 1876. He was appointed major in the Hunts Militia in 1852, but retired in 1880, and was lieutenant-colonel of Huntingdon Light Horse Voltmteers. The late Duhe was fond of travelling in the colonies, and it is said that he acquired large tracts of land in Australia. He took an active interest in the prosperity of the Royal Colonial Institute of which he was the head. He was also well known as a Freemason. The `present Dike was formerly in the House of Commons, hav- ing sat for Huntingdonshire from July, 1877, to March, 1880, when he was an unsuccessful candi- date.

"The new Duke of Manchester is" says the Star "about to start on a tour of inspection over his Australian estates. The lane duke had a profound faith in the future of the great Southern Continent, and invested as largely as he could in Australian land, securing some twenty-five thousand acres in Queensland, and ten thousand in West Australia. This will be his first visit to Australia. His father went out there-no less than fiTe times, and always- travelled in the ortho- dox bushman's costume when he paid periodical visits to his estates."

-- WEStEYAN BAND OF FlOPE.—The weekly meeting was held on Monday evening, and conducted by Mr. F. 0. Moston. The programme was of a pleasing character. BAPTIST MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY.—The weekly meeting of the members of the above took place on Wednesday night. There was a good attendance. Mr. Brundritt occupied occupied the chair. The subject of the evening, "The Wesleys and their work," was intro- duced in an admirable speech by Mr. Briggs, who was fol- lowed by Messrs. E. Clarke, Hurstfield, and Robinson. CONGREGATIONAL BAND OF Hope.—A public meeting under the auspices of this society was held in the Congre- gational Schoolroom, on Monday evening, the chair being occupied by Mr. Dutton. The programme included a number of recitations and a trio of dialogues by the members of the band. Songs were given by Misses Moston and Stone, Mr. Joynson, Master Arthur Astley, and an instrumental duet by the Misses Brearley. Mr. Evans, of Thelwall, delivered a suitable address. DEATH OF MISS DEWHIIRST.—MISS May Dewhurst, I youngest daughter of Mr. J. B. Dewhurst, of Oughtring- ton House, and grandchild of Mr. G. C. Dewhurst, J.P., of Beechwood, died after a brief illness, on Friday after- noon at Windsor, where she was being educated. She caught a cold a short time since, which ultimately developed into an acute attack of inflammation of the lungs, and although everything that medical skill could devise was procured, it proved of no avail. The intelli- gence of the young lady's death was not generally known in the village until Sunday, when much sympathy was expressed for the bereaved family. hut POPULAR CONCERTS. —The fifth of the series of popular concerts took place in the Bridgewater rooms, which were again well filled, on Saturday evening. Mr. Richard Dutton occupied the chair, and Mr. Jas. Dodds gave the customary "ten minutes address." The pro- gramme, which was fully up to the standard of its pre- decessors, was opened by a piano solo by Miss M.Thorpe. Songs were subsequently given by Mr. Peters, Miss Moston, Miss Warburton, Miss Brown, Mr. Thomason, Mrs. Dutton, and Mr. Smith. Mr. and Mrs. Dutton and Mr. and Miss Warburton also contributed vocal duets, the Warburtoris also giving an instrumental selection. Mr. Dutton, Mr. Hall, and Mrs. Dodds each gave a read- ing; and a couple of glees,by Mr. Warburton and party, completed a well-arranged programme. ALLEGED THEME. —At the Lymm Police Court, on Saturday, before Mr. Charles Lister and Dr. Brabazon, a youth named Wm. Goulden, of Bollington. was charged with stealing, on or about the 23rd January, a measur- ing tape, value 10s., the property of Robert Brigham, of High Legh. Jelin Harrison, also of Bollington, was charged with receiving the same knowing it to have been stolen. On tho 23rd ult. Brigham was at work at High Legh, and forgot his measuring tape. Goulden subsequently gained possession of it, and Harrison ' pledged it at Altrineham for Is. 6d. Information was given to the police, and the defendants were arrested by P.C.'s Arthern and Ennion, of the Lymm Police force. As there was some doubt as to whether Goulden took the tape knowing it to be Brigham's, or merely found it, the defendants were discharged.

div.head: LIBERAL MEETING AT LYMM.
div.p: LIBERAL MEETING AT LYMM.

The annual public meeting of the Lymm Liberal Club was held in the Congregational Schoolroom, Lymm, on Tuesday night, when the president of the club, Mr. Richard Dutton, occupied the chair. With him on the platform were Mr. J. S. Leadam,. Liberal candidate for the division; Mr. James Tomkinson, J.P., of Tarporley.,Liberal candidate for the Edisbury Division; Mrs. Tomkinson,. the Rev. Wm. Evans, and Messrs. James Dodds, G. L. Welford, John Thompson, Geo. Manning, and J. Swanwick. There was a large attendance in the body of the hall. -The Chairman said the Liberal party at Lymm were ready for the great fight whenever it came, and they wouid make a better fight than ever they had done before.— The Rev. William Evans moved a resolution giving a cordial welcome to Mr. Leadam• and to Mr. and Mrs. Tomkinson, recording increased affection for and confidence in Mr. Gladstone and in the great principle of Home Rule for Ireland with which his political life was identified, and looking for- ward to the settlement of the Irish question by giving to the Irish people free control of all purely Irish affairs, and therefore to promote legislation for the many English, Scotch, and Welsh griev- ances which were crying out for remedy.—The Rev. Charles Clay seconded the resolution.—Mrs. Tomkinson, in rising to support the resolution, met with a very cordial reception. She referred to the last part of the resolution, remarking that it was instinct With the feeling that, there waa good time coming all over England, anct judging by that crowded meeting, it was apparent that there was a good time coming for the Liberals of Lym-m. The resolution was put to the meeting and carried enthusiastically. Mr. Leadam said their Conserva- tive friends had had a regular campaign of jollifica- tion, and they gave the contest the appearance of a contest between stomach and brains. Mr. Tomkin- son and other speakers followed, and the usual votes. ot confidence and thanks terminated the proceed— ings. A musical programme was efficidntly gone through at intervals during the meeting.

div.head: PENKETH.
div.p: PENKETH.
THE HISTORY OF PENNY POSTAGE.

On Wednesday evening in connetAion with the Mutual Improvement Association, Mr. Alfred Duna- bin read a paper on the above subject. The chair as occupied by Mr. T. Gandy. In. a most able and interesting manner Mr. Dunahin gave an account of our postal system from the time of Oliver Crom- welrto the present century. He gave a detailed description of the difficulties which letter writers of past times experienced, and then spoke of the system formulated by Mr. Rowland Hill whereby letters posted to any part of the United Kingdom were conveyed for one penny. At the conclusion Messrs. T. Gandy, Snoddy. White, and Peers spoke of the pleasure they had experienced in hearing the paper. CHAPEL EXTENSION SCHMID. _

On Thursday eve-nin-g-a—l-a-r-g-e-' and-i-m-p-o-rtant meet- ing of the congregation worshipping , in the Wesleyan Chapel was held in No. 1 vestry. After a short address by the Rev. Mr. Waterworth, a scheme for enlarging and beautifying the chapel was explained by Mr. R. Cook and Mr. R. Garnett. When the proposed alterations are carried out a considerable number of new sittings will be added to the chapel. The approximate cost is estimated from .1850 to to £1,150. Coffee and sandwiches were handed round at 8.15 p.m. and afterwards a sun- scription list was opened and promises were given amounting to £789 10s. 6d. A building committee has been appointed. Mr. D. Garnett was unanimously elected treasurer and Mr. K Davies secretary. SUNDAY SCHOOL TREAT AT GREAT SANKEY.

_ On Monday and Tuesday evenings the annual treat in connection with St. Mary's Church Sunday Schools, Sankey and Penketh, was held in the Sun- day School, Greet Sankey. On Monday afternoon the junior scholars were provided with tea com- mencing at 4 p.m. The tables were presided over by the teachers, and the children did full justice to the good things provided. After tea games of various kinds were indulged in and greatly enjoyed, and before the children left, each scholar was pre- sented with a gift of some kind provided by several ladies in connection with the congregation. On Tuesday evening the senior scholars had their treat. ,Tea was commenced at G o'clock,and as on the pre- vious evening the wants of the scholars were looked after by the teachers. After tea an entertidnment provided by the teachers and other friends was gone through. Much amusement was caused by two sketches in character which were contributed by Mr. Robinson. At the conclusion of the programme prizes were presented to all the scholars, and a most pleasant evening was shortly afterwards brought to a termination. ,
Reid's biscuit fa.ctnrv, in Glasgow, was destroyed by fire on Saturday morning. The damage is estimated at £20,000.

div.head: MR. GLADSTONE ON BUM LIBRARIES.
div.p: MR. GLADSTONE ON BUM LIBRARIES.

Mr. Gladstone, on Thursday afternoon, opened the Free Public Library in St. Martin's-in-the-Fields,. West- minister. There was a large gathering of spectators. The right hon. gentleman, after signing the visitors' book was presented with a silver key, with which he unlocked the reference library. In declaring it open, he referred to the progress which had been made in institutions of this kind since the passing of the Libraries Act in 1864. It was a matter of great satisfaction that in recent years the condition of the working-man had been greatly im- proved by the shorting of the hours of labour, and such institutions as these would , enable him to employ his leisure hours to the greatest advantage of himself and

div.head: DARING JEWELLERY ROBBERY AT NORTON PRIORY..
div.p: DARING JEWELLERY ROBBERY AT NORTON PRIORY..

Between seven and nine o'Clock,. on Thursday night, a daring robbery took place atNorton Priory, the residence of Sir Richard Brooke, Bart., and, from the elaborate preparations made, the robbery was effected by expert and experienced thieves.. The gates approaching the hall and the lawn were wired, and the 'thieves had effected an entrance to Lady Brooke's dressing-room by placing a ladder against the wind Ow. The only article stolen was a dressing case containing four gold lockets, threeset with pearls and one with diamonds ; two gold brace- lets, set with pearls, and a large silver cross and a silver necklet. The dressing case was found lying on the lawn, smashed and its contents gone. The county police, have the matter in hand.
RAILWAY ACCIDENT AT ST. HELENS.
AN INSURANCE AGENT KILLED-.

Mr. William Crick, insurance agent for the Royal London Friendly Society, residing at Reeleston Villa,. Thatto Heath, was killed at St. Helens rail- way station, on Wednesday night. About nine o'clock Foreman-porter James Wilding spoke to de- ceased on the platform, and he then appeared to be waiting for the 9.18 train for Thatto Heath. Nothing was afterwards seen of him until the arrival of the Widnes train, due at 10.33. When the train was draw- ing up the engine driver noticed the body of a man lying across the rail, and attempted to stop, but was un- able to do so before the wheels had passed oventhe body. It was then found that the body was that of Mr. Crick, and the lower part of the body was dreadfully Muti- lated. How deceased came into the position:in which he was found is a mystery. It is said that he was very short-sighted, and one theory is that he was cros- sing to the wall on the back side. of the station, and that, miscalculating the edge of the platform, fell across the rail, and, was. stunned. Deceased was thirty-one years of age, and had several children, the youngest being only a, few weeks old. He had been in the service of the Royal London Friendly Society about ten years, and was generally respected by his fellow-collectors and officials. Upon him there was found a current number of" Answers," with its insur- ance of £l,OOO, and a current _number of "Tit-bits," with its insurance of £lOO. If the unfortunate man fell on the line, it is most singular that he was not discovered as there were both porters and several passengers on the platform near the place. The facts have been commu- nicated to Mr. Brighouse, the coroner, and an inquest will be held.

div.head: SALVATION ARMY AT EARLES-
div.p: THE SALVATION ARMY AT EARLES-
TOWN.

The progress of the Salvation Army it: Earlestown is most extraordinary,and people express unbounded surprise that its influence in so short a period should have become so widespread. commencing in a very insignificant manner,. it has gradually crept along, gathering in a convert here and there, and always, be it understood;,of the worst class, until at the present time it numbers 100 members, with 60 standing " solAiers." Every night in the week, in all sorts of weather,, the- army turns out, and shows the people .by its increasing strength, that it loses nothing in influence, in energy and in perseverance. The want of accommodation however for a meeting room, has for some time been much felt, and an agitation is on foot for the erection of barracks. Mr. Thomas Molyneux.,-. who is always to the front in philanthropic matters,, and another prominent townsman,have kindly undertaken to assist the members in their endeavours to obtain a site for the erection of the barracks, and negotiations are now in progress with Mr. W. J. Legh, with that object in view. On the other hand the members of the army are working with might and main to raise £5O tawards the building, as when that , amount has been got together, the remainder of the cost will be defrayed by the Building Department of the Army at headquarters, who will hold a mortgage over the building to be repaid by the local corps. Up to the present over £4O has been got together, and the members are hopeful that the remainder will be subscribed very shortly. To assist in this object a public tea meeting was held in the Co-operative Hall, on Monday night, when about 350 were present, a good number coming from St. Helens. The tea was excel- lently served, all the provisions being contributed by the tradesmen of Earlestown, and the tables were pre- sided over by lady members of the corps. After tea the members had a march out headed by the band of the St. Helens corps, and a short meeting was held in the market place. A return was afterwards made to the hall, which was cempletely packed with people scores being unable to gain admission. The usual Salvation Army meeting was held, led by Captain Cloud, Lieut. Malltry, Lieut. Skinner, (St. Helens), Ensigns Turner, and Bartlett, (Liverpool). The meeting throughout was most enthusiastic. Several young men belonging to Earlestown are wearingthe red jersey having declared their faith in God. Captain Cloud in the course of a few remarks said they wanted in Earlestown a room as big as that they were in. They wanted to raise £5O, so that they could erect a building for the local corps, and they had been making special efforts to do so. .With the proceeds from the tea he thought they should have raised something like £4O. Headquarters had given them until the end of March to raise the sum, when the property department in London would proceed with the erection of a building, and when completed and opened, the local corps would have to give another £5O, and the building would be mortgaged. When the building was erected and qleared, it would be the property ot Earles- town, and wit of a committee, or Trust in Chancery. A collection was then made, and realised 10s. 2d. Staff captain and Mrs. Hoggard of Liverpool arrived at this point, and after a few remarks, Captain Hoggard, com- missioned John Bassett (a reformed drunkard) as a ser- geant over the junior branch of the Army in Earlestown. S. Bothwell was commissioned as Sergeant Major of the Earlestown Corps. Captain Hoggard said that Bothwell had been accepted as a candidate, and would leave very shortly for the Training Home.
THE LATE BISHOP OF WINCHESTER. i

Dr. Harold Browne, who during last year resigned' the Bishopric of Winchester, had filled the office of a bishop since 1864. In that ' yearhe was consecrated bishop of Ely, bnt, after the death of Dr. Wilberforce, he was, in 1873, translated to the see of Winchester, and appointed Prelate of the Order of the Garter. He was the young- est son of Colonel Robert Browne, of Morton House, born in 1811. Educated at Emmanuel College, Cambridge, he graduated as wrangler in 1832, obtained the Crosse Theological Scolarship in 1833, the first Hebrew scholarship in 1834, and the Norrisian Prize for a theological essay in 1E35. He became fellow and tutor of his college; incumbent of St. James's and of St. Sidwell's,Exeter, in 1841 ; was vice-Principal and Professor of Hebrew at St. David's College, Lampeter, from 1843 to 1849, when he was appointed Vicar of Kenwyn, Cornwall, and Prebendary of Exeter. The vicarage of Ken- wyn he resigned for that of Heavitree, Devon- shire, in 1857. In 1854 he was elected Norrisian Professor of Divinity in the University of Cam- bridge, and, in 1857 Canon Residentiary of Exeter Cathedral, when he resigned the living of Heavi- tree. Dr. Browne has taken a warm interest in the "Old Catholic" movement in Germany, and at- tended the Congress of "Old Catholics" held at Cologne in September, 1872. He published in 1850- 53 an "Exposition of the Thirty-nine articles "in two volumes, since reprinted in one volume an re- edited for the used the American Church by Bishop William, of Middletown, Connecticut ; two volumes of sermons preached before the University of Cam- bridge; and a volume on. the "Pentateuch and Elohistic Psalms; in reply to Dr. Colenso." He is also the author of articles in‘ "Aids to Faith," in "Smith's Dictionary of the Bible," and in the "Speaker's Commentary," and of various sermons, pamphlets, and charges. Oh the 16th of July last Dr. and Mrs. Browne celebrated their golden wed- ding, and on that occasion there was a presentation of an address and a sum of upwards of £7OO for diocesian objects. The Queen also sent a telegram of congratulation.
THE LANCASHIRE, DERBYSHIRE AND EAST COAST RATI#WAY.

During the week a deputation representing the Warrington Corporation have had an interview in London with the promoters of the propoSed ne w Lancashire, Derbyshire and East Coast railway,with the tesult that the promoters have agreed to the proposals of the Corporation as to the width of the bridges to be constructea. over Wilderspool-road. The promoters have also undertaken not to make any level crossings on Wilderspobl-road. We under- stand that a meeting is to be held shortly in War- rington, with a view to ascertaining the opinions of the ratepayers as to the new railway.. As we have before mentioned, the new station for Warrington will be built on the football ffeld,. and it is,we understand, intended to carry the line of rails to Liverpool, the Mersey at Warrington being crossed on a bridge to the south of .the present iron rail- way bridge.

div.head: JACK-THE-RIPPER AGAIN.
div.p: JACK-THE-RIPPER AGAIN.
ANOTHER SHOCKING MURDER. LywELTE- CHAPEL,

Shortly after two o'clock yesterdaymorningi.a woman was found in Chamber-street,. Whitechapel,. with her throat horribly cut and other injuries: She was quite dead. The body was first found by the poliaeman osi the beat, who immediately raised an alarm: Assistance arrived, and the body was removed, to the mortuary. Mere is little doubt that the victim belonged to the un- fortunate class. Detectives are inquiring at Hotels, and lodging-houses in search of a clue to the murderer. The Press Association says that the murder is evidently an- other of the series of crimes asseciated.with.East London although in this case the revoltingleatures which have characterized the former atrocious murders are happily a.bseat.-- LATEST DETAILSI

It appears that shortly after two o'clock- yesterday morning at fifteen minutes past the hour,as nearly aacan be ascertained,Constable 240 H,while passing through. an archway of the Great Eastern Railway,, which leads from Swallow-gardens to Orman-street, two•thorough- fares running parallel with the Whitechapel-road, but lying more towards the river, observed a woman ex- tended on her back in the centre of the 'thoroughfare. He had passed the spot fifteen minutes previously, arid there was no one there. On turning his, lamp on the prostrate figure he was horrified to find that the woman lay in a pool of blood; which was flowing from a terrible wound in the throat,. ex.tending literally from ear to ear. He immediately sounded his whistle for assistance, and within a few minutes he was joined by Constable 327:H; :whoseheat is adjoin- The Woman gave no sign of life;.but the body was quite warm, and the constable felt that the pulse was beating faintly. A messenger was despatched to the residence of Dr. Phillip, surgeon to that division,, who resides near at hand.

In the meantime, the police allowedthe body to remain undisturbed, in accordance with. instructions issued dur- ing the panic at the East-end nearly two years ago, and took careful note of the surroundings witba.view to trac- ing any possible clue. The deceased woman. was about 27. She lay in the roadway, her feet being- towards the footpath, and crossed one over the other. One arm was bent over her breast, and the other- lay extended by her side. A black crape hat lay beside her hand, and several pieces of crape or black lace were• found in her dress pocket. The Scotland Yard officials, including Detective-in- spectors Swanson and Moore, oanferred with the local Police at Leman-st. at ten o'clock for the p.urpose of ar- riving at a tangible clue: It was stated that the de- ceased had been identified as an unfortunate known as •• Carroty Nell," and that a man has been arrested on suspicion, and detlined pending inquiries.. The Thames police have visited various cattle ships ly- ing in the port of London, and ascertained that no per- son has boarded the vessel since thefinding of the body. On the arrival of Dr. Phillips he pronounced the woman not quite dead, but she expired before she could be placed on a stretcher for- removal. The body was conveyed to Whitechapel mortuary, to await an in- quest.

- Intelligence of the murder having been telegraphed to the adjacent police stations, Supt. Arnold, Inspector Reed, and several detectives were soon on the scene, in- vestigating the affair.. The archway in which the body was found is at the end of Orman-st.' and is dimly lighted. After nightfall it is frequented by women of the unfortunate class. One side of the arch is boarded off, and used as a builder's store. The deceased was seen in Leman-st. early in the evening. Inpector Swanson has carge of further in- vestigation. Deceased is described as 25 years old, sft in height, eyes and hair brown, complexion pale. Shell was wearing a black dress, rather worn, and a dirty black crape hat. IMPORTANT DISCOVERY.

One of the most extraordinary discoveries, which sug- gests a totally new clue, was the finding of a woman's hat on the body besides the crape hat which she had evidently been wearing. This fact has caused no little surprise to the police, for it goes to support the sugges- tion that the crime might be perpetrated by a woman,or, at any rate, by a man in female attire. This important information was at once telegraphed to the headquarters at Scotland-yard. Several persons have been found Who speak to having seen the woman near the site of the murder a few minutes before it happened; and the victim has been definitely identified as Mrs. Francis, 18, Thrawl-st., Spitalfields. . _

-The inquest on the deceased will tako place at half- past four this (Saturday) afternoon. This makes the ninth in the horrible series of White- chapel murders. Five of the women were slain within a period of eight weeks.
A_AIILITARY FUNERAL.

The remains of Sergeant Wm. Shaw, .of the 2nd V.B. South Lancashire Regiment, who died suddenly on Wed- nesday week were interred with military honours in the St. Helens Cemetery on Saturday afternoon. About 200 members of the corps, including the cyclists' section, preceded the hearse and mourning coaches, and were headed by the band of the regiment, under bandmaster Hall. A large number of floral tributes were received from friends of the deceased gentleman. The Rev. J. Brown conducted the funeral service, and Captain David Gamble, jun., was in command of the firing party. FALL FROM A HOUSE TOP—MIRACULOUS ESCAPH, On Thursday evening a bricklayer's labourer. named John Thornton, living in Gas-st., Newton, fell from the roof of a house and had a most mar- vellous escape from injury. He was engaged in cleaning the spouts of some houses in Rathbone-st., and at the time was some little way up the roof of one, when he slipped and fell over into the back yard of the house. He alighted on his feet, and after a short rest, resumed his work. Strange to say he received no injury, although he fell a distance I of about 20 feet.

LATEST NEWS. A GAMEKEEPER SflOT. A garraekeeper was shot dead on Thursday at Glenga- riff, co. Cork. He is supposed to have been shot by poachers.

CHARGE OF FRATRICIDE. At Leeds, yesterday, Alfred Mann, sweep, was re- manded on the charge of causing his brother'3, death during a quarrel at Holbeck. MESSRS. DILLON AND O'BRIEN. The Press Association Holyhead correspondent tele- graphs that Messrs. Dillon and O'Brien passed through there yesterday afternoon on their way (under arrest) th Ireland. toth appeared in good spirits. MURDER WITH A CRICKET BAT. Samuel Mason, a shopkeeper, of Godmanchester, Huntingdonshire murdered his wife yesterday, by beat- ing her about ttrehead with a cricket bat in a back room. He is under arrest and said to be of unsound mind. FATAL FIRE ON SHIPBOARD. A fire broke out early yesterday morning at Newport,, Monmouthshire, on board the steamer Calliope. The ship was much dkroaged, and two of the crew perished, it is supposed from suffocation, as they were found dead in the forecastle.

THE BURSTING OF A CANAL. , r5O LIVES LOST. NEW YORK, VarDa.v.—Advices received here from Buenos Ayres give details of the bursting of a canal at Cordova on December 20 last, and of fearful loss of life caused by that catastrophe. Half of the city was inun- dated and houses were washed away by the score. More than 150 persons. perished. The damage was esti- mated at three million dollars.

div.head: YESTERDAYS PARLIAMENT.
div.p: YESTERDAYS PARLIAMENT.
HOUSE OF LORDS.

Theilouse metat a quarter-past four. In reply to Lord Herschell as to the interests and rights of British companies in Africa, Lord SALISBURY said there was some confusion between sovereign and political rights and private rights in a particular terri- tory—private rights, fully acquired by individuals or a company would be unaffected by any arrangement which Government might make with :Portugal. The Hbuss adjourned at live o'clock. HOUSE OF COMMONS.
. - The Speaker took the charrat seven minutes past three, o'clock.
The Lancashire, Derbyshire, and East Coast Railway Bill was read a second time:.

QUESTIONS.-Mr. MATTrows replying to Mr. Moreton said he had no information respecting playing baccarat at Tanby Court, Doncaster, beyond newspaper paragraphs. It was not an offence against the gaming laws to play baccarat h private houses.. Mr. BALFOUR answering Mr. Healy said the Irish Relief Fund was private benevolence:. Neither he nor Lord Zetland were pre- cluded from using the volantary subscriptions of officials.

TRADE PRIMES.—On going-into. committee of supply Mr. BUXTON moved against sub-contracting in Govern- ment contracts and in favourof the payment of trade prices. In Mt. Buxton's opinion the present system of contracts was' injurious to the country at large.—Mr. FENWICE seconded the motion,, and said illpaid labour invariably resulted in scamped'and unsatisfactory work. Mr. PLuNitEr, on behalf of the 6overnment, suggested the re-wording of the motion to give power to deal with the evils of "sweating," and make every effort to secure the payment of current rates. After a few words from Mr. Playfair9 Mr. Buxton readily accepted Mr. Plunket's resolution. Mr.Buxton's resolution was then negatived, and Mr. Plunket's resolution agreed to. The House was counted out at half-past seven.

LANCASHIRE WATCH COMPANY.

The annual general meeting of the shareholders of the Lancashire Watch enrapany, Limked, was held in the Watch Factory, Prescot, last evening week. Mr; S. H. Hartley,,chairman of the board of directors, presided, and there was a good attendance. The directors, in their report, said there was a net balanced profit of £4,399 18s. lid. (including £1,291! ss. 91d from last year) to be dealt with at the end of the secondiyear's working,, and they recommended a divi-- dend cf 6 per cent. on the ordinary shares of the corn, pany,, the payment of the-dividend on the 8 per cent. preference shares issued during the year, and interest at the rate of 5 per cont, on, sums received in advance of calls, on ordinary shares. These payments would, absorb the sum of £24065 6s. 3d., and leave a balance of £2,334 12s. Bd. In the early pert of last year the whole of the machinery acquired from the vendors was. removed from several workshops, overhauled, renovated, and re-fixed in the new factory, and notwithstanding , thefact that that machinery was to-day in better work.- ing conditioa than it was then, the directors stronoy urged the recognition of the principle of depreciation,aud they therefore suggested that the sum of £5OO be written off machinery account. They further felt justified, in suggesting that a like sum of £5OO should be deducted from goodwill and trade-marks account, and that there be carried forward a, balance of £1,334 12s. 8d.,. which ' would be sufficient to secure the 6 per cent. dividend , on three times the value of preference shares issued last year, even if they were all immediately allotted. The Chairman moved the adoption of the report and balance sheet, and the payment of the dividend recom- mended.—The Rev. B. A. W. Norrie seconded,, and the resolution was adopted.—Mr. A. Menzies, the retiring director, was unanimously re-appointed on, the proposi- tion of Mr. H. Makin, seconded by Mr.. A.. H. Hale.— Messrs. Bander, Spencer, and Co., Liverpool, were re- elected auditors.—Mr. F. Smith considered that the directors had served them very, well and satisfactory duringthe past year, and he moved that thesum of £2OO ; be voted to them.—The Rev. B. A. W. Norrie seconded, arid the motion was agreed to.—The Chairman paid a high compliment to the managing director, Mr. T. P. Hewitt, for the services he had rendered during the year. —Mr. Hewitt responded, and referred to, the assistance be had received from the leading bands in the works..—. On the motion of the Rev. Mr. Norrie, seconded by Mr. Hale, and supported by Mr. Smith, a vote of thanks was tendered to the chairman, and the proceedings termin- ated.

div.head: EARLESTOWN CHORAL CLASS.
div.p: EARLESTOWN CHORAL CLASS.

A social evening in connection with this this class took place in the Co-operative Hall, Earlestown on Tuesday evening, when _about 40 members were ptesent. Being Shrove Tuesday, pancakes were servdd,up, and much amusement was caused during the " tossing " operations. A light meal was also provided, and the remainder of the evening was spent in dancing and games. Mrs. Latimer kindly provided the music.

MANCHESTER TRADE, FRIDAY.—The best one can say of the market is that it is no worse. Some people report rather more inquiry, but nobody gets any more business. Cotton seems to be in rather better form ; the estimate has been_ raised from 6,000 to 7,000 bales. Yarns are no be ter ill price. Some sellers say they find a little more inquiry, and seem more hopeful, but they are in a small minority, and the general report puts things mueh as they were yesterday. Good Cheshire makes of printers and finishing cloths are steady and fairly well engaged. Burnley qualities are no better, and business is difficult to get. The home houses are keeping up assortments. TWENTY PERSONS DEVOURED BY WOLVFS. The " Wiener Allegemeine Zeitung " publishes intelli- gence front Szoluck, Hungary, giving an account of the depredations of a pack of wolves on the estate of Baron Woodianer, at Szandanist. The animals attacked and killed over twenty peasants,the unfortunate people being devoured with the exception of the feet and boots. A hunting party has been organised, and will set out to extermimate the wolves.
